The feeding bag is labeled with the date and time it was hung
The assistive personnel lowered the head of the bed flat for linen change without pausing the feeding
The tube's external length matches the documented mark

questions.stem: A client's parenteral nutrition (PN) bag is empty, and the pharmacy says the new bag will not be ready for 2 hours. What should the nurse do?
questions.rationale: Abruptly stopping PN can cause rebound hypoglycemia because of high circulating insulin. D10W provides a similar dextrose concentration. Rates are never increased to catch up.

options.text: Hang 0.9% sodium chloride at the same rate
Hang 10% dextrose in water at the PN rate until the new bag arrives
Stop the infusion and flush the line
Double the rate of the new bag when it arrives

questions.stem: A severely malnourished client started enteral nutrition 2 days ago. Which lab result is most important for the nurse to report?
questions.rationale: Refeeding syndrome causes intracellular shifts of phosphorus, potassium, and magnesium when nutrition resumes. Severe hypophosphatemia can cause heart failure, respiratory failure, and dysrhythmias. Nutrition is advanced slowly with electrolyte monitoring.

options.text: Phosphorus 1.4 mg/dL
Sodium 138 mEq/L
Albumin 2.8 g/dL
Glucose 128 mg/dL

questions.stem: A client with cirrhosis and hepatic encephalopathy is receiving lactulose. Which finding indicates the medication is effective?
questions.rationale: Lactulose traps ammonia in the colon and removes it through stool. The goal is typically 2–3 soft stools daily with improved cognition. Worsening asterixis and a rising ammonia indicate progression.

options.text: One hard stool every 3 days
Two to three soft stools per day and improved mental status
Increased asterixis
Serum ammonia rising from 80 to 110 mcg/dL

questions.stem: A client with cirrhosis is vomiting large amounts of bright red blood. Which medication does the nurse anticipate?
questions.rationale: Octreotide reduces splanchnic blood flow and portal pressure during acute variceal bleeding. Antibiotic prophylaxis and urgent endoscopy with band ligation follow. Nonselective beta blockers are used for long-term prevention, not active bleeding.

options.text: Octreotide IV infusion
Oral propranolol
Ibuprofen
Oral lactulose

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing a client for abdominal paracentesis. Which action is most important before the procedure?
questions.rationale: Emptying the bladder reduces the risk of puncturing it. The client sits upright or in high-Fowler's position. After the procedure, the nurse monitors for hypotension caused by fluid shifts.

options.text: Have the client void
Place the client in Trendelenburg position
Insert a nasogastric tube
Keep the client NPO for 12 hours

questions.stem: Which findings does the nurse expect in a client with acute pancreatitis? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Pancreatitis causes epigastric pain radiating to the back and an elevated lipase. Cullen's (periumbilical) and Grey Turner's (flank) signs indicate retroperitoneal hemorrhage. Hypocalcemia results from fat saponification. Pain is often relieved by sitting up and leaning forward, not by lying flat.

options.text: Severe epigastric pain radiating to the back
Elevated serum lipase
Bluish discoloration around the umbilicus
Bluish discoloration of the flanks
Serum calcium 7.6 mg/dL
Pain relieved by lying flat

questions.stem: Which finding supports a diagnosis of acute cholecystitis?
questions.rationale: Gallbladder inflammation causes RUQ pain after fatty meals, often radiating to the right shoulder. Murphy's sign is inspiratory arrest during RUQ palpation. McBurney's point pain suggests appendicitis.

options.text: Pain in the right lower quadrant at McBurney's point
Right upper quadrant pain after a fatty meal with a positive Murphy's sign
Left lower quadrant pain relieved by bowel movements
Epigastric pain relieved by eating

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client diagnosed with hepatitis A. Which client statement indicates a need for further teaching?
questions.rationale: Hepatitis A spreads by the fecal-oral route. Household contacts should not share utensils, and they may need post-exposure vaccination or immune globulin.

options.text: "I'll wash my hands well after using the bathroom."
"I won't prepare food for others while I'm contagious."
"It's fine for my family to share my utensils and cups."
"My family members may need a vaccine or immune globulin."

questions.stem: For each characteristic, indicate whether it is more typical of Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis.
questions.rationale: Crohn's can affect any part of the GI tract with transmural, patchy inflammation that leads to fistulas and strictures. Ulcerative colitis is limited to the colon mucosa, starts in the rectum, spreads continuously, and causes bloody diarrhea. Removing the colon cures UC.
questions.answer_summary: Crohn's: skip lesions, fistulas, transmural inflammation. UC: continuous from rectum, bloody diarrhea, curable by colectomy.

rows.text: "Skip lesions" with areas of normal bowel between
Continuous inflammation beginning in the rectum
Inflammation through all layers of the bowel wall

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a client 12 hours after creation of an ileostomy. Which finding requires immediate action?
questions.rationale: A dusky, purple, or black stoma indicates compromised blood supply and necrosis, which requires immediate surgical evaluation. A pink, moist, slightly edematous stoma with liquid output is expected.

options.text: Stoma is pink and moist
Small amount of liquid output in the pouch
Stoma is dark purple to black
Mild edema of the stoma

questions.stem: A client is being treated at home for an acute episode of uncomplicated diverticulitis. Which diet does the nurse anticipate during the acute phase?
questions.rationale: Bowel rest with clear liquids, then low-fiber foods, reduces inflammation during the acute phase. Once recovered, a high-fiber diet helps prevent recurrence. Current evidence does not require avoiding nuts and seeds long term.

options.text: High-fiber diet with bran
Clear liquids, advancing to low-fiber foods as symptoms improve
High-fat diet
Regular diet with nuts and seeds

questions.stem: A client is diagnosed with Clostridioides difficile infection. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: C. difficile spores are not killed by alcohol-based rubs, so soap and water and sporicidal cleaning are required. Antidiarrheals can trap toxins and increase the risk of toxic megacolon.

options.text: Place the client on contact precautions
Wear a gown and gloves when entering the room
Wash hands with soap and water after care
Clean the room with a sporicidal (bleach-based) disinfectant
Use alcohol-based hand rub as the only hand hygiene
Administer an antidiarrheal to stop the diarrhea

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client with gastroesophageal reflux disease. Which client statement indicates a need for further teaching?
questions.rationale: Lying down within 2–3 hours after eating promotes reflux. Head-of-bed elevation, small meals, and avoiding trigger foods reduce symptoms.

options.text: "I'll raise the head of my bed on 6-inch blocks."
"I'll lie down for a nap right after lunch."
"I'll eat smaller meals."
"I'll limit caffeine, alcohol, and chocolate."

questions.stem: A client reports dizziness, sweating, and cramping 20 minutes after meals following a partial gastrectomy. Which instruction should the nurse provide?
questions.rationale: Dumping syndrome results from rapid emptying of hypertonic food into the small intestine. Small meals, limited simple sugars, fluids between rather than with meals, and lying down after eating slow gastric emptying.

options.text: "Drink plenty of fluids with each meal."
"Eat small, high-protein, low-carbohydrate meals and lie down briefly after eating."
"Eat three large meals high in simple sugars."
"Sit upright and walk right after meals."

questions.stem: After a percutaneous liver biopsy, how should the nurse position the client?
questions.rationale: Lying on the right side applies pressure to the puncture site and reduces the risk of bleeding. The nurse monitors vital signs frequently for hemorrhage.

options.text: On the left side
On the right side with a pillow under the costal margin
Prone
High-Fowler's

questions.stem: Highlight (circle) the findings that require immediate follow-up.
questions.rationale: Tachycardia, hypotension, poor peripheral perfusion, and a low hemoglobin indicate significant blood loss and shock. Normal platelets and INR mean coagulopathy is not contributing, and a soft abdomen argues against perforation.
questions.answer_summary: HR 122; BP 88/52; cool, clammy skin; capillary refill 4 seconds; hemoglobin 7.2
questions.correct_text: HR 122; BP 88/52; cool, clammy skin; capillary refill 4 seconds; hemoglobin 7.2

questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it primarily reflects the body's compensatory response to blood loss or is a direct result of upper GI bleeding.
questions.rationale: Sympathetic activation increases heart rate, constricts peripheral vessels, and increases respirations to maintain oxygen delivery. Blood partially digested by gastric acid appears as coffee grounds or melena, and absorption of digested blood proteins raises BUN.
questions.answer_summary: Compensatory: tachycardia, cool clammy skin, tachypnea. Direct result: melena, coffee-ground emesis, elevated BUN with normal creatinine.

rows.text: Elevated BUN with a normal creatinine

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.rationale: Chronic high-dose ibuprofen damages the gastric mucosa and causes ulcers. Melena and coffee-ground emesis indicate an upper GI source, and hemodynamic instability with a low hemoglobin reflects hypovolemic shock. There is no history of liver disease or fever.
questions.answer_summary: 1: hypovolemic shock; 2: a bleeding peptic ulcer associated with NSAID use
questions.template: The client is most likely experiencing ___1___ caused by ___2___.

options: a bleeding peptic ulcer associated with NSAID use
blanks.correct: a bleeding peptic ulcer associated with NSAID use

questions.stem: Which interventions does the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Management includes large-bore access, fluid resuscitation, transfusion (commonly when hemoglobin is below 7–8 g/dL or the client is unstable), IV PPI to stabilize clots, and endoscopy to find and treat the bleeding. The client stays NPO for the procedure. NSAIDs caused the bleeding and are stopped.
questions.answer_summary: A, B, C, D, E, F

options.text: Insert two large-bore IV catheters
Infuse isotonic crystalloid solution
Type and crossmatch for packed red blood cells
Administer an IV proton pump inhibitor
Prepare the client for upper endoscopy
Keep the client NPO
Administer ibuprofen for the epigastric pain

questions.stem: Which action should the nurse take first?
questions.rationale: Restoring circulating volume is the priority in hypovolemic shock. The airway is currently intact. Consent and history follow, and the stool is already visibly bloody, so occult blood testing adds nothing.

options.text: Obtain informed consent for endoscopy
Insert two large-bore IV catheters and begin isotonic fluids
Collect a stool specimen for occult blood
Complete a detailed medication history

questions.stem: The client receives 2 units of packed red blood cells, and a bleeding ulcer is cauterized during endoscopy. Six hours later, the nurse reassesses. For each finding, indicate whether it shows improvement or no improvement.
questions.rationale: Stable vital signs, adequate urine output, improved perfusion, and an expected hemoglobin rise (about 1 g/dL per unit) show a response. A new large bloody stool with dizziness suggests rebleeding and requires immediate reporting.
questions.answer_summary: Improved: HR 92, BP 118/70, Hgb 9.0, urine output 45 mL/hr, warm dry skin. Not improved: large maroon stool with new dizziness.

rows.text: Large maroon stool with new dizziness

questions.stem: The nurse on an orthopedic unit receives report on four clients. Which client should the nurse assess first?
questions.rationale: Pain out of proportion to the injury, unrelieved by opioids and worsened by passive stretch, suggests acute compartment syndrome. Permanent muscle and nerve damage can occur within hours.

options.text: A client with a new long-leg cast who reports pain not relieved by IV morphine that worsens when the toes are moved
A client 1 day after total knee arthroplasty who rates pain 5/10
A client with gout who is requesting a lower-purine meal tray
A client with osteoporosis who has questions about calcium supplements

questions.stem: The nurse is monitoring a client with a tibial fracture for compartment syndrome. Which finding is the earliest indicator?
questions.rationale: Severe pain, especially with passive stretch, is the earliest and most reliable sign. Pulselessness, pallor, and paralysis are late signs that indicate advanced ischemia. The extremity is kept at heart level, not elevated above it, and the provider is notified immediately.

options.text: Absent pedal pulse
Pale, cold foot
Increasing pain with passive stretching of the toes
Inability to move the toes

questions.stem: An 82-year-old client fell at home and is brought to the emergency department. Which finding supports a suspected hip fracture?
questions.rationale: A displaced hip fracture typically causes shortening and external rotation of the affected leg, with groin or hip pain and inability to bear weight.

options.text: Affected leg lengthened and internally rotated
Affected leg shortened and externally rotated
Bilateral lower leg edema
Pain in the lower back only

questions.stem: A client had a total hip arthroplasty through a posterior approach 2 days ago. Which observation requires the nurse to intervene?
questions.rationale: After a posterior approach, the client avoids hip flexion beyond 90 degrees, crossing the legs, and internal rotation to prevent dislocation. Low chairs and bending forward exceed the flexion limit. Precautions vary by surgical approach and surgeon.

options.text: The client has an abduction pillow between the legs while in bed
The client is sitting in a low chair, bending forward to tie shoes
The client is using a raised toilet seat
The client is using a reacher to pick up items from the floor

questions.stem: A client is 2 days postoperative after total knee arthroplasty. Which finding requires the nurse's immediate action?
questions.rationale: Sudden dyspnea, chest pain, and tachycardia after lower-extremity joint replacement suggest pulmonary embolism, which requires emergency intervention. Low-grade fever, bruising, and controlled pain are expected.

options.text: Incisional pain rated 4/10 after analgesic
Temperature of 99.5°F (37.5°C)
Sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, and HR 118/min
Moderate bruising around the knee

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client in skeletal traction. Which finding requires the nurse to intervene?
questions.rationale: Weights must hang freely to maintain continuous, effective traction. Weights on the floor eliminate the pull. The nurse never removes skeletal traction weights without a prescription.

options.text: The weights are hanging freely
The client's body is aligned with the line of pull
The traction weights are resting on the floor
The ropes move freely through the pulleys

questions.stem: The nurse is performing pin site care for a client with an external fixator. Which finding should the nurse report?
questions.rationale: Purulent drainage and spreading erythema indicate pin site infection, which can progress to osteomyelitis. Clear drainage, mild crusting, and slight tenderness are expected.

options.text: Small amount of clear serous drainage
Slight crusting at the pin sites
Thick yellow-green drainage with spreading redness
Mild tenderness during cleaning

questions.stem: A client is receiving a 6-week course of IV antibiotics for osteomyelitis. Which lab trend indicates a positive response to treatment?
questions.rationale: ESR and CRP are inflammatory markers used to monitor osteomyelitis. Declining values indicate a response. A rising creatinine suggests nephrotoxicity from antibiotics such as vancomycin.

options.text: Rising erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein
Declining erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein
Increasing white blood cell count
Rising serum creatinine

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client who is starting alendronate for osteoporosis. Which instruction is correct?
questions.rationale: Alendronate is poorly absorbed and can cause esophagitis. It is taken on an empty stomach with plain water, and the client stays upright for at least 30 minutes before eating, drinking, or taking other medications.

options.text: "Take it at bedtime with a snack."
"Take it first thing in the morning with a full glass of plain water and remain upright for at least 30 minutes before eating."
"Take it with your calcium supplement and orange juice."
"Lie down for 30 minutes after taking it."

questions.stem: Which factors increase a client's risk for osteoporosis? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Estrogen loss, smoking, steroids, inactivity, alcohol, and low calcium and vitamin D reduce bone density. Weight-bearing exercise builds and maintains bone.
questions.answer_summary: A, B, C, D, F, G

options.text: Postmenopausal status
Cigarette smoking
Long-term corticosteroid therapy
Sedentary lifestyle
Regular weight-bearing exercise
Excessive alcohol intake
Low calcium and vitamin D intake

questions.stem: A client with gout asks which foods to limit. Which foods should the nurse identify?
questions.rationale: Organ meats, shellfish, and beer are high in purines, which increase uric acid. High-fructose drinks should also be limited. Low-fat dairy may lower uric acid levels.

options.text: Low-fat dairy products
Organ meats, shellfish, and beer
Fresh vegetables
Whole grains

questions.stem: For each characteristic, indicate whether it is more typical of rheumatoid arthritis or osteoarthritis.
questions.rationale: RA is a systemic autoimmune disease causing symmetric synovitis with prolonged stiffness and systemic symptoms. OA is degenerative, affecting weight-bearing joints and distal finger joints, with pain related to use.
questions.answer_summary: RA: prolonged morning stiffness, symmetric small-joint involvement, systemic symptoms. OA: Heberden's nodes, activity-related pain, brief stiffness.

rows.text: Morning stiffness lasting more than 1 hour
Symmetric involvement of small joints of the hands
Heberden's nodes on the distal finger joints
Fatigue, low-grade fever, and weight loss
Pain that worsens with activity and improves with rest
Morning stiffness lasting less than 30 minutes

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client with rheumatoid arthritis who is starting oral methotrexate. Which client statement indicates a need for further teaching?
questions.rationale: For RA, methotrexate is taken once weekly. Daily dosing is a serious, potentially fatal error causing bone marrow suppression and toxicity. Folic acid, alcohol avoidance, contraception, and monitoring of the CBC and liver function are correct teaching.

options.text: "I'll take my folic acid as prescribed."
"I'll take my methotrexate every morning."
"I'll avoid drinking alcohol."
"I'll keep my appointments for blood tests."

questions.stem: A client with rheumatoid arthritis is scheduled to begin adalimumab. Which test should the nurse verify has been completed before the first dose?
questions.rationale: TNF inhibitors can reactivate latent tuberculosis, so TB screening is required before therapy. Hepatitis B screening is also recommended. Live vaccines are avoided during treatment.

options.text: Tuberculosis screening
Hemoglobin A1C
Thyroid-stimulating hormone
Urine drug screen

questions.stem: A client is 3 days postoperative after a below-the-knee amputation. Which intervention helps prevent hip flexion contracture?
questions.rationale: Lying prone extends the hip and prevents flexion contracture. After the first 24–48 hours, the residual limb is not elevated on a pillow, and prolonged sitting is avoided.

options.text: Keep a pillow under the residual limb at all times
Place the client prone for 20–30 minutes several times a day, if tolerated
Keep the head of the bed elevated 60 degrees continuously
Encourage the client to sit in a chair most of the day

questions.stem: The nurse observes a client walking with axillary crutches. Which observation requires correction?
questions.rationale: Weight is supported on the hands, not the axillae. Leaning on the pads can compress the brachial plexus and cause crutch palsy.

options.text: The crutch pads are 2–3 fingerbreadths below the axillae
The client is leaning on the axillary pads to support body weight
The elbows are flexed about 20–30 degrees
The client moves the crutches and the injured leg forward together

questions.stem: A client was trapped under debris for several hours. The urine is dark reddish-brown, and the creatine kinase (CK) is 48,000 units/L. What is the nurse's priority intervention?
questions.rationale: Rhabdomyolysis releases myoglobin, which can cause acute kidney injury. Aggressive IV hydration maintains urine output and flushes myoglobin. Potassium is often elevated from muscle breakdown, so supplements are contraindicated.

options.text: Restrict fluids to prevent edema
Administer aggressive IV fluids as prescribed and monitor urine output
Encourage ambulation
Administer potassium supplements

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client with a new fiberglass arm cast. Which client statement indicates a need for further teaching?
questions.rationale: Inserting objects under a cast can break the skin and cause infection. Elevation, finger movement, and reporting odor or warm spots (which may indicate infection or pressure injury) are correct.

options.text: "I'll keep my arm elevated above my heart for the first couple of days."
"I'll use a coat hanger to scratch under the cast if it itches."
"I'll report any foul odor or warm spots on the cast."
"I'll wiggle my fingers often."

questions.stem: How should the nurse reposition a client after a lumbar spinal fusion?
questions.rationale: Log-rolling moves the head, shoulders, and hips as one unit to prevent twisting of the surgical site. A pillow between the knees helps maintain alignment.

options.text: Have the client twist at the waist to turn
Log-roll the client with assistance, keeping the spine aligned
Raise the head of the bed to 90 degrees before turning
Have the client use the overhead trapeze to pull up and turn

questions.stem: Highlight (circle) the findings that require immediate follow-up.
questions.rationale: New neurological changes, petechial rash, hypoxemia, tachypnea, tachycardia, fever, and falling platelets are new, serious findings. Moderate fracture pain and clear pin-site drainage are expected.
questions.answer_summary: New confusion; petechiae; SpO2 86%; RR 30; HR 124; T 101.2°F; platelets dropped to 98,000

passage_segments.text: Petechiae on the chest, axillae, and conjunctivae

questions.correct_text: New confusion; petechiae; SpO2 86%; RR 30; HR 124; T 101.2°F; platelets dropped to 98,000

questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is consistent with fat embolism syndrome or expected after a femur fracture.
questions.rationale: Fat embolism syndrome classically causes a triad of respiratory distress, neurological changes, and petechial rash, typically 24–72 hours after long-bone fractures. Thrombocytopenia is common. Swelling and pain at the fracture site are expected.
questions.answer_summary: FES: petechiae, acute confusion, hypoxemia, falling platelets. Expected: thigh swelling, fracture-site pain.

rows.text: Petechiae in the axillae and on the conjunctivae
Moderate pain at the fracture site

questions.stem: Complete the sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.rationale: The timing, petechiae, confusion, and hypoxemia after a long-bone fracture point to fat embolism syndrome. Distal perfusion is intact, which argues against compartment syndrome, and BP is stable, which argues against hypovolemic shock. Hypoxemia is the most immediate threat.
questions.answer_summary: 1: fat embolism syndrome; 2: impaired gas exchange
questions.template: The client is most likely experiencing ___1___. The priority problem is ___2___.

questions.stem: Which interventions does the nurse anticipate for this client? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Treatment for fat embolism syndrome is supportive: oxygenation, positioning, ventilatory support if needed, and neurological monitoring. Minimizing fracture movement and early stabilization reduce further fat release. Moving the fracture or changing traction without a prescription can worsen embolization.

options.text: Administer high-flow oxygen
Elevate the head of the bed
Prepare for possible intubation and mechanical ventilation
Minimize movement of the fractured leg
Perform frequent neurological assessments
Begin active range-of-motion exercises of the left leg
Increase the traction weight to realign the bone

questions.stem: Which action should the nurse take first?
questions.rationale: Correcting hypoxemia is the immediate priority. The nurse applies oxygen per protocol while calling for the provider or rapid response team. Diagnostic tests follow once oxygenation is supported.

options.text: Obtain a portable chest x-ray
Apply high-flow oxygen and raise the head of the bed
Draw blood for arterial blood gases
Document the petechiae with a photograph

questions.stem: Forty-eight hours later, the nurse reassesses the client. For each finding, indicate whether it shows improvement or no improvement.
questions.rationale: Better oxygenation, orientation, respiratory rate, and fading rash show improvement. Falling platelets and new crackles with rising oxygen requirements suggest ongoing lung injury, possibly progressing to ARDS.
questions.answer_summary: Improved: SpO2 95% on 4 L, oriented, RR 20, petechiae fading. Not improved: platelets 86,000, new crackles with rising oxygen needs.

rows.text: Oriented to person, place, and time
New bilateral crackles with increasing oxygen requirements

questions.stem: The nurse on an oncology unit receives report on four clients. Which client should the nurse assess first?
questions.rationale: Low back pain and chills during a transfusion suggest an acute hemolytic reaction, which can rapidly cause shock, DIC, and kidney failure. The morphine needs time to work, and the others are stable.

options.text: A client 30 minutes into a packed red blood cell transfusion who reports new low back pain and chills
A client with sickle cell disease in pain crisis who received IV morphine 20 minutes ago
A client with iron deficiency anemia who has questions about iron supplements
A client receiving chemotherapy who reports mild nausea

questions.stem: Fifteen minutes into a unit of packed red blood cells, the client develops chills, a temperature increase from 98.6°F to 101°F (37°C to 38.3°C), and anxiety. What should the nurse do first?
questions.rationale: With any suspected reaction, the nurse stops the transfusion immediately and keeps the IV open with saline through new tubing, so no more blood enters the client. The nurse then notifies the provider and blood bank and returns the bag and tubing.

options.text: Slow the transfusion and recheck vital signs in 15 minutes
Stop the transfusion and maintain IV access with 0.9% sodium chloride using new tubing
Administer acetaminophen and continue the transfusion
Flush the blood tubing with normal saline

questions.stem: Which actions are correct when administering packed red blood cells? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Two-person verification, saline priming, filtered tubing, baseline vital signs, close observation early (when severe reactions usually occur), and completion within 4 hours are standard. Dextrose causes hemolysis of red cells.
questions.answer_summary: A, B, C, D, F, G

options.text: Verify the client and blood product with another licensed nurse at the bedside
Prime the tubing with 0.9% sodium chloride
Stay with the client for the first 15 minutes
Use tubing with a blood filter
Prime the tubing with 5% dextrose in water
Complete the transfusion within 4 hours of spiking the bag
Obtain baseline vital signs before starting

questions.stem: A client has been receiving heparin for 7 days. The platelet count has dropped from 260,000 to 110,000/mm³, and a new DVT is found in the left leg. What does the nurse anticipate?
questions.rationale: A platelet drop of more than 50% 5–10 days after starting heparin, with new thrombosis, suggests heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. All heparin, including flushes and low-molecular-weight heparin, is stopped, and a direct thrombin inhibitor is started.

options.text: Increasing the heparin dose
Stopping all heparin and starting a non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban
Transfusing platelets
Switching to enoxaparin

questions.stem: A client with septic shock develops oozing from IV sites. Which set of lab results supports disseminated intravascular coagulation?
questions.rationale: DIC consumes clotting factors and platelets while activating fibrinolysis. This causes thrombocytopenia, prolonged clotting times, low fibrinogen, and elevated D-dimer. Treating the underlying cause is key.

options.text: Increased platelets, shortened PT, elevated fibrinogen
Decreased platelets, prolonged PT and aPTT, decreased fibrinogen, elevated D-dimer
Normal platelets, normal PT, normal D-dimer
Elevated hemoglobin, decreased D-dimer

questions.stem: Which interventions should the nurse include for a client admitted in vaso-occlusive sickle cell crisis? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Hydration, aggressive pain control, oxygen for hypoxemia, and infection monitoring are core interventions. Cold causes vasoconstriction and increases sickling, and prolonged bed rest increases the risk of complications. Warm compresses may help.

options.text: IV fluids as prescribed
Scheduled or patient-controlled opioid analgesia
Oxygen if SpO2 is below the prescribed target
Apply cold packs to painful joints
Monitor for fever and signs of infection
Encourage strict bed rest for several days

questions.stem: A client with sickle cell disease develops chest pain, fever, cough, and SpO2 of 89%. The chest x-ray shows a new infiltrate. What is the nurse's priority?
questions.rationale: Acute chest syndrome is a leading cause of death in sickle cell disease and requires urgent oxygen, antibiotics, pain control, incentive spirometry, and possibly transfusion.

options.text: Encourage oral fluids and reassess in 4 hours
Recognize acute chest syndrome and notify the provider immediately for urgent treatment
Discharge the client with oral antibiotics
Apply a cold compress to the chest

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client who is starting oral ferrous sulfate. Which instruction is correct?
questions.rationale: Vitamin C enhances iron absorption. Dark stools are expected. Milk, antacids, and calcium reduce absorption. If GI upset occurs, iron can be taken with a small amount of food.

options.text: "Take it with milk to reduce stomach upset."
"Take it with orange juice, and expect your stools to become dark green or black."
"Take it with an antacid."
"Stop taking it if your stools darken."

questions.stem: A client is diagnosed with pernicious anemia. Which statement by the client indicates understanding of the treatment?
questions.rationale: Pernicious anemia results from a lack of intrinsic factor, so dietary B12 cannot be absorbed. Lifelong B12 replacement, by injection or high-dose oral or nasal forms, is needed to prevent anemia and neurological damage.

options.text: "I'll need vitamin B12 injections or high-dose supplements for the rest of my life."
"Eating more red meat will cure this."
"I'll take iron pills for 3 months."
"I only need treatment until my energy improves."

questions.stem: A client's absolute neutrophil count is 400/mm³. Which interventions should the nurse implement? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Severe neutropenia (ANC below 500) greatly increases infection risk. Hand hygiene is most important. Rectal procedures can cause mucosal injury and infection, and ill visitors should not visit. Fever may be the only sign of infection.

options.text: Place the client in a private room
Perform meticulous hand hygiene before and after contact
Avoid rectal temperatures and suppositories
Screen visitors for signs of illness
Allow a visitor with a cold to visit if wearing a mask
Monitor temperature closely and report fever promptly

questions.stem: A client's platelet count is 18,000/mm³. Which prescription should the nurse clarify with the provider?
questions.rationale: IM injections can cause hematomas and bleeding when platelets are severely low. The other measures are appropriate bleeding precautions.

options.text: Use an electric razor
Administer the influenza vaccine intramuscularly today
Use a soft-bristled toothbrush
Apply pressure to venipuncture sites for 5 minutes

questions.stem: During a peripheral infusion of a vesicant chemotherapy drug, the client reports burning at the site, and the nurse notes swelling. What should the nurse do first?
questions.rationale: The infusion is stopped first. The catheter is left in place so residual drug can be aspirated and a prescribed antidote can be given if indicated. Warm or cold compresses depend on the specific agent, and flushing pushes more drug into the tissue.

options.text: Remove the IV catheter immediately
Stop the infusion
Apply warm compresses
Flush the line with normal saline

questions.stem: A client with a high-grade lymphoma started chemotherapy 24 hours ago. Which lab pattern indicates tumor lysis syndrome?
questions.rationale: Rapid tumor cell breakdown releases potassium, phosphate, and nucleic acids (converted to uric acid). Phosphate binds calcium, causing hypocalcemia. Prevention includes aggressive hydration and allopurinol or rasburicase.

options.text: Hypokalemia, hypophosphatemia, hypercalcemia
Hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hyperuricemia, hypocalcemia
Hyponatremia only
Normal electrolytes with elevated hemoglobin

questions.stem: A client with lung cancer reports increasing shortness of breath and a feeling of fullness in the head. Which finding suggests superior vena cava syndrome?
questions.rationale: Tumor compression of the superior vena cava impairs venous return from the upper body, causing facial, neck, and arm edema with prominent veins. It is an oncologic emergency.

options.text: Swelling of the face, neck, and arms with distended neck and chest veins
Bilateral ankle edema only
Hypotension with warm, flushed extremities
Severe low back pain

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client receiving external beam radiation to the chest. Which client statement indicates a need for further teaching?
questions.rationale: Skin markings guide accurate radiation delivery and must not be removed. Gentle care, sun avoidance, and using only approved products protect the irradiated skin.

options.text: "I'll wash the area gently with mild soap and lukewarm water."
"I'll scrub off the markings on my skin after each treatment."
"I'll avoid sun exposure to the treatment area."
"I'll ask before using any lotion on the area."

questions.stem: A client has a sealed radioactive cervical implant. The nurse finds the implant in the bed linens. What should the nurse do?
questions.rationale: A dislodged source is never touched by hand. Long forceps and the lead container minimize exposure (time, distance, shielding). The nurse notifies the radiation safety officer and provider.

options.text: Pick it up with gloved hands and reinsert it
Use long-handled forceps to place it in the lead container in the room and notify radiation safety
Discard it in the biohazard container
Leave it in place and continue care

questions.stem: A client taking warfarin is admitted with active GI bleeding and an INR of 8.9. Which treatment does the nurse anticipate?
questions.rationale: Serious bleeding with a high INR requires rapid reversal with IV vitamin K and PCC (or plasma if PCC is unavailable). Protamine reverses heparin.

options.text: Protamine sulfate
IV vitamin K and 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate
Increased warfarin dose
Oral aspirin

questions.stem: A client with atrial fibrillation is prescribed apixaban. Which statement by the client indicates understanding?
questions.rationale: DOACs do not need routine INR monitoring or vitamin K restriction. Stopping abruptly increases stroke risk, and bleeding should be reported. Missed doses are handled per specific instructions; doubling is not recommended.

options.text: "I'll need weekly INR blood tests."
"I won't stop taking it without talking to my provider, and I'll report any unusual bleeding."
"I need to avoid all green vegetables."
"I can double my next dose if I miss one."

questions.stem: A 46-year-old client at average risk for colorectal cancer asks when screening should begin. What is the nurse's best response?
questions.rationale: U.S. guidelines (USPSTF and American Cancer Society) recommend starting colorectal cancer screening at age 45 for average-risk adults, using colonoscopy or other approved tests.

options.text: "Screening begins at age 60."
"Current guidelines recommend starting screening at age 45."
"Screening is only needed if you have symptoms."
"You only need screening if a parent had colon cancer."

questions.stem: Highlight (circle) the findings that require immediate follow-up.
questions.rationale: Fever in severe neutropenia is a medical emergency. Tachycardia, a falling BP, and elevated lactate suggest sepsis with hypoperfusion, and the PICC site is a likely source. SpO2 is acceptable, and fatigue is expected with anemia.
questions.answer_summary: Fever; chills; HR 118; BP 96/58; PICC-site redness; ANC 200; lactate 2.8

passage_segments.text: Redness and tenderness around the PICC site

questions.correct_text: Fever; chills; HR 118; BP 96/58; PICC-site redness; ANC 200; lactate 2.8

questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it primarily reflects infection/sepsis, low platelets (thrombocytopenia), or anemia.
questions.rationale: Chemotherapy suppresses all bone marrow lines. Neutropenia causes infection risk, low platelets cause bleeding, and low hemoglobin causes fatigue and pallor. Lactate reflects tissue hypoperfusion from sepsis.
questions.answer_summary: Infection/sepsis: fever, PICC redness, lactate. Thrombocytopenia: petechiae, gum bleeding. Anemia: pallor and fatigue.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.rationale: Fever with an ANC of 200 and signs of hypoperfusion indicate neutropenic sepsis. Redness and tenderness at the central line insertion site point to a catheter-related bloodstream infection. Classic signs of infection may be muted in neutropenia.
questions.answer_summary: 1: febrile neutropenia with sepsis; 2: the PICC line

questions.stem: Which interventions does the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Febrile neutropenia requires cultures from each lumen and a peripheral site, then broad-spectrum antibiotics within 60 minutes. Fluids treat hypoperfusion, and repeat lactate tracks response. Rectal temperatures are avoided, and delaying antibiotics increases mortality.

options.text: Obtain blood cultures from the PICC and a peripheral site
Start broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour
Administer an isotonic IV fluid bolus as prescribed
Repeat the lactate level
Maintain neutropenic precautions
Take a rectal temperature every 2 hours
Withhold antibiotics until culture results return

questions.stem: The provider has written all prescriptions. Which action should the nurse take first?
questions.rationale: Blood cultures are drawn immediately before antibiotics so the organism can be identified, but antibiotics must not be delayed beyond 60 minutes. The PICC is not removed until the provider decides, and acetaminophen is a lower priority.

options.text: Administer acetaminophen for the fever
Obtain the blood cultures
Administer the broad-spectrum IV antibiotic
Send the PICC tip for culture

questions.stem: Twenty-four hours later, the nurse reassesses the client. For each finding, indicate whether it shows improvement or no improvement.
questions.rationale: Improved temperature, BP, heart rate, and lactate show response to therapy. Rigors after flushing suggest bacteria seeding from the catheter, which may need to be removed. Low urine output suggests ongoing hypoperfusion or acute kidney injury.
questions.answer_summary: Improved: T 99.1°F, BP 118/70, lactate 1.4, HR 90. Not improved: rigors after PICC flush, urine output 20 mL/hr.

rows.text: Rigors immediately after the PICC is flushed
Urine output 20 mL/hr for the past 3 hours

questions.set_title: Set 9: Immune System and Infectious Disease
questions.stem: The charge nurse in the emergency department is reviewing the status of four clients. Which situation requires the nurse's action first?
questions.rationale: Fever, cough, conjunctivitis, and a rash suggest measles, which is highly contagious by the airborne route. The client needs a mask and immediate placement in an airborne infection isolation room to protect others.

options.text: A client with an MRSA wound infection on contact precautions in a private room
A client with fever, cough, conjunctivitis, and a new blotchy rash seated in the waiting room
A client with HIV who is asking about medication refills
A client with Clostridioides difficile on contact precautions who is resting

questions.set_title: Set 9: Immune System and Infectious Disease
questions.stem: For each infection, indicate the transmission-based precautions required in addition to standard precautions.
questions.rationale: Airborne pathogens remain suspended in the air and require a negative-pressure room and N95 respirator. Droplet pathogens travel short distances and require a surgical mask. Contact pathogens spread by direct or indirect touch and require a gown and gloves. Varicella requires both airborne and contact precautions.
questions.answer_summary: Airborne: measles, TB. Droplet: influenza, pertussis. Contact: MRSA wound, scabies.

questions.set_title: Set 9: Immune System and Infectious Disease
questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to enter the room of a client who requires contact and droplet precautions. In what order should the nurse put on personal protective equipment?
questions.rationale: CDC donning order is gown, mask or respirator, eye protection, then gloves, with gloves pulled over the gown cuffs. Doffing typically begins with gloves, the most contaminated item.

options.text: Gloves, gown, mask, goggles
Gown, mask, goggles or face shield, gloves
Mask, gloves, gown, goggles
Goggles, gloves, mask, gown

questions.set_title: Set 9: Immune System and Infectious Disease
questions.stem: A nurse sustains a needlestick from a used needle after giving an injection to a client with HIV. What should the nurse do first?
questions.rationale: Immediate washing with soap and water is the first step. The nurse then reports the exposure right away, because HIV post-exposure prophylaxis is most effective when started as soon as possible, ideally within hours and no later than 72 hours. Squeezing and caustic agents are not recommended.

options.text: Report the injury to the employee health department
Wash the site thoroughly with soap and water
Squeeze the site to make it bleed
Apply bleach to the site

questions.set_title: Set 9: Immune System and Infectious Disease
questions.stem: A client with HIV has a CD4 count of 160 cells/mm³. Which prescription does the nurse anticipate in addition to antiretroviral therapy?
questions.rationale: A CD4 count below 200 defines AIDS and increases the risk of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, so prophylaxis with TMP-SMX is started. Live vaccines are contraindicated with severe immunosuppression.

options.text: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for Pneumocystis pneumonia prophylaxis
Live varicella vaccine
Discontinuation of antiretroviral therapy
High-dose corticosteroids

questions.set_title: Set 9: Immune System and Infectious Disease
questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client who is starting antiretroviral therapy. Which client statement indicates understanding?
questions.rationale: Consistent daily adherence maintains viral suppression, prevents resistance, and means the client cannot sexually transmit HIV (undetectable = untransmittable). Therapy is lifelong.

options.text: "I can skip doses on weekends if I feel well."
"If I take my medicine every day and my viral load stays undetectable, I won't transmit HIV to sexual partners."
"I can stop the medication once my CD4 count is normal."
"Missing doses won't affect whether the medication works."

questions.set_title: Set 9: Immune System and Infectious Disease
questions.stem: A client with systemic lupus erythematosus reports new swelling of the ankles and foamy urine. What does the nurse suspect?
questions.rationale: Foamy urine (proteinuria) and edema suggest lupus nephritis, a serious complication that can lead to kidney failure. Urinalysis and renal function tests are needed.

options.text: Lupus nephritis
Expected medication side effect
Dehydration
Raynaud's phenomenon

questions.set_title: Set 9: Immune System and Infectious Disease
questions.stem: A client with lupus is starting hydroxychloroquine. Which instruction should the nurse include?
questions.rationale: Hydroxychloroquine can cause retinal toxicity. A baseline eye exam and periodic screening are recommended.

options.text: "Have regular eye exams while taking this medication."
"Take it with grapefruit juice."
"Expect your urine to turn orange."
"Stop the medication if you feel better."

questions.set_title: Set 9: Immune System and Infectious Disease
questions.stem: A client scheduled for surgery reports allergies to bananas, avocados, and kiwi. What should the nurse do?
questions.rationale: These foods share proteins with natural rubber latex (latex-fruit syndrome). The client may be latex-sensitive, so the team should use a latex-free environment.

options.text: Document the food allergies only
Notify the surgical team of a possible latex allergy and plan for a latex-free environment
Give a test dose of latex
No action is needed

questions.set_title: Set 9: Immune System and Infectious Disease
questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client with a severe peanut allergy how to use an epinephrine auto-injector. Which instruction is correct?
questions.rationale: Epinephrine is injected into the anterolateral thigh and can be given through clothing. It is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis. Emergency care is still needed because symptoms can recur.

options.text: "Inject into your upper arm muscle."
"Press the injector firmly against the outer thigh, even through clothing, hold it in place as directed, then call 911."
"Use it only if taking an antihistamine doesn't work."
"After using it, you don't need further medical care."

questions.set_title: Set 9: Immune System and Infectious Disease
questions.stem: A client receiving chemotherapy for breast cancer is due for several vaccines. Which vaccine should the nurse question?
questions.rationale: MMR is a live attenuated vaccine and is contraindicated in immunocompromised clients and during pregnancy. Inactivated vaccines are generally safe, though response may be reduced.

options.text: Inactivated influenza vaccine
Measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine
Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine
Tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis (Tdap) vaccine

questions.set_title: Set 9: Immune System and Infectious Disease
questions.stem: A client meets criteria for sepsis with a lactate of 4.6 mmol/L and BP 84/48 mm Hg. Which actions are part of the initial sepsis bundle? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: The Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour-1 bundle includes lactate, cultures, broad-spectrum antibiotics, 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate of 4 or higher, and vasopressors to maintain MAP of at least 65 mm Hg. Delaying antibiotics increases mortality.

options.text: Measure a lactate level
Obtain blood cultures before antibiotics
Administer broad-spectrum antibiotics
Give 30 mL/kg of IV crystalloid
Start a vasopressor if hypotension persists during or after fluid resuscitation
Wait for culture results before starting antibiotics

questions.set_title: Set 9: Immune System and Infectious Disease
questions.stem: A client in septic shock remains hypotensive after adequate fluid resuscitation. Norepinephrine is started. Which goal is appropriate?
questions.rationale: A MAP of at least 65 mm Hg maintains organ perfusion in septic shock. Adequate urine output (at least 0.5 mL/kg/hr) and falling lactate also indicate improved perfusion.

options.text: MAP of 65 mm Hg or higher
Systolic BP above 180 mm Hg
HR above 120/min
Urine output of 10 mL/hr

questions.set_title: Set 9: Immune System and Infectious Disease
questions.stem: A client asks how to remove a tick found on the leg after hiking. Which instruction is correct?
questions.rationale: Steady removal with tweezers reduces the chance of leaving mouthparts behind. The client should clean the area and watch for an expanding "bull's-eye" rash (erythema migrans), fever, or joint pain.

options.text: "Burn it off with a match."
"Grasp the tick close to the skin with fine-tipped tweezers and pull upward with steady, even pressure."
"Cover it with petroleum jelly and wait for it to fall off."
"Twist it quickly while squeezing its body."

questions.set_title: Set 9: Immune System and Infectious Disease
questions.stem: A client with localized herpes zoster (shingles) is admitted. Which staff member should not be assigned to this client?
questions.rationale: Contact with zoster lesions can transmit varicella-zoster virus to people who are not immune. Varicella in pregnancy can cause severe maternal and fetal complications.

options.text: A nurse who had chickenpox as a child
A pregnant nurse who has never had chickenpox or the varicella vaccine
A nurse who received the varicella vaccine
A nurse who had shingles last year

questions.set_title: Set 9: Immune System and Infectious Disease
questions.stem: During an IV vancomycin infusion, the client develops flushing and a red rash on the face, neck, and upper chest. BP is stable, and there is no respiratory distress. What should the nurse do?
questions.rationale: Vancomycin infusion reaction (formerly "red man syndrome") is related to rapid infusion, not true allergy. It is managed by slowing the rate (over at least 60 minutes) and giving antihistamines. The client's stable BP and breathing distinguish it from anaphylaxis.

options.text: Continue the infusion at the same rate
Stop or slow the infusion and notify the provider, anticipating a slower infusion rate and possibly an antihistamine
Administer epinephrine IM
Discontinue vancomycin permanently

questions.set_title: Set 9: Immune System and Infectious Disease
questions.stem: A client is receiving IV gentamicin. Which finding should the nurse report to the provider?
questions.rationale: Aminoglycosides are ototoxic and nephrotoxic. Tinnitus or hearing loss indicates ototoxicity. Drug levels and renal function are monitored.

options.text: Ringing in the ears
Improved urinary symptoms
Mild injection-site tenderness
Creatinine of 0.8 mg/dL

questions.set_title: Set 9: Immune System and Infectious Disease
questions.stem: In which situation must the nurse wash hands with soap and water rather than use an alcohol-based hand rub?
questions.rationale: Soap and water are needed when hands are visibly soiled and after caring for clients with spore-forming or alcohol-resistant organisms such as C. difficile and norovirus. Alcohol rub is appropriate for most other situations.

options.text: Before taking a blood pressure
After caring for a client with norovirus
After touching a clean over-bed table
Before entering a room on contact precautions for MRSA

questions.set_title: Set 9: Immune System and Infectious Disease
questions.stem: A client is prescribed amoxicillin-clavulanate. During the medication history, the client reports developing hives the last time they took amoxicillin. What should the nurse do?
questions.rationale: Amoxicillin-clavulanate contains amoxicillin. A prior hypersensitivity reaction means the drug should be held and the provider notified to select an alternative. The allergy and reaction type are documented.

options.text: Administer the medication with diphenhydramine
Hold the medication and clarify the prescription with the provider
Give a half dose to test for a reaction
Administer the medication, since hives are a minor reaction

questions.set_title: Set 9: Immune System and Infectious Disease
questions.stem: Highlight (circle) the findings that require immediate follow-up.
questions.rationale: Airway edema (hoarseness, angioedema), bronchospasm, hypoxemia, and hypotension indicate life-threatening anaphylaxis. The low-grade fever is related to the pyelonephritis.
questions.answer_summary: Hoarse voice; wheezing; BP 78/42; HR 128; SpO2 89%; lip and eyelid swelling; widespread hives

passage_segments.text: Swelling of the lips and eyelids

questions.correct_text: Hoarse voice; wheezing; BP 78/42; HR 128; SpO2 89%; lip and eyelid swelling; widespread hives

questions.set_title: Set 9: Immune System and Infectious Disease
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate the body system primarily affected.
questions.rationale: Mast cell mediators such as histamine cause laryngeal edema and bronchoconstriction, vasodilation and capillary leak (distributive shock), and skin manifestations. Anaphylaxis is diagnosed when multiple systems are involved.
questions.answer_summary: Airway/breathing: hoarseness, wheezing. Circulation: hypotension, tachycardia. Skin/mucosa: hives, itching.

questions.set_title: Set 9: Immune System and Infectious Disease
questions.stem: Complete the sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.rationale: Sudden onset of multi-system symptoms within minutes of a first-dose antibiotic indicates anaphylaxis. Septic shock does not cause hives, angioedema, and wheezing this abruptly. Hoarseness signals laryngeal edema, which can progress to complete airway obstruction.
questions.answer_summary: 1: anaphylaxis caused by ceftriaxone; 2: airway obstruction from laryngeal edema
questions.template: The client is most likely experiencing ___1___. The most immediate threat to the client is ___2___.

questions.set_title: Set 9: Immune System and Infectious Disease
questions.stem: Which interventions does the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Anaphylaxis treatment is stopping the trigger, IM epinephrine (repeated every 5–15 minutes as needed), oxygen, fluid resuscitation for distributive shock, and airway readiness. Antihistamines, corticosteroids, and albuterol are adjuncts only. The antibiotic is never restarted.

options.text: Stop the ceftriaxone infusion
Epinephrine 0.5 mg IM (1 mg/mL) in the anterolateral thigh
High-flow oxygen
Rapid IV bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride
Prepare for advanced airway management
Continue the ceftriaxone at a slower rate
Oral diphenhydramine as the only treatment

questions.set_title: Set 9: Immune System and Infectious Disease
questions.stem: The nurse has stopped the ceftriaxone and called for help. Which medication should the nurse administer first?
questions.rationale: Epinephrine reverses bronchospasm, laryngeal edema, and vasodilation, and it is the only first-line drug for anaphylaxis. Delaying it increases mortality. The other drugs are adjuncts.

options.text: Diphenhydramine IV
Epinephrine IM
Methylprednisolone IV
Nebulized albuterol

questions.set_title: Set 9: Immune System and Infectious Disease
questions.stem: The client receives two doses of IM epinephrine, IV fluids, and oxygen. For each finding, indicate whether it shows improvement or requires immediate follow-up.
questions.rationale: Improved BP, oxygenation, airway, and skin show response to treatment. Symptom recurrence hours later is a biphasic reaction, which is why clients are observed after anaphylaxis and discharged with an epinephrine auto-injector and a documented allergy.
questions.answer_summary: Improved: BP 112/70, SpO2 96%, wheezing resolved, normal voice, hives fading. Follow-up: recurrent symptoms at 4 hours.

rows.text: Four hours later: new throat tightness and hives recurring

questions.stem: The nurse in the emergency department receives four clients. Which client should the nurse assess first?
questions.rationale: Facial burns, singed nasal hair, and hoarseness indicate inhalation injury with airway edema, which can quickly progress to complete obstruction. Early intubation may be needed.

options.text: A client with burns to the face who has singed nasal hair and a hoarse voice
A client with a stage 2 pressure injury on the sacrum
A client with cellulitis of the lower leg and a temperature of 100.6°F (38.1°C)
A client with a psoriasis flare requesting topical medication

questions.stem: A client rescued from an enclosed burning building has a headache and confusion. The pulse oximeter reads 99%. What should the nurse do?
questions.rationale: Standard pulse oximetry cannot tell carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin, so SpO2 can be falsely normal. The treatment is 100% oxygen, which shortens the half-life of carbon monoxide. Hyperbaric therapy may be considered in severe cases.

options.text: Document the normal oxygen saturation
Apply 100% oxygen by nonrebreather mask and anticipate a carboxyhemoglobin level
Apply oxygen at 2 L/min by nasal cannula
Encourage deep breathing and reassess in 1 hour

questions.stem: Using the rule of nines, what is the total body surface area burned in an adult with burns to the entire right arm and the entire anterior trunk?
questions.rationale: Each entire arm is 9% and the anterior trunk is 18%, so 9% + 18% = 27%. Superficial (first-degree) burns are not included in TBSA calculations.

questions.stem: Which description is consistent with a full-thickness burn?
questions.rationale: Full-thickness burns destroy the epidermis, dermis, and nerve endings, leaving dry, leathery eschar with little pain. They usually require grafting. Moist, blistered, painful burns are partial-thickness.

options.text: Red, painful, blanches with pressure, no blisters
Moist, red, blistered, and very painful
White or charred, dry, leathery, and painless to touch
Pink with mild peeling after 3 days

questions.stem: A client has circumferential full-thickness burns of the left arm. Which finding requires immediate action?
questions.rationale: Inelastic eschar combined with swelling can compress vessels and nerves, similar to compartment syndrome. Loss of pulses or sensation requires emergency escharotomy. Edema and leathery eschar are expected.

options.text: Edema of the arm
Diminishing radial pulse by Doppler and increasing numbness of the fingers
Pain at the edges of the burn
Dry, leathery appearance of the burn

questions.stem: Which laboratory findings does the nurse expect during the first 24 hours after a major burn?
questions.rationale: During the emergent phase, capillary leak shifts plasma out of the vessels, which concentrates the blood and raises hematocrit. Cell destruction releases potassium. Later, hypokalemia often develops as fluid shifts back and diuresis begins.

options.text: Decreased hematocrit and hypokalemia
Elevated hematocrit and hyperkalemia
Normal hematocrit and hypernatremia
Decreased hematocrit and hypercalcemia

questions.stem: A client with partial-thickness burns is prescribed silver sulfadiazine cream. Which information in the client's history should the nurse report before applying it?
questions.rationale: Silver sulfadiazine is a sulfonamide and may cause reactions in clients with sulfa allergy. It can also cause transient leukopenia.

options.text: Allergy to sulfonamide antibiotics
Allergy to shellfish
History of hypertension
Seasonal allergies

questions.stem: Which dietary plan does the nurse anticipate for a client recovering from a major burn?
questions.rationale: Major burns cause a hypermetabolic state with greatly increased calorie and protein needs for wound healing and immune function. Early enteral feeding is preferred.

options.text: Low-calorie, low-protein diet
High-calorie, high-protein diet with supplemental vitamins and minerals
Clear liquids only for 2 weeks
Low-fat, low-sodium diet only

questions.stem: A client sustained a high-voltage electrical injury. There are small entry and exit wounds on the hand and foot. What is the nurse's priority?
questions.rationale: Electrical current can cause dysrhythmias and cardiac arrest. Small skin wounds often hide extensive deep tissue damage, which can release myoglobin and cause kidney injury, so urine color is also monitored.

options.text: Dress the small wounds
Place the client on continuous cardiac monitoring
Calculate the TBSA using the rule of nines
Apply cool compresses to the wounds

questions.stem: A worker is brought in with dry lime powder on the arms. What should the nurse do first?
questions.rationale: Dry chemicals are brushed off first, because water can activate some powders. The area is then irrigated with copious water. Neutralizing agents can cause heat injury.

options.text: Immediately flush the arms with water
Brush off the dry powder, then flush with large amounts of water
Apply a neutralizing acid
Cover the arms with dry dressings

questions.stem: The nurse assesses a sacral wound with full-thickness tissue loss. Subcutaneous fat is visible, but no bone, tendon, or muscle is exposed. How should the nurse document this wound?
questions.rationale: Stage 3 involves full-thickness skin loss with visible fat. Stage 4 exposes bone, tendon, or muscle. Stage 2 is partial-thickness, and wounds obscured by slough or eschar are unstageable.

options.text: Stage 1
Stage 2
Stage 3
Stage 4

questions.stem: Four clients have the following Braden Scale scores. Which client is at highest risk for developing a pressure injury?
questions.rationale: Lower Braden scores indicate higher risk. A score of 9 or less is very high risk, and scores of 18 or less generally indicate risk.

options.text: Score of 20
Score of 17
Score of 13
Score of 9

questions.stem: Which interventions help prevent pressure injuries in an immobile client? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Repositioning, limiting head elevation (to reduce shear), moisture control, and pressure-redistribution surfaces reduce risk. Massaging reddened areas damages tissue, and donut cushions concentrate pressure around the edges.

options.text: Reposition at least every 2 hours
Keep the head of the bed at 30 degrees or lower when possible
Manage incontinence promptly
Use a pressure-redistribution mattress
Massage reddened bony prominences
Use a donut-shaped cushion when sitting

questions.stem: A client's negative-pressure wound therapy device has been off for 3 hours because of a power issue. What should the nurse do?
questions.rationale: If the device is off for more than about 2 hours (per manufacturer and facility policy), the foam can trap drainage and bacteria. It is replaced with a moist dressing, and the provider is notified.

options.text: Restart the device over the existing foam dressing
Remove the foam dressing and apply a moist saline dressing, then notify the provider
Leave the foam dressing in place until the next scheduled change
Increase the suction pressure when restarting

questions.stem: A client is admitted with cellulitis of the lower leg. Which action helps the nurse monitor the response to treatment?
questions.rationale: Marking the border allows objective tracking of spread or improvement. The leg is elevated to reduce swelling.

options.text: Apply a tight compression bandage
Outline the border of redness with a skin marker and note the date and time
Keep the leg in a dependent position
Massage the area to reduce swelling

questions.stem: A client with a small leg wound reports severe pain far out of proportion to the appearance of the wound. The redness has spread rapidly over 3 hours, and the client is tachycardic and febrile. What does the nurse suspect?
questions.rationale: Pain out of proportion, rapid spread, and systemic toxicity suggest necrotizing soft tissue infection. It requires emergency surgical debridement and broad-spectrum antibiotics.

options.text: Simple cellulitis
Necrotizing fasciitis requiring emergency surgical evaluation
Contact dermatitis
Normal healing

questions.stem: Two weeks after starting lamotrigine, a client develops fever, painful red skin with blisters, and sores in the mouth and eyes. What should the nurse anticipate?
questions.rationale: These findings suggest Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis, a severe drug reaction. The causative drug is stopped immediately, and care focuses on fluid management, wound care, pain control, and infection prevention, often in a burn unit.

options.text: Continuing the medication with an antihistamine
Stopping the medication and providing care similar to that for a major burn
Applying hydrocortisone cream and discharging the client
Doubling the dose

questions.stem: A 19-year-old female client is starting isotretinoin for severe acne. Which statement indicates understanding?
questions.rationale: Isotretinoin is highly teratogenic. The iPLEDGE program requires contraception and pregnancy testing. Vitamin A supplements increase toxicity, and blood donation is prohibited during treatment and for 1 month after.

options.text: "I can get pregnant while taking this if I stop the medicine as soon as I find out."
"I'll use two forms of birth control and have regular pregnancy tests as required by the program."
"I'll take extra vitamin A supplements."
"I can donate blood while taking this."

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client how to apply a high-potency topical corticosteroid for psoriasis plaques. Which instruction is correct?
questions.rationale: Thin application to affected areas reduces the risk of skin atrophy and systemic absorption. High-potency steroids are avoided on the face and skin folds. Occlusion increases absorption and is used only if prescribed.

options.text: "Apply a thick layer to the face daily."
"Apply a thin layer only to the affected areas as prescribed."
"Cover the area with plastic wrap overnight unless your provider tells you not to."
"Use it on all skin to prevent new plaques."

questions.stem: Highlight (circle) the findings that require immediate follow-up.
questions.rationale: Tachycardia, low BP, oliguria, and hemoconcentration indicate burn shock from capillary leak. Severe pain needs prompt treatment. The clear airway, intact pulses, and normal SpO2 are reassuring.
questions.answer_summary: HR 128; BP 96/60; urine output 15 mL/hr; hematocrit 54%; pain 9/10

passage_segments.text: Urine output 15 mL in the first hour
Voice clear, no soot in the mouth or nose

questions.correct_text: HR 128; BP 96/60; urine output 15 mL/hr; hematocrit 54%; pain 9/10

questions.stem: Complete the sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.rationale: Anterior trunk (18%) plus the anterior surfaces of both legs (9% each) equals 36%. Parkland: 4 mL × 80 kg × 36 = 11,520 mL. Half (5,760 mL) is given in the first 8 hours from the time of injury, not arrival, and the rest over the next 16 hours. Rates are then adjusted to urine output.
questions.template: Using the rule of nines, the client's total body surface area burned is ___1___. Using the Parkland formula (4 mL × kg × %TBSA), the total volume of lactated Ringer's for the first 24 hours is ___2___.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.rationale: Burns over about 20% TBSA cause massive capillary leak, which shifts fluid and protein into the interstitial space and depletes intravascular volume. There are no signs of inhalation injury, and the burns occurred outdoors.
questions.answer_summary: 1: hypovolemic (burn) shock; 2: increased capillary permeability with plasma shifting into the tissues
questions.template: The client is at greatest risk for ___1___ because of ___2___.

options: increased capillary permeability with plasma shifting into the tissues
blanks.correct: increased capillary permeability with plasma shifting into the tissues

questions.stem: Which interventions does the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Burn resuscitation uses isotonic crystalloid titrated to urine output. IV opioids treat pain, because IM absorption is unreliable with poor perfusion. Clients with large burns lose heat rapidly, so warmth is maintained. Tetanus prophylaxis is standard. Ice causes vasoconstriction, deepens the injury, and causes hypothermia.

options.text: Infuse warmed lactated Ringer's per the Parkland formula
Titrate fluids to maintain urine output of about 0.5 mL/kg/hr (30–50 mL/hr)
Administer IV opioids for pain
Keep the client warm and cover burns with clean, dry sheets
Give tetanus prophylaxis if immunization is not current
Apply ice to the burned areas
Administer morphine intramuscularly

questions.stem: Two large-bore IV catheters are in place. Which action should the nurse take first?
questions.rationale: With a patent airway and adequate breathing, circulation is the priority. Fluid resuscitation prevents progression of burn shock and organ damage. Wound care and other measures follow.

options.text: Apply topical antimicrobial cream to all burns
Begin lactated Ringer's infusion at the calculated rate
Administer tetanus toxoid
Obtain photographs of the burns for the record

questions.stem: Eight hours into resuscitation, the nurse reassesses the client. For each finding, indicate whether it shows effective treatment or requires follow-up.
questions.rationale: Adequate urine output, improving hemodynamics, normal mentation, and falling hematocrit show effective resuscitation. Loss of a distal pulse with increasing edema under burned tissue suggests compromised circulation and may require escharotomy.
questions.answer_summary: Effective: urine output 45 mL/hr, HR 104, BP 118/72, alert, Hct 44%. Follow-up: loss of left pedal pulse with increasing edema.

rows.text: Left pedal pulse no longer detectable by Doppler, with increasing leg edema

questions.set_title: Set 11: Fluids, Electrolytes, and Acid-Base Balance
questions.stem: The nurse reviews morning lab results for four clients. Which client should the nurse assess first?
questions.rationale: Hypokalemia with ventricular ectopy increases the risk of lethal dysrhythmias. The other values are mildly abnormal, and those clients are stable. A low total calcium with low albumin may reflect a normal ionized calcium.

options.text: A client with potassium 2.9 mEq/L who has new frequent PVCs on the monitor
A client with sodium 133 mEq/L who is alert and asymptomatic
A client with total calcium 8.4 mg/dL and low albumin
A client with magnesium 1.6 mg/dL who is receiving oral supplements

questions.set_title: Set 11: Fluids, Electrolytes, and Acid-Base Balance
questions.stem: For each IV solution, indicate whether it is isotonic, hypotonic, or hypertonic.
questions.rationale: Isotonic fluids expand intravascular volume. Hypotonic fluids shift water into cells. Hypertonic fluids pull water out of cells. D5W is isotonic in the bag but acts as hypotonic once the dextrose is metabolized.
questions.answer_summary: Isotonic: 0.9% NaCl, LR. Hypotonic: 0.45% NaCl, 0.225% NaCl. Hypertonic: 3% NaCl, D5 0.9% NaCl.

questions.set_title: Set 11: Fluids, Electrolytes, and Acid-Base Balance
questions.stem: A client with a traumatic brain injury and cerebral edema has a new IV fluid prescription. Which solution should the nurse question?
questions.rationale: Hypotonic fluids move water into brain cells and worsen cerebral edema and ICP. Isotonic or hypertonic solutions are used.

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride
0.45% sodium chloride
3% sodium chloride
Lactated Ringer's

questions.set_title: Set 11: Fluids, Electrolytes, and Acid-Base Balance
questions.stem: Which potassium chloride prescription should the nurse question?
questions.rationale: IV potassium is never given by IV push because it can cause cardiac arrest. It is diluted and infused by pump, typically no faster than 10 mEq/hr through a peripheral line unless a policy allows faster central-line rates with cardiac monitoring.

options.text: Potassium chloride 10 mEq in 100 mL over 1 hour via infusion pump
Potassium chloride 20 mEq IV push over 2 minutes
Potassium chloride 20 mEq orally twice daily
Potassium chloride 20 mEq added to 1,000 mL 0.9% sodium chloride at 100 mL/hr

questions.set_title: Set 11: Fluids, Electrolytes, and Acid-Base Balance
questions.stem: Which ECG changes are consistent with hypokalemia?
questions.rationale: Hypokalemia causes flattened or inverted T waves, ST depression, and U waves. Peaked T waves indicate hyperkalemia, and a short QT suggests hypercalcemia.

options.text: Tall, peaked T waves and widened QRS
Flattened T waves and prominent U waves
Shortened QT interval
ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF

questions.set_title: Set 11: Fluids, Electrolytes, and Acid-Base Balance
questions.stem: A client with severe symptomatic hyponatremia is receiving 3% sodium chloride. The sodium was 114 mEq/L at 0800 and is 128 mEq/L at 2000. What should the nurse do?
questions.rationale: Correcting chronic hyponatremia too quickly can cause osmotic demyelination syndrome. The rise is generally limited to about 8–10 mEq/L in 24 hours. A 14 mEq/L rise in 12 hours exceeds safe limits.

options.text: Continue the infusion, since the sodium is still below normal
Notify the provider immediately because the sodium is rising too quickly
Increase the infusion rate
Encourage the client to drink more water

questions.set_title: Set 11: Fluids, Electrolytes, and Acid-Base Balance
questions.stem: An older adult with dementia who has had poor fluid intake has a serum sodium of 156 mEq/L. Which findings does the nurse expect?
questions.rationale: Hypernatremia draws water out of brain cells, causing thirst, dry mucosa, irritability, confusion, and in severe cases seizures. Older adults may have a blunted thirst response.

options.text: Weight gain and bounding pulses
Thirst, dry mucous membranes, restlessness, and confusion
Muscle cramps and U waves
Positive Trousseau's sign

questions.set_title: Set 11: Fluids, Electrolytes, and Acid-Base Balance
questions.stem: Which findings are consistent with hypocalcemia? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Low calcium increases neuromuscular excitability, causing tetany, paresthesias, cramps, hyperactive reflexes, and a prolonged QT. It can progress to laryngospasm and seizures. Diminished reflexes suggest hypercalcemia or hypermagnesemia.

options.text: Carpal spasm when a BP cuff is inflated (Trousseau's sign)
Facial twitching when the facial nerve is tapped (Chvostek's sign)
Numbness and tingling around the mouth
Muscle cramps
Diminished deep tendon reflexes
Prolonged QT interval

questions.set_title: Set 11: Fluids, Electrolytes, and Acid-Base Balance
questions.stem: A client with metastatic breast cancer has a serum calcium of 13.2 mg/dL. Which findings does the nurse expect?
questions.rationale: Hypercalcemia depresses neuromuscular activity (weakness, hyporeflexia, lethargy) and causes constipation, polyuria, kidney stones, and a shortened QT. Treatment includes IV fluids and medications such as bisphosphonates.

options.text: Tetany and seizures
Muscle weakness, constipation, confusion, and polyuria
Hyperactive reflexes
Diarrhea and positive Chvostek's sign

questions.set_title: Set 11: Fluids, Electrolytes, and Acid-Base Balance
questions.stem: A client with alcohol use disorder has persistent hypokalemia despite several days of potassium replacement. Which lab value should the nurse check?
questions.rationale: Hypomagnesemia causes renal potassium wasting and makes hypokalemia difficult to correct. Magnesium must be replaced first. Low magnesium also increases the risk of torsades de pointes.

options.text: Magnesium
Sodium
Chloride
Albumin

questions.set_title: Set 11: Fluids, Electrolytes, and Acid-Base Balance
questions.stem: A client with chronic kidney disease has been taking magnesium-containing laxatives. The serum magnesium is 5.8 mg/dL. Which finding does the nurse expect?
questions.rationale: Magnesium depresses neuromuscular transmission, causing hyporeflexia, lethargy, hypotension, bradycardia, and respiratory depression. IV calcium gluconate is the antidote.

options.text: Hyperactive deep tendon reflexes
Diminished deep tendon reflexes and respiratory depression
Tetany
Tachycardia and hypertension

questions.set_title: Set 11: Fluids, Electrolytes, and Acid-Base Balance
questions.stem: A client with chronic kidney disease has a serum phosphorus of 7.9 mg/dL. Which additional lab finding does the nurse expect?
questions.rationale: Phosphorus and calcium have an inverse relationship. High phosphorus binds calcium and lowers the serum level, which contributes to renal bone disease.

options.text: Elevated calcium
Decreased calcium
Elevated sodium
Decreased potassium

questions.set_title: Set 11: Fluids, Electrolytes, and Acid-Base Balance
questions.stem: A client with severe diarrhea for 4 days has the following ABG: pH 7.30, PaCO2 30 mm Hg, HCO3 15 mEq/L. How should the nurse interpret this?
questions.rationale: The low pH and low HCO3 indicate metabolic acidosis from bicarbonate loss in stool. The low PaCO2 shows respiratory compensation that has not normalized the pH.

options.text: Uncompensated respiratory acidosis
Partially compensated metabolic acidosis
Fully compensated metabolic alkalosis
Partially compensated respiratory alkalosis

questions.set_title: Set 11: Fluids, Electrolytes, and Acid-Base Balance
questions.stem: Which conditions increase a client's risk for metabolic alkalosis? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Loss of gastric acid, diuretic-induced chloride and potassium loss, and excess base intake cause metabolic alkalosis. Diarrhea and DKA cause metabolic acidosis.

options.text: Prolonged vomiting
Continuous nasogastric suctioning
Loop diuretic therapy
Excessive use of antacids
Severe diarrhea
Diabetic ketoacidosis

questions.set_title: Set 11: Fluids, Electrolytes, and Acid-Base Balance
questions.stem: Which findings indicate fluid volume excess? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Excess fluid causes bounding pulses, JVD, pulmonary crackles, rapid weight gain, and edema. Hemodilution lowers hematocrit. A weak pulse and elevated hematocrit suggest fluid volume deficit.

options.text: Bounding pulses
Jugular venous distention
Crackles in the lungs
Weight gain of 2 kg in 2 days
Weak, thready pulse
Elevated hematocrit

questions.set_title: Set 11: Fluids, Electrolytes, and Acid-Base Balance
questions.stem: Which is the most accurate indicator of fluid balance changes in an older adult?
