questions.stem: The nurse notices the power cord on a client's IV pump is frayed. What should the nurse do?
questions.rationale: Damaged electrical equipment can cause shocks or fires. It is removed from use, tagged as defective, and replaced.

options.text: Wrap the frayed area with tape
Remove the pump from service, label it, and report it to biomedical engineering
Continue using it until the shift ends
Unplug it only when the client is sleeping

questions.stem: When should the surgical team perform the "time-out" to prevent wrong-site surgery?
questions.rationale: The Universal Protocol includes preprocedure verification, site marking by the person performing the procedure with the client's involvement, and a time-out immediately before starting.

options.text: The day before surgery
Immediately before the incision, with all team members pausing to confirm the client, procedure, and site
During recovery in the PACU
Only if the surgeon requests it

questions.stem: At the end of surgery, the sponge count is incorrect. What should the circulating nurse do?
questions.rationale: Retained surgical items are preventable sentinel events. A count discrepancy requires immediate communication, a recount, a search, and imaging per policy before the client leaves the OR.

options.text: Document the discrepancy and let the team close the incision
Notify the surgeon, repeat the count, and follow the facility protocol, which may include an x-ray before closure
Assume the sponge was discarded
Ignore it if only one sponge is missing

questions.stem: Which principles of sterile technique should the nurse follow? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Items below the waist, the outer border, anything out of view, and questionable items are considered unsterile. Reaching across the field and turning away risk contamination.

options.text: Only items above waist level are considered sterile
The 1-inch (2.5-cm) border around a sterile field is considered unsterile
Keep the sterile field in view at all times
If sterility is in doubt, consider the item contaminated
Reaching across the sterile field is acceptable if the nurse is careful
Turning your back on a sterile field is acceptable if it is brief

questions.stem: Which interventions help prevent central line-associated bloodstream infection? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Hand hygiene, hub disinfection ("scrub the hub"), proper dressing care with chlorhexidine, and prompt removal reduce CLABSI. Routine catheter replacement and routine antibiotic ointment are not recommended.

options.text: Perform hand hygiene before accessing the line
Scrub the needleless connector hub with antiseptic before each access
Change a transparent dressing at least every 7 days and whenever it is damp, loose, or soiled
Assess daily whether the line is still needed
Replace the central line routinely every 72 hours
Apply antibiotic ointment to the insertion site routinely

questions.stem: Which action related to preventing surgical site infection requires the nurse to intervene?
questions.rationale: Razor shaving causes microabrasions that increase infection risk. If hair removal is needed, clippers are used close to the time of surgery. Glucose control is also part of prevention.

options.text: The client showers with chlorhexidine the night before surgery
An assistive personnel shaves the surgical site with a razor the night before surgery
Prophylactic antibiotics are given within 60 minutes before the incision
Normothermia is maintained during surgery

questions.stem: Several clients arrive with suspected inhalation anthrax after exposure to a suspicious powder. Which precautions does the nurse use?
questions.rationale: Inhalation anthrax is not transmitted person-to-person, so standard precautions are used. Decontamination of exposed people and surfaces follows public health guidance. Smallpox, in contrast, requires airborne and contact precautions.

options.text: Airborne precautions in negative-pressure rooms
Standard precautions, because inhalation anthrax is not spread person-to-person
Droplet precautions only
Strict reverse isolation

questions.stem: Victims of a radiological "dirty bomb" arrive at the emergency department. After life-threatening injuries are addressed, which action is the most effective initial decontamination step?
questions.rationale: Removing outer clothing eliminates most external contamination. Gentle washing with soap and water follows, avoiding skin abrasion, which could allow internal contamination. Life-saving care is never delayed for decontamination.

options.text: Scrubbing the skin vigorously with a brush
Removing the victims' clothing and placing it in labeled bags
Applying lotion to the skin
Waiting for radiation levels to be measured before any action

questions.stem: A container of an unfamiliar cleaning chemical spills in the utility room. What should the nurse do first?
questions.rationale: The SDS provides hazard, PPE, and cleanup information. Securing the area protects staff and clients. Mixing chemicals with water can cause dangerous reactions.

options.text: Wipe it up with paper towels immediately
Keep people away from the area and consult the Safety Data Sheet (SDS) for handling instructions
Pour water on it to dilute it
Leave it for housekeeping without warning anyone

questions.stem: A bag of IV chemotherapy leaks onto the floor. What should the nurse do?
questions.rationale: Hazardous drug spills require spill kits with absorbent materials, chemotherapy-tested gloves, gowns, eye protection, and respiratory protection as indicated. Waste goes in hazardous drug containers, and the spill is reported.

options.text: Clean it with regular paper towels and trash
Obtain the chemotherapy spill kit, put on the required PPE, and contain and clean the spill per protocol
Mop it with the unit mop
Call the family to help

questions.stem: A client who weighs 120 kg and cannot bear weight needs to move from the bed to a chair. What should the nurse do?
questions.rationale: Safe patient handling programs use mechanical lifts for dependent clients to prevent injury to staff and clients. The nurse verifies the lift's weight capacity and sling size.

options.text: Lift the client with one assistant using good body mechanics
Use a mechanical lift with at least two trained staff members
Have the client pivot using a gait belt
Wait until the client can stand

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching an older adult about preventing burns at home. Which instruction is most appropriate?
questions.rationale: Older adults may have reduced sensation and slower reaction times. Lower water heater settings prevent scald injuries. Working smoke and carbon monoxide detectors are essential.

options.text: "Set your water heater to 140°F (60°C)."
"Set your water heater to 120°F (49°C) or lower and test the water before bathing."
"Use a heating pad on high while sleeping."
"Remove smoke detector batteries to prevent false alarms."

questions.stem: A visitor in the hallway becomes enraged and pulls out a knife. What should the nurse do first?
questions.rationale: Staff safety comes first. The nurse leaves the area, alerts others, and activates the emergency response. Nurses do not attempt to disarm someone.

options.text: Try to take the knife away
Move away to a safe location, keep others away, and call security or activate the facility's emergency code
Argue with the visitor to calm them
Continue with client care

questions.stem: A client is colonized with Candida auris. Which action is most important to prevent its spread?
questions.rationale: C. auris is a multidrug-resistant fungus that persists on surfaces and spreads in healthcare settings. Contact precautions and effective disinfectants (such as those on EPA List P) are required, even for colonized clients.

options.text: Standard precautions only
Contact precautions and cleaning with a disinfectant proven effective against C. auris
Droplet precautions only
No special precautions are needed for colonization

questions.stem: A newly hired nurse asks why hepatitis B vaccination is recommended. What is the best response?
questions.rationale: Healthcare workers with potential blood exposure should complete the hepatitis B series and have post-vaccination antibody testing. Vaccination does not replace standard precautions.

options.text: "It protects against hepatitis A and C."
"It protects against a bloodborne infection you could be exposed to through needlesticks or splashes, and a titer can confirm immunity."
"It is only needed for surgical staff."
"It replaces the need for standard precautions."

questions.stem: A client with dementia cannot be found on the unit during the 1400 rounds. What should the nurse do first?
questions.rationale: A missing client with cognitive impairment is an emergency with a high risk of harm. The facility's search protocol is activated immediately.

options.text: Wait 1 hour to see if the client returns
Immediately notify the charge nurse and initiate the facility's missing-client code and search
Call the family and ask if the client went home
Document the absence in the chart

questions.stem: When the nurse scans a client's medication, the bar-code system displays a "wrong patient" alert. What should the nurse do?
questions.rationale: Bar-code alerts are safety checks. Workarounds and overrides without investigation cause medication errors. The nurse verifies the client, order, and medication before proceeding.

options.text: Override the alert and give the medication
Stop, do not give the medication, and investigate the discrepancy
Scan the medication again until the alert clears
Give the medication and report the alert later

questions.stem: Highlight (circle) the findings that require immediate follow-up.
questions.rationale: An acute change in cognition with agitation suggests delirium and creates an immediate fall and injury risk. Urinary retention, hypoxemia, fever, and an anticholinergic medication are likely causes. BP is stable.
questions.answer_summary: Acute disorientation; climbing over rails; pulling at IV; bladder 650 mL; SpO2 91%; T 100.6°F; diphenhydramine given

passage_segments.text: Oriented to person only (yesterday oriented x3)
Trying to climb over the side rails

questions.correct_text: Acute disorientation; climbing over rails; pulling at IV; bladder 650 mL; SpO2 91%; T 100.6°F; diphenhydramine given

questions.stem: For each factor contributing to this client's delirium and fall risk, indicate whether it is modifiable or nonmodifiable.
questions.rationale: Delirium prevention targets modifiable causes: medications (especially anticholinergics), retention, hypoxia, infection, pain, and sensory deprivation. Age and baseline cognitive impairment increase risk but cannot be changed.
questions.answer_summary: Modifiable: diphenhydramine, urinary retention, hypoxemia, sensory aids not in use. Nonmodifiable: age, preexisting cognitive impairment.

rows.text: Eyeglasses and hearing aids not in use

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.rationale: Acute onset of fluctuating confusion after surgery, with identifiable triggers, indicates delirium rather than progression of dementia. Climbing over rails after hip surgery risks falls, fractures, dislocation, and device removal.
questions.answer_summary: 1: postoperative delirium; 2: falls and injury, including dislodging the IV and hip dislocation
questions.template: The client is most likely experiencing ___1___, and the priority is preventing ___2___.

options: falls and injury, including dislodging the IV and hip dislocation
blanks.correct: falls and injury, including dislodging the IV and hip dislocation

questions.stem: Which interventions should the nurse implement? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Supervision, sensory aids, reorientation, a low bed with an alarm, and treating underlying causes (catheterization, oxygen, evaluating for infection, stopping anticholinergics) are evidence-based. Four raised rails increase fall severity when clients climb over them. More anticholinergics worsen delirium, and restraints are a last resort.

options.text: Stay with the client or arrange continuous observation
Put on the client's eyeglasses and hearing aids and reorient calmly
Lower the bed to the lowest position and activate a bed alarm
Contact the provider about urinary retention, low SpO2, fever, and the diphenhydramine
Raise all four side rails
Give another dose of diphenhydramine to help the client sleep
Apply wrist restraints as the first intervention

questions.stem: The nurse finds the client with one leg over the side rail. What should the nurse do first?
questions.rationale: Immediate physical safety comes first. The nurse does not leave a client at imminent risk of falling. After the client is safe, the nurse notifies the provider and addresses the causes.

options.text: Leave to call the provider
Stay with the client, lower the bed, guide the client safely back, and call for assistance
Apply soft wrist restraints
Administer PRN haloperidol

questions.stem: By morning, the nurse evaluates the plan. For each finding, indicate whether it shows the plan was effective or requires follow-up.
questions.rationale: Improved cognition, oxygenation, and bladder emptying, with no injury, show effective care. A disabled alarm is a safety gap to address with staff. The provider should be asked to discontinue diphenhydramine to prevent recurrence.
questions.answer_summary: Effective: improved orientation with sensory aids, SpO2 94%, retention relieved, no falls. Follow-up: alarm turned off, diphenhydramine still active.

rows.text: Oriented to person and place, wearing glasses and hearing aids
650 mL drained by straight catheterization; client now resting
Bed alarm found turned off at 0500 by an unknown person
Diphenhydramine still listed as an active PRN on the MAR

questions.stem: The nurse in an eye and ear clinic receives four telephone messages. Which client should the nurse call back first?
questions.rationale: Flashes, floaters, and a curtain-like shadow indicate retinal detachment, which requires emergency treatment to preserve vision. Mild scratchiness after cataract surgery is expected.

options.text: A client who reports sudden flashes of light, new floaters, and a "curtain" coming down over the vision in one eye
A client 1 day after cataract surgery who reports mild scratchiness
A client whose hearing aid is whistling
A client with Ménière's disease requesting a refill of meclizine

questions.stem: A client arrives with sudden severe eye pain, blurred vision with halos around lights, nausea, and a firm, reddened eye. Which prescription should the nurse question?
questions.rationale: These findings suggest acute angle-closure glaucoma. Atropine dilates the pupil, which can further block aqueous outflow and raise intraocular pressure. The other drugs lower intraocular pressure.

options.text: Timolol ophthalmic drops
Acetazolamide IV
Atropine ophthalmic drops
Pilocarpine ophthalmic drops

questions.stem: The nurse is providing discharge teaching after cataract surgery. Which client statement indicates a need for further teaching?
questions.rationale: Bending at the waist, straining, and heavy lifting raise intraocular pressure. The client should bend at the knees or use slip-on shoes. Sudden pain or vision loss may indicate hemorrhage, infection, or increased pressure.

options.text: "I'll wear the eye shield at night."
"I'll bend over at the waist to tie my shoes."
"I'll call if I have sudden eye pain or decreased vision."
"I'll avoid lifting anything heavy for now."

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client with Ménière's disease. Which instruction is appropriate?
questions.rationale: Lying still reduces vertigo and prevents falls. Limiting sodium, caffeine, and alcohol can reduce endolymphatic fluid and the frequency of attacks. Driving is unsafe during episodes.

options.text: "Follow a high-sodium diet to maintain fluid balance."
"During a vertigo attack, lie still in a safe position and keep your eyes fixed on a stationary object."
"Increase caffeine intake to improve alertness."
"Drive as usual during attacks."

questions.stem: A client reports sharp chest pain that worsens when lying down and when taking a deep breath. The pain improves when sitting up and leaning forward. Which additional finding does the nurse expect?
questions.rationale: Acute pericarditis causes positional, pleuritic chest pain and a scratchy friction rub, often with diffuse ST elevation. Treatment typically includes NSAIDs and colchicine.

options.text: A pericardial friction rub
An S4 heart sound only
Unilateral leg swelling
Tearing back pain radiating to the abdomen

questions.stem: A client with known severe aortic stenosis is being followed in a cardiology clinic. Which symptom should the nurse instruct the client to report immediately?
questions.rationale: Exertional syncope, angina, and heart failure symptoms in aortic stenosis indicate severe obstruction and poor prognosis without valve replacement.

options.text: Occasional mild fatigue in the evening
Fainting or near-fainting during exertion
Increased appetite
A mild seasonal cough

questions.stem: A client with Raynaud's phenomenon asks how to prevent attacks. Which instruction should the nurse give?
questions.rationale: Cold exposure, stress, smoking, and caffeine trigger vasospasm. Staying warm, including the body core, and wearing gloves (even when handling cold items from the freezer) prevent attacks.

options.text: "Hold ice packs to toughen your fingers."
"Keep your hands and body warm, wear gloves in cold places, and avoid smoking."
"Drink more caffeine."
"Soak your fingers in cold water daily."

questions.stem: A client is 1 day postoperative after a right pneumonectomy. How should the nurse position the client?
questions.rationale: After pneumonectomy, lying on the operative side or back allows the remaining lung to expand fully and helps prevent mediastinal shift. Complete side-lying on the nonoperative side is usually avoided.

options.text: Completely on the left side
Supine or partially turned onto the right (operative) side, as prescribed
Prone
Trendelenburg

questions.stem: A client with obstructive sleep apnea is prescribed CPAP. Which statement indicates understanding?
questions.rationale: CPAP keeps the airway open only while it is worn, so consistent nightly use is needed. Sedatives worsen airway collapse. Weight loss and avoiding alcohol before bed also help.

options.text: "I'll use CPAP only when I feel tired."
"I'll wear the CPAP every night, including during naps, and clean the mask and tubing regularly."
"I'll take a sleeping pill so I can tolerate the mask."
"CPAP will cure my sleep apnea in a few weeks."

questions.stem: A client with confirmed influenza asks about oseltamivir. What is the nurse's best response?
questions.rationale: Neuraminidase inhibitors shorten illness and reduce complications when started early, ideally within 48 hours. High-risk and hospitalized clients may benefit even later. It does not replace vaccination.

options.text: "It is most effective when started within 48 hours of symptom onset."
"It cures influenza within 24 hours."
"It replaces the need for a yearly flu vaccine."
"It works only if started after a week of symptoms."

questions.stem: A client with trigeminal neuralgia has severe facial pain triggered by eating. Which intervention is most appropriate?
questions.rationale: Temperature extremes, chewing, and touch can trigger attacks. Soft, lukewarm foods and chewing on the unaffected side reduce triggers. Carbamazepine is commonly prescribed.

options.text: Serve very hot foods to relax the muscles
Offer lukewarm, soft foods and encourage chewing on the unaffected side
Encourage vigorous brushing of the teeth
Apply an ice pack to the face before meals

questions.stem: A client with advanced amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) has increasing difficulty swallowing and a weak cough. Which is the nurse's priority concern?
questions.rationale: ALS progressively weakens bulbar and respiratory muscles, increasing the risk of aspiration pneumonia and respiratory failure. These are the leading causes of death. Cognition is often preserved.

options.text: Impaired verbal communication
Aspiration and respiratory compromise
Disturbed body image
Constipation

questions.stem: A client whose father has Huntington's disease asks about the chance of inheriting it. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
questions.rationale: Huntington's disease is autosomal dominant. Genetic counseling is recommended before and after testing because of the significant psychological and family implications.

options.text: "There is no genetic risk."
"It is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, so each child of an affected parent has a 50% chance of inheriting the gene."
"Only sons can inherit it."
"The chance is 25%."

questions.stem: A client with immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) has a platelet count of 22,000/mm³. Which instruction should the nurse include?
questions.rationale: In ITP, autoantibodies destroy platelets. Avoiding antiplatelet drugs and trauma reduces bleeding risk. Corticosteroids are often the first-line treatment.

options.text: "Take ibuprofen for headaches."
"Avoid aspirin and NSAIDs, use a soft toothbrush, and report any bleeding."
"Take up contact sports to strengthen your body."
"Floss vigorously twice a day."

questions.stem: A client with polycythemia vera has a hematocrit of 58%. Which complication is the nurse most concerned about?
questions.rationale: Excess red cells increase blood viscosity and the risk of clotting. Treatment includes therapeutic phlebotomy, hydration, and low-dose aspirin as prescribed. Itching after warm baths is a common symptom.

options.text: Hypotension from anemia
Thrombosis such as stroke, MI, or DVT
Hypoglycemia
Hyperkalemia only

questions.stem: A client has an ileal conduit after cystectomy for bladder cancer. Which finding should the nurse report?
questions.rationale: A dusky or dark stoma indicates impaired blood flow. Continuous urine flow and mucus (from the intestinal segment) are expected with an ileal conduit.

options.text: Continuous flow of urine into the pouch
Mucus threads in the urine
A dark purple stoma
A moist, pink stoma

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a 20-year-old male about testicular self-examination. Which instruction is correct?
questions.rationale: Testicular cancer is most common in young men. Warmth relaxes the scrotum, making it easier to feel changes. Most cancers present as a painless lump.

options.text: "Perform the exam once a year."
"Examine each testicle monthly, ideally after a warm shower, and report any lump, swelling, or heaviness."
"Only examine if you have pain."
"Squeeze the testicles firmly to check for pain."

questions.stem: A client is treated for chlamydia with a single dose of azithromycin. Which instruction should the nurse include?
questions.rationale: Abstaining for 7 days and until partners are treated prevents reinfection. Retesting in about 3 months is recommended because reinfection is common. Doxycycline is now the preferred first-line treatment in most cases.

options.text: "You can resume sexual activity tonight."
"Avoid sexual activity for 7 days after treatment and until your partners are treated, and consider retesting in about 3 months."
"Your partners don't need treatment."
"You'll be immune to chlamydia now."

questions.stem: A client is brought to the emergency department after using cocaine. Which findings does the nurse expect?
questions.rationale: Cocaine causes sympathetic stimulation, which can lead to chest pain, MI, dysrhythmias, stroke, and seizures. Benzodiazepines are commonly used to control agitation and sympathetic effects.

options.text: Pinpoint pupils, bradycardia, and hypothermia
Dilated pupils, tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, and agitation
Slow, shallow respirations and sedation
Hypotension and constricted pupils

questions.stem: Highlight (circle) the findings that require follow-up.
questions.rationale: Regular contractions with cervical change before 37 weeks indicate preterm labor, and a positive fetal fibronectin supports it. The UTI may be a trigger, and unknown GBS status requires prophylaxis. The FHR tracing and BP are reassuring.
questions.answer_summary: Contractions every 5 minutes; cervical change; positive fetal fibronectin; positive urinalysis; unknown GBS status
questions.correct_text: Contractions every 5 minutes; cervical change; positive fetal fibronectin; positive urinalysis; unknown GBS status

questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it supports a diagnosis of preterm labor or reflects reassuring fetal status.
questions.rationale: Preterm labor is diagnosed by regular contractions with cervical change before 37 weeks. A baseline of 110–160, moderate variability, and accelerations indicate a well-oxygenated fetus (Category I tracing).
questions.answer_summary: Preterm labor: regular contractions, cervical change, positive fFN. Reassuring: normal baseline, moderate variability, accelerations.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.rationale: Braxton Hicks contractions do not cause cervical change. There is no bleeding, uterine rigidity, or hypertension to suggest abruption or preeclampsia. Genitourinary infections are a known trigger of preterm labor.
questions.answer_summary: 1: preterm labor; 2: a urinary tract infection
questions.template: The client is most likely experiencing ___1___, possibly triggered by ___2___.

questions.stem: Which interventions does the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Before 34 weeks, corticosteroids reduce neonatal respiratory distress and other complications. Magnesium before 32 weeks reduces the risk of cerebral palsy. Short-term tocolysis buys time for steroids, and GBS prophylaxis is given when status is unknown in preterm labor. The FDA warns against prolonged terbutaline use, and prolonged bed rest is not recommended.

options.text: Betamethasone IM, two doses 24 hours apart
Magnesium sulfate IV for fetal neuroprotection
Short-term tocolysis (such as nifedipine) to allow time for corticosteroids
IV penicillin G for GBS prophylaxis
Antibiotic treatment for the UTI
Oral terbutaline for long-term maintenance tocolysis
Strict bed rest for the remainder of pregnancy

questions.stem: The nurse has prescriptions for all of the anticipated interventions. Which medication has the greatest impact on neonatal outcomes if delivery occurs?
questions.rationale: Antenatal corticosteroids accelerate fetal lung maturity and reduce neonatal respiratory distress, intraventricular hemorrhage, and mortality. They are most effective 24 hours to 7 days after the first dose, so timely administration is critical.

options.text: Betamethasone
Acetaminophen
Nifedipine
Docusate

questions.stem: Twenty-four hours later, the nurse reassesses the client. For each finding, indicate whether it shows the plan was effective or requires follow-up.
questions.rationale: Decreased contractions, a completed steroid course, and a reassuring tracing show success. Respiratory depression with absent reflexes suggests magnesium toxicity. Crackles and hypoxemia suggest pulmonary edema, a known complication of magnesium and tocolytic therapy.
questions.answer_summary: Effective: fewer contractions, completed steroid course, reassuring FHR, adequate urine output. Follow-up: RR 10 with absent reflexes, new crackles with SpO2 90%.

rows.text: Second dose of betamethasone given on time
New crackles with SpO2 90% on room air

questions.stem: The nurse on a urology unit receives report on four clients. Which client should the nurse assess first?
questions.rationale: Absent nephrostomy drainage with new flank pain suggests obstruction or dislodgement, which can cause hydronephrosis and kidney damage. Mild hematuria after lithotripsy is expected.

options.text: A client with a nephrostomy tube that has had no drainage for 2 hours who reports new severe flank pain
A client 4 hours after shock wave lithotripsy with pink-tinged urine
A client with polycystic kidney disease requesting a BP medication refill
A client with benign prostatic hyperplasia who reports nocturia

questions.stem: A client with atrial fibrillation of about 1 week's duration is scheduled for elective synchronized cardioversion. Which finding is most important for the nurse to verify before the procedure?
questions.rationale: Atrial fibrillation lasting more than 48 hours can form atrial clots that may embolize when sinus rhythm is restored. Adequate anticoagulation or a TEE is required. The client should also be NPO, and potassium should be normal.

options.text: The client ate a light breakfast
The client has received adequate anticoagulation or had a transesophageal echocardiogram to rule out atrial thrombus
The client took their digoxin this morning
The client's potassium is 3.1 mEq/L

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client with a new implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD). Which instruction is correct?
questions.rationale: A single shock with no symptoms should be reported. Repeated shocks or symptoms such as chest pain or fainting require emergency care. A person touching the client may feel a tingle but will not be harmed.

options.text: "If the device shocks you once and you feel fine afterward, contact your cardiology provider. If you receive multiple shocks or feel unwell, call 911."
"Ignore shocks unless you have more than five in a day."
"Avoid all physical activity for life."
"Family members will be seriously injured if they touch you during a shock."

questions.stem: The nurse is checking the cuff pressure of a client's cuffed tracheostomy tube. Which range is generally recommended?
questions.rationale: A cuff pressure of about 20–30 cm H2O seals the airway to reduce aspiration without compressing tracheal capillaries. Excessive pressure can cause tracheal ischemia and stenosis.

options.text: 5–10 cm H2O
20–30 cm H2O
40–50 cm H2O
60–70 cm H2O

questions.stem: A client arrives with severe, one-sided pain around the eye, tearing, and nasal congestion that began 15 minutes ago. The client has a history of cluster headaches. Which treatment does the nurse anticipate first?
questions.rationale: High-flow oxygen is a first-line abortive therapy for cluster headaches and often relieves pain within about 15 minutes. Subcutaneous or intranasal triptans are also used.

options.text: 100% oxygen at 12–15 L/min by nonrebreather mask
Oral ibuprofen
A warm compress to the eye
IV fluids only

questions.stem: A client with resistant hypertension is being evaluated for primary hyperaldosteronism. Which lab finding supports this diagnosis?
questions.rationale: Excess aldosterone causes sodium and water retention (hypertension) and potassium excretion (hypokalemia). Treatment may include surgery or an aldosterone antagonist such as spironolactone.

options.text: Hyperkalemia
Hypokalemia
Hypoglycemia
Hypercalcemia

questions.stem: A client with type 2 diabetes takes empagliflozin and is scheduled for elective surgery. Which information should the nurse include?
questions.rationale: SGLT2 inhibitors can cause euglycemic DKA, especially during fasting, surgery, or illness, so they are typically held about 3 days before surgery. They increase glucose excretion in the urine, which raises the risk of genital yeast infections.

options.text: "Take a double dose the morning of surgery."
"This medication is usually stopped several days before surgery because it can cause ketoacidosis even with near-normal glucose levels."
"It lowers blood sugar by increasing insulin release."
"It prevents urinary tract infections."

questions.stem: A client with an insulin pump notices the infusion tubing was disconnected for several hours overnight. Why is the nurse most concerned?
questions.rationale: Because pumps contain only rapid- or short-acting insulin, there is no long-acting insulin reserve. Interruption can lead to DKA within hours. Clients check glucose and ketones and have a backup plan.

options.text: Pumps use long-acting insulin, so glucose will drop
Pumps deliver only rapid-acting insulin, so the client can develop hyperglycemia and ketoacidosis quickly
Disconnection has no effect
The client will develop hypoglycemia

questions.stem: A client newly diagnosed with chronic hepatitis C asks about treatment. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
questions.rationale: Direct-acting antivirals cure more than 95% of hepatitis C infections. There is no vaccine for hepatitis C. Clients should avoid alcohol and be vaccinated against hepatitis A and B.

options.text: "There is no effective treatment."
"Direct-acting antiviral medications taken for 8–12 weeks cure most people."
"A vaccine will cure the infection."
"Treatment is only for people with liver failure."

questions.stem: An 80-year-old client is completing a bowel preparation for colonoscopy. Which finding is most important for the nurse to report?
questions.rationale: Bowel preparation can cause dehydration and electrolyte imbalances, especially in older adults. Watery, clear stools indicate an effective prep. Red and purple liquids are avoided because they can look like blood.

options.text: Frequent watery stools
Dizziness when standing, dry mouth, and decreased urine output
Clear yellow liquid stools
Mild abdominal fullness

questions.stem: Which findings does the nurse expect in a client with an early mechanical small bowel obstruction?
questions.rationale: Early obstruction causes cramping pain, vomiting, and high-pitched bowel sounds as the bowel works against the blockage. Later, bowel sounds may become absent. Treatment includes NG decompression, IV fluids, and electrolyte correction.

options.text: Absent bowel sounds and a rigid abdomen
Colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, distention, and high-pitched bowel sounds
Diarrhea with blood
Left lower quadrant pain relieved by defecation

questions.stem: A client with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency asks what to avoid. Which items should the nurse include?
questions.rationale: Oxidative stress from fava beans, certain medications, and infections can trigger hemolytic anemia in G6PD deficiency.

options.text: Dairy products
Fava beans and certain drugs such as sulfonamides and primaquine
All fruits
Acetaminophen at any dose

questions.stem: Which lab pattern does the nurse expect in a client with aplastic anemia?
questions.rationale: Aplastic anemia is bone marrow failure affecting all cell lines. Care includes infection and bleeding precautions, transfusions, immunosuppression, or stem cell transplant.

options.text: Elevated WBC, normal hemoglobin, and elevated platelets
Low WBC, low hemoglobin, and low platelets (pancytopenia)
Isolated low platelets
Elevated hemoglobin

questions.stem: A client is being discharged after a total laryngectomy. Which instruction should the nurse include?
questions.rationale: After total laryngectomy, the client breathes only through the neck stoma. Water entering the stoma can go directly into the lungs. Humidification replaces the nose's warming and moistening function. Speech options include an electrolarynx or a tracheoesophageal prosthesis.

options.text: "You'll be able to speak normally in a few days."
"Protect your stoma with a shower shield, use humidification, and avoid swimming."
"Keep the stoma tightly covered with plastic wrap."
"You can still breathe through your nose and mouth."

questions.stem: A client at 34 weeks' gestation with preeclampsia reports right upper quadrant pain and nausea. Which lab findings suggest HELLP syndrome?
questions.rationale: HELLP stands for Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, and Low Platelets. It is a severe form of preeclampsia that can cause liver rupture, DIC, and death, and delivery is the definitive treatment.

options.text: Elevated platelets and low liver enzymes
Hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets
Low hemoglobin with normal liver enzymes only
Elevated glucose and ketones

questions.stem: During delivery, the fetal head emerges and then retracts against the perineum ("turtle sign"). Which action should the nurse take?
questions.rationale: McRoberts positioning and suprapubic pressure help dislodge the anterior shoulder. Fundal pressure worsens impaction and increases the risk of uterine rupture and brachial plexus injury.

options.text: Apply fundal pressure
Assist with the McRoberts maneuver (sharply flexing the client's thighs onto the abdomen) and apply suprapubic pressure as directed
Push the fetal head back into the vagina
Place the client in Trendelenburg position

questions.stem: A client had a suction evacuation for a hydatidiform mole. Which statement indicates understanding of follow-up care?
questions.rationale: Serial hCG levels are monitored until normal to detect persistent disease or choriocarcinoma. Pregnancy would raise hCG and interfere with monitoring, so reliable contraception is needed.

options.text: "I can try to get pregnant again right away."
"I'll have regular hCG blood tests and use reliable contraception during the follow-up period."
"I don't need any follow-up."
"A rising hCG level is a good sign."

questions.stem: A client with opioid use disorder is starting buprenorphine. Which timing is most important for the first dose?
questions.rationale: Buprenorphine is a partial agonist with high receptor affinity. Given too early, it displaces full agonists and precipitates withdrawal. Waiting for moderate withdrawal prevents this.

options.text: Immediately after the last opioid use
When the client shows objective signs of moderate withdrawal (for example, by the Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale)
Only after 2 weeks of abstinence
At the same time as a full-agonist opioid

questions.stem: A client is admitted after an overdose of amitriptyline. The ECG shows a widening QRS complex. Which medication does the nurse anticipate?
questions.rationale: Tricyclic toxicity blocks sodium channels, causing QRS widening, dysrhythmias, seizures, and hypotension. Sodium bicarbonate counteracts the sodium channel blockade. Anticholinergic effects are also common.

options.text: Sodium bicarbonate IV
Flumazenil
Physostigmine as first-line
Naloxone

questions.stem: Highlight (circle) the findings that require immediate follow-up.
questions.rationale: Tearing pain, unequal arm pressures and pulses, and a new aortic regurgitation murmur are hallmarks of aortic dissection. Tachycardia increases shear stress on the aortic wall. The lungs, temperature, and SpO2 are normal.
questions.answer_summary: Tearing pain to the back; BP difference between arms; new diastolic murmur; weaker left radial pulse; HR 112

passage_segments.text: BP difference of 46 mm Hg between the arms

questions.correct_text: Tearing pain to the back; BP difference between arms; new diastolic murmur; weaker left radial pulse; HR 112

questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it more strongly suggests aortic dissection or acute myocardial infarction.
questions.rationale: Distinguishing the two is critical, because anticoagulants and thrombolytics used for MI can be fatal in dissection. A dissection can occasionally involve a coronary artery and cause MI findings.
questions.answer_summary: Dissection: tearing back pain, arm BP difference, aortic regurgitation murmur, unequal pulses. MI: ST elevation, crushing pressure with troponin rise.

rows.text: Sudden tearing pain radiating to the back
Significant BP difference between the arms
New diastolic murmur of aortic regurgitation
ST elevation in two contiguous leads
Crushing substernal pressure with elevated troponin

questions.stem: Complete the sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.rationale: Type A dissections involve the ascending aorta and carry high early mortality without surgery. They can rupture into the pericardium, occlude branch arteries, or cause acute aortic regurgitation.
questions.answer_summary: 1: type A (ascending) aortic dissection requiring emergency surgery; 2: aortic rupture, cardiac tamponade, or organ malperfusion
questions.template: The client has a ___1___. The greatest immediate threat is ___2___.

options: type A (ascending) aortic dissection requiring emergency surgery
type B dissection managed only with oral medications
blanks.correct: type A (ascending) aortic dissection requiring emergency surgery

options: aortic rupture, cardiac tamponade, or organ malperfusion
blanks.correct: aortic rupture, cardiac tamponade, or organ malperfusion

questions.stem: Which interventions does the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Management is rapid heart rate and BP control (a beta blocker first, then a vasodilator if needed), pain control that also reduces sympathetic surge, close monitoring, blood availability, and emergency surgery. Thrombolytics, aspirin, and heparin can cause catastrophic bleeding.

options.text: IV esmolol or labetalol to lower HR (goal about 60/min or less) and systolic BP (goal about 100–120 mm Hg)
IV opioid analgesia
Preparation for emergency surgical repair
Two large-bore IVs and type and crossmatch
Arterial line for continuous BP monitoring
IV alteplase
Chewable aspirin 325 mg and a heparin infusion

questions.stem: Which medication should the nurse administer first?
questions.rationale: A beta blocker is given first to reduce heart rate and the force of ejection (shear stress). Starting a vasodilator alone first can cause reflex tachycardia and extend the dissection. Antiplatelet and anticoagulant drugs are contraindicated.

options.text: Chewable aspirin 325 mg
IV esmolol
Heparin IV bolus
Nitroprusside infusion before any beta blocker

questions.stem: While the client awaits transfer to the OR, the nurse reassesses. For each finding, indicate whether it shows the treatment was effective or requires immediate follow-up.
questions.rationale: Achieved HR and BP targets, pain control, and adequate renal perfusion show effective initial management. A pulseless limb indicates branch artery malperfusion. Hypotension with JVD and muffled heart sounds suggests rupture into the pericardium, which is immediately life-threatening.
questions.answer_summary: Effective: HR 58, SBP 112, pain 3/10, urine output 50 mL/hr. Follow-up: new limb ischemia, signs of cardiac tamponade.

rows.text: New pallor and absent pulse in the left foot
Sudden BP 78/40 mm Hg with distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds

questions.stem: The emergency department nurse is assigned four new clients. Which client should the nurse assess first?
questions.rationale: Rapid atrial fibrillation with hypotension and chest pain indicates hemodynamic instability, which requires immediate intervention. The other clients are stable.

options.text: A client with new-onset atrial fibrillation, HR 152/min, BP 78/40 mm Hg, and chest pain
A client with a laceration on the forearm with controlled bleeding
A client with a sprained ankle rating pain 6/10
A client with a urinary tract infection and a temperature of 100.4°F (38°C)

questions.stem: A client with supraventricular tachycardia at 190/min becomes confused, with BP 76/42 mm Hg. Vagal maneuvers and adenosine have not been attempted. Which intervention does the nurse anticipate first?
questions.rationale: Tachycardia with signs of instability (hypotension, altered mental status) and a pulse is treated with synchronized cardioversion. Synchronization avoids delivering a shock during the vulnerable T wave. Defibrillation is for pulseless rhythms such as VF.

options.text: Oral metoprolol
Synchronized cardioversion
Unsynchronized defibrillation
Observation for 30 minutes

questions.stem: A client in cardiac arrest has asystole on the monitor, confirmed in two leads. Which action is appropriate?
questions.rationale: Asystole is not a shockable rhythm. Management is CPR, epinephrine every 3–5 minutes, and identifying reversible causes (the H's and T's).

options.text: Deliver a defibrillation shock immediately
Continue high-quality CPR and administer epinephrine as prescribed
Perform synchronized cardioversion
Administer adenosine

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client who had a heart transplant 2 months ago. Which statement indicates understanding?
questions.rationale: The transplanted heart is denervated, so heart rate increases slowly in response to circulating catecholamines rather than nerve signals. Prolonged warm-up and cool-down periods are needed. Endomyocardial biopsies monitor for rejection, and immunosuppression is lifelong.

options.text: "My heart rate will increase immediately when I start exercising."
"I'll warm up gradually before exercise and cool down slowly, because my new heart takes longer to respond."
"I won't need any more heart biopsies."
"I can stop my immunosuppressants once I feel well."

questions.stem: A client is 8 hours postoperative after a femoral-popliteal bypass graft. Which finding requires immediate action?
questions.rationale: A diminishing pulse and cooler extremity suggest graft occlusion, which requires emergency intervention. Mild edema is common after revascularization as blood flow returns.

options.text: Incisional pain rated 4/10
Pedal pulse present by Doppler but weaker than 1 hour ago, with a cooler foot
Mild swelling of the operative leg
Serosanguineous drainage on the dressing

questions.stem: The nurse is assisting with chest tube removal. What should the nurse instruct the client to do as the tube is pulled?
questions.rationale: Holding the breath or performing a Valsalva maneuver increases intrathoracic pressure and prevents air from entering the pleural space during removal. An occlusive dressing is applied immediately, and a chest x-ray may follow.

options.text: Breathe in and out rapidly
Take a deep breath and hold it or bear down (Valsalva), as directed by the provider
Cough forcefully
Lie flat and relax completely

questions.stem: Which situation is most likely to cause a falsely high pulse oximetry reading?
questions.rationale: Standard oximeters read carboxyhemoglobin as oxyhemoglobin, overestimating saturation. Poor perfusion, cold extremities, motion, and dark nail polish usually cause inaccurate or low readings. Oximeters may also overestimate saturation in clients with darker skin.

options.text: Warm fingers with good perfusion
Carbon monoxide poisoning
Clean, unpolished fingernails
A client at rest

questions.stem: A client with a severe brain injury is being evaluated for brain death. Which action by the nurse is correct regarding organ donation?
questions.rationale: Federal regulations require timely referral of imminent deaths to the organ procurement organization. Trained requesters approach families, which respects the family and improves consent rates.

options.text: Ask the family about organ donation before the evaluation is complete
Notify the organ procurement organization according to hospital policy and allow its trained staff to approach the family
Decide that the client is not a candidate because of age
Wait until after the ventilator is removed to discuss donation

questions.stem: A client had 20 minutes of right arm weakness and slurred speech yesterday, which resolved completely. Which statement by the nurse is most accurate?
questions.rationale: TIAs signal a high short-term risk of stroke. Urgent evaluation (imaging, carotid studies, cardiac monitoring) and prevention measures, such as antiplatelet therapy and risk factor control, are needed.

options.text: "Since the symptoms went away, no follow-up is needed."
"This may have been a transient ischemic attack, which is a warning sign for stroke and needs urgent evaluation."
"This was probably anxiety."
"You should wait for it to happen again before seeing a provider."

questions.stem: A client develops permanent hypoparathyroidism after neck surgery. Which long-term treatment does the nurse anticipate?
questions.rationale: Without parathyroid hormone, calcium levels fall. Oral calcium and activated vitamin D maintain calcium levels. The client is taught to recognize tingling and muscle cramps, which suggest hypocalcemia.

options.text: Potassium supplements
Calcium supplements and active vitamin D (calcitriol)
Levothyroxine only
A low-calcium diet

questions.stem: A client is recovering from a bilateral adrenalectomy for Cushing's syndrome. Which medication will the client need long term?
questions.rationale: Removing both adrenal glands eliminates cortisol and aldosterone production. Lifelong hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone replacement is needed, with stress dosing during illness.

options.text: Insulin
Glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement
Levothyroxine
Potassium chloride only

questions.stem: While a central venous catheter is being changed, a client suddenly becomes short of breath, has chest pain, and becomes hypotensive. The nurse suspects an air embolism. What should the nurse do first?
questions.rationale: Clamping stops more air from entering. Left lateral Trendelenburg positioning traps air in the right atrium away from the pulmonary outflow tract. The nurse then gives oxygen and notifies the provider.

options.text: Place the client in high-Fowler's position
Clamp the catheter and place the client on the left side in Trendelenburg position
Flush the catheter with saline
Remove the catheter completely

questions.stem: A client returns from a percutaneous kidney biopsy. Which finding should the nurse report immediately?
questions.rationale: Bleeding is the major complication after kidney biopsy. Gross hematuria with clots, increasing flank pain, and hypotension suggest hemorrhage. Bed rest and frequent vital signs are standard after the procedure.

options.text: Mild soreness at the site
Gross hematuria with clots, flank pain, and a falling BP
Slightly pink urine on the first void
The client asks for food

questions.stem: A client with metastatic prostate cancer reports worsening back pain for a week and new leg weakness. What should the nurse do?
questions.rationale: New or worsening back pain with neurological deficits in a client with cancer suggests metastatic spinal cord compression. Prompt corticosteroids, imaging, and radiation or surgery are needed to preserve function.

options.text: Give a PRN analgesic and reassess tomorrow
Report the findings immediately because they suggest spinal cord compression, an oncologic emergency
Encourage the client to walk more
Apply heat to the back

questions.stem: A client is starting oral capecitabine at home. Which instruction should the nurse include?
questions.rationale: Oral chemotherapy is hazardous. Safe handling protects the client and family. Tablets are not crushed, missed doses are not doubled, and hand-foot syndrome and diarrhea are reported.

options.text: "Crush the tablets if they're hard to swallow."
"Handle the tablets carefully, wash your hands after taking them, and caregivers should wear gloves if they handle them."
"Store the tablets in a shared pill organizer with your spouse's medicines."
"Double the next dose if you miss one."

questions.stem: A client received an allogeneic stem cell transplant 4 weeks ago. Which findings suggest acute graft-versus-host disease?
questions.rationale: Donor immune cells attack host tissues, most often the skin, GI tract, and liver. GVHD is managed with immunosuppression.

options.text: Rash on the palms and soles, diarrhea, and elevated bilirubin
Bradycardia and hypothermia
Hyperglycemia only
Clear lungs and normal stools

questions.stem: A client at 10 weeks' gestation has persistent vomiting, a 6% weight loss, and ketones in the urine. Which treatment does the nurse anticipate?
questions.rationale: Hyperemesis gravidarum causes dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, and ketosis. Thiamine prevents Wernicke encephalopathy, especially before dextrose is given.

options.text: Encourage three large meals a day
IV fluids with electrolyte replacement, thiamine, and antiemetics as prescribed
Discharge with no treatment
A high-fat diet

questions.stem: A client attempting a vaginal birth after a previous cesarean suddenly reports severe abdominal pain. The fetal heart rate drops to 70/min, and the presenting part is no longer palpable on vaginal exam. What does the nurse suspect?
questions.rationale: Sudden pain, fetal bradycardia, and loss of fetal station suggest uterine rupture, an obstetric emergency requiring immediate cesarean delivery. Uterine scar is the main risk factor.

options.text: Normal second-stage labor
Uterine rupture
Placenta previa
Cord prolapse

questions.stem: A 10-year-old is being treated for DKA. After 6 hours of therapy, the child reports a severe headache, becomes confused, and has a slowing heart rate. What does the nurse suspect?
questions.rationale: Cerebral edema is the most serious complication of pediatric DKA treatment, often linked to rapid shifts in osmolality. It typically presents 4–12 hours into therapy. Treatment includes reducing the fluid rate, raising the head of the bed, and giving mannitol or hypertonic saline.

options.text: Hypoglycemia
Cerebral edema
Expected fatigue
Hyperkalemia only

questions.stem: Highlight (circle) the findings that require immediate follow-up.
questions.rationale: Bradycardia with hypotension indicates shock, and a reduced vital capacity with shallow breathing warns of respiratory failure. The negative FAST, normal hemoglobin, and intact mental status argue against hemorrhage and brain injury.
questions.answer_summary: HR 48; BP 78/44; shallow abdominal breathing; vital capacity 1.2 L; SpO2 93% on oxygen
questions.correct_text: HR 48; BP 78/44; shallow abdominal breathing; vital capacity 1.2 L; SpO2 93% on oxygen

questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is more consistent with neurogenic shock or hypovolemic shock.
questions.rationale: Cervical or high thoracic cord injury disrupts sympathetic outflow, causing vasodilation and unopposed vagal tone (hypotension with bradycardia and warm skin). Hemorrhage triggers compensatory tachycardia and vasoconstriction. Trauma clients can have both, so bleeding must be ruled out.
questions.answer_summary: Neurogenic: bradycardia, warm dry skin, normal Hgb with negative FAST. Hypovolemic: tachycardia, cool clammy skin, delayed refill with narrow pulse pressure.

rows.text: Warm, dry, flushed skin below the injury
Normal hemoglobin with a negative FAST exam
Delayed capillary refill with a narrow pulse pressure

questions.stem: Complete the sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.rationale: A C6 injury paralyzes intercostal and abdominal muscles, leaving the diaphragm to do the work. Cord swelling can extend upward toward the phrenic nerve (C3–C5). A falling vital capacity signals impending respiratory failure.
questions.answer_summary: 1: neurogenic shock from loss of sympathetic tone; 2: respiratory failure from weakened respiratory muscles and possible ascending cord edema
questions.template: The client is experiencing ___1___. The most immediate threat to life is ___2___.

options: neurogenic shock from loss of sympathetic tone
blanks.correct: neurogenic shock from loss of sympathetic tone

options: respiratory failure from weakened respiratory muscles and possible ascending cord edema
blanks.correct: respiratory failure from weakened respiratory muscles and possible ascending cord edema

questions.stem: Which interventions does the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Care focuses on preventing secondary cord injury, maintaining spinal cord perfusion (MAP goals of about 85–90 for several days are common), treating bradycardia, monitoring respiratory function, and managing the neurogenic bladder. High-dose steroids are no longer routinely recommended. The collar stays in place until cleared.

options.text: Maintain spinal immobilization and log-roll with in-line stabilization
IV fluids, followed by a vasopressor such as norepinephrine to maintain the prescribed MAP (often 85–90 mm Hg)
Atropine for symptomatic bradycardia
Monitor vital capacity frequently and prepare for intubation
Insert an indwelling urinary catheter
Routine high-dose methylprednisolone
Remove the cervical collar to assess the neck

questions.stem: One hour later, the client's vital capacity has decreased to 0.9 L, RR is 32/min, and the chest moves inward as the abdomen rises. What should the nurse do first?
questions.rationale: A vital capacity below about 15 mL/kg, rising RR, and paradoxical breathing indicate impending respiratory failure. Intubation is performed with in-line stabilization to prevent further cord injury.

options.text: Apply warm blankets
Call the airway team or provider immediately to prepare for intubation with manual in-line cervical stabilization
Insert the urinary catheter
Administer an oral analgesic

questions.stem: Forty-eight hours later, the intubated client is in the ICU. For each finding, indicate whether it shows effective management or requires follow-up.
questions.rationale: Meeting perfusion goals, a controlled heart rate, adequate renal perfusion, and normal temperature show effective management. A pressure injury and paralytic ileus are common complications of spinal cord injury and require prompt intervention, such as more frequent repositioning and NG decompression.
questions.answer_summary: Effective: MAP 88, HR 64, urine output 45 mL/hr, normothermia. Follow-up: sacral stage 1 pressure injury, paralytic ileus signs.

rows.text: Absent bowel sounds with increasing abdominal distention

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four postoperative clients. Which client should the nurse assess first?
questions.rationale: Neck swelling with hoarseness and dysphagia after carotid surgery suggests an expanding hematoma that can compress the airway. Shoulder pain after laparoscopy is referred pain from CO2 gas and is expected.

options.text: A client 4 hours after carotid endarterectomy with new hoarseness, difficulty swallowing, and increasing neck swelling
A client 1 day after laparoscopic cholecystectomy with right shoulder pain
A client 2 days after hernia repair who has not had a bowel movement
A client 6 hours after cataract surgery requesting eye drops

questions.stem: A client is 12 hours after open abdominal aortic aneurysm repair. Which finding requires the nurse's immediate action?
questions.rationale: Aortic cross-clamping can reduce renal blood flow, and oliguria may signal acute kidney injury, hypovolemia, or graft problems. Hypoactive bowel sounds and low-grade fever are expected after major abdominal surgery.

options.text: Incisional pain rated 5/10
Urine output of 15 mL/hr for 2 consecutive hours
Hypoactive bowel sounds
Temperature of 99.5°F (37.5°C)

questions.stem: A client with a new DVT started warfarin 2 days ago and is also receiving enoxaparin. The INR is 1.6. The client asks why both drugs are needed. What is the nurse's best response?
questions.rationale: Warfarin's full effect takes several days, and it can initially cause a brief hypercoagulable state. Overlap with a parenteral anticoagulant for at least 5 days, until the INR is therapeutic, prevents clot extension.

options.text: "The enoxaparin will be stopped today because warfarin has started."
"Warfarin takes several days to work fully, so enoxaparin continues until your INR is in the target range for at least 24 hours."
"The two drugs cancel each other out."
"Enoxaparin is only for pain."

questions.stem: A client taking clonidine for hypertension says, "I stopped my pills 2 days ago because they made my mouth dry." Which finding is the nurse most concerned about?
questions.rationale: Abrupt discontinuation of clonidine can cause rebound hypertension, which can be severe. Clonidine should be tapered. Dry mouth is a common side effect that can be managed.

options.text: BP 212/118 mm Hg with headache and agitation
Mild dry mouth
HR 68/min
Mild drowsiness

questions.stem: A client with stable angina uses a nitroglycerin transdermal patch. Which instruction helps prevent nitrate tolerance?
questions.rationale: Continuous nitrate exposure leads to tolerance. A daily nitrate-free interval, usually overnight, maintains effectiveness.

options.text: "Wear two patches at a time."
"Apply the patch in the morning and remove it at bedtime to allow a patch-free period of 10–12 hours."
"Never remove the patch."
"Apply the patch only when you have chest pain."

questions.stem: A client with active tuberculosis has a history of missing medication doses. Which strategy does the nurse anticipate the health department will use?
questions.rationale: Directly observed therapy improves adherence, prevents drug resistance, and protects public health. Video-observed therapy is an option in many areas.

options.text: Stopping treatment until the client is motivated
Directly observed therapy, in which a health care worker watches the client take each dose
Doubling doses on the days the client remembers
Giving the full supply of pills to a neighbor

questions.stem: A client on a mechanical ventilator is undergoing a spontaneous breathing trial. Which finding indicates the nurse should stop the trial?
questions.rationale: Tachypnea above about 35/min, hypoxemia, a significant rise in heart rate or BP, diaphoresis, and agitation indicate trial failure. Ventilatory support is resumed and the provider notified.

options.text: RR 22/min
SpO2 94%
RR 38/min with SpO2 86%, increased HR, and anxiety
Calm and following commands

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to administer IV phenytoin. Which action is correct?
questions.rationale: Phenytoin precipitates in dextrose solutions. Rapid administration can cause hypotension and dysrhythmias. Fosphenytoin can be infused faster and causes less tissue irritation.

options.text: Mix it with 5% dextrose in water
Dilute it in 0.9% sodium chloride, infuse no faster than 50 mg/min in adults (using a filter per policy), and monitor ECG and BP
Give it as a rapid IV push
Give it through the same line as a dextrose infusion

questions.stem: A client with Guillain-Barré syndrome is receiving plasmapheresis. The client reports tingling around the mouth and in the fingers. What does the nurse suspect?
questions.rationale: Citrate used during plasmapheresis binds calcium and causes hypocalcemia. The nurse reports it, and calcium replacement and slowing the procedure may be needed. Hypotension and bleeding are other complications.

options.text: Hypocalcemia from the citrate anticoagulant
Hyperkalemia
Worsening of the Guillain-Barré syndrome
An expected finding that needs no action

questions.stem: A client taking evening NPH insulin has high fasting glucose levels each morning. Which action best helps identify the cause?
questions.rationale: A low 0300 glucose suggests the Somogyi effect (rebound hyperglycemia after nighttime hypoglycemia), which requires less evening insulin. A normal or high 0300 glucose suggests the dawn phenomenon, which may require more insulin or different timing.

options.text: Increase the evening NPH dose immediately
Check blood glucose around 0200–0300 for several nights
Stop the evening insulin
Check glucose only at bedtime

questions.stem: A client with Graves' disease is taking methimazole. Which symptom should the nurse instruct the client to report immediately?
questions.rationale: Methimazole and propylthiouracil can cause agranulocytosis. A sore throat or fever requires prompt CBC evaluation. PTU is preferred in the first trimester of pregnancy, and methimazole is preferred otherwise.

options.text: Weight gain
Sore throat and fever
Mild itching
Feeling cold

questions.stem: A client with a history of peptic ulcer disease reports sudden, severe epigastric pain that spreads across the abdomen. The abdomen is rigid, and the client lies very still with knees drawn up. What does the nurse suspect?
questions.rationale: Sudden severe pain with a board-like abdomen suggests perforation and chemical peritonitis, a surgical emergency. The client is kept NPO, and NG suction, IV fluids, and surgical evaluation follow.

options.text: Gastroesophageal reflux
Perforated ulcer with peritonitis
Irritable bowel syndrome
Gastroenteritis

questions.stem: A client's percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) tube, placed 10 days ago, has come out. What should the nurse do?
questions.rationale: Before the tract matures (about 4–6 weeks), reinserting a tube blindly can place it in the peritoneal cavity and cause peritonitis. The provider must replace it, often under endoscopic or radiologic guidance.

options.text: Reinsert the tube immediately
Cover the site with a sterile dressing and notify the provider immediately
Insert an indwelling urinary catheter into the tract
Wait until the next day to report it

questions.stem: A client has a tunneled central venous catheter used for hemodialysis. The nurse needs to give an IV antibiotic, and no peripheral access is available. What should the nurse do?
questions.rationale: Dialysis catheters are locked with high-concentration heparin and reserved for dialysis to reduce infection and occlusion. Using them for other purposes requires specific orders.

options.text: Use the dialysis catheter for the antibiotic
Contact the provider or follow policy, because dialysis catheters are reserved for dialysis
Flush the catheter with a large volume of saline first and then use it
Remove the heparin lock and use it freely

questions.stem: An adult with sickle cell disease is starting hydroxyurea. Which instruction should the nurse include?
questions.rationale: Hydroxyurea increases fetal hemoglobin and reduces crises. It can cause bone marrow suppression and is teratogenic, so CBC monitoring and contraception are required. It is taken daily.

options.text: "No blood tests are needed."
"You'll need regular blood counts, and you should use effective contraception because the drug can harm a developing baby."
"It cures sickle cell disease."
"Take it only during pain crises."

questions.stem: A client is taking tamoxifen after breast cancer treatment. Which symptom should the nurse instruct the client to report?
questions.rationale: Tamoxifen increases the risk of endometrial cancer and venous thromboembolism. Hot flashes are a common, expected side effect.

options.text: Hot flashes
Abnormal vaginal bleeding or unilateral leg pain and swelling
Mild fatigue
Occasional headache

questions.stem: A client starting HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) asks about follow-up. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
questions.rationale: Regular HIV testing ensures infection hasn't occurred (which would require full treatment). Other STI screening and kidney monitoring are also needed. PrEP does not prevent other STIs, so condoms are still recommended.

options.text: "No follow-up is needed once you start."
"You'll need HIV and STI testing and kidney function checks regularly, usually every 3 months for oral PrEP."
"PrEP protects against all sexually transmitted infections."
"You can take it only when you remember."

questions.stem: An Rh-negative client with an Rh-positive partner had an amniocentesis at 16 weeks. Which action is most important after the procedure?
questions.rationale: Amniocentesis can cause fetal-maternal blood mixing, so Rh-negative clients receive Rh immune globulin. Complications include rupture of membranes, infection, and pregnancy loss.

options.text: Encourage strict bed rest for a week
Administer Rh(D) immune globulin as prescribed and teach the client to report leaking fluid, bleeding, cramping, or fever
Give a laxative
Schedule a repeat amniocentesis in 1 week

questions.stem: A 4-year-old with nephrotic syndrome is receiving prednisone. Which finding indicates the treatment is working?
questions.rationale: Remission is shown by reduced proteinuria and resolving edema as albumin rises. Children on steroids are at increased risk of infection, and live vaccines are avoided.

options.text: Increasing proteinuria
Decreasing edema and urine protein, with weight returning to baseline
Worsening periorbital swelling
Serum albumin decreasing further

questions.stem: Highlight (circle) the findings that require immediate follow-up.
questions.rationale: Extreme hyperglycemia and hyperosmolality cause neurological changes and severe dehydration, leading to hypotension, tachycardia, and prerenal kidney injury. The near-normal pH, trace ketones, and SpO2 do not require immediate action.
questions.answer_summary: Altered mental status; glucose 986; osmolality 362; hypotension with tachycardia; creatinine 2.1
questions.correct_text: Altered mental status; glucose 986; osmolality 362; hypotension with tachycardia; creatinine 2.1

questions.stem: For each feature, indicate whether it is more characteristic of hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS) or diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA).
questions.rationale: In HHS, enough insulin is present to prevent significant ketogenesis, so acidosis is absent. The result is profound dehydration and hyperosmolality developing over days. DKA develops quickly with ketoacidosis.
questions.answer_summary: HHS: extreme glucose and osmolality, minimal ketones, pH above 7.30, gradual onset in older adults. DKA: Kussmaul respirations, fruity breath.

rows.text: Glucose above 600 mg/dL with osmolality above 320 mOsm/kg
Gradual onset over days in an older adult with type 2 diabetes

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.rationale: Infection increases stress hormones and glucose, while poor intake and osmotic diuresis cause severe dehydration. Older adults often have an impaired thirst response. The normal pH and HCO3 make lactic acidosis unlikely.
questions.answer_summary: 1: hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state; 2: infection with decreased fluid intake
questions.template: The client is experiencing ___1___ triggered by ___2___.

questions.stem: Which interventions does the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: HHS management centers on aggressive fluid replacement, a controlled insulin infusion, close monitoring, dextrose once glucose reaches about 300 mg/dL, and treating the trigger. Bicarbonate is not indicated without acidosis, and rapid glucose correction risks cerebral edema.

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride IV to restore volume, then adjust based on corrected sodium
IV regular insulin infusion after fluids are started and potassium is confirmed adequate
Hourly blood glucose monitoring and frequent neurological checks
Add dextrose to IV fluids when glucose falls to about 300 mg/dL
IV antibiotics for the urinary tract infection
Sodium bicarbonate IV
Lowering glucose to normal within the first 2 hours

questions.stem: Two hours after treatment begins, the glucose has dropped from 986 to 520 mg/dL. What should the nurse do?
questions.rationale: Glucose should generally fall about 50–75 mg/dL per hour. A drop of about 233 mg/dL per hour increases the risk of rapid osmolality shifts and cerebral edema, so rates need adjustment.

options.text: Continue the current rates since the glucose is still high
Notify the provider, because the glucose is falling faster than the recommended rate
Increase the insulin infusion rate
Stop IV fluids

questions.stem: Eighteen hours after admission, the nurse reassesses the client. For each finding, indicate whether it shows the treatment was effective or requires follow-up.
questions.rationale: Controlled glucose, improving osmolality, restored perfusion, and improved mental status show response. A rising sodium indicates free water deficit requiring fluid adjustment, and a seizure suggests a neurological complication such as cerebral edema.
questions.answer_summary: Effective: glucose 280 with dextrose, osmolality 304, urine output 60 mL/hr, oriented. Follow-up: rising sodium, seizure.

rows.text: Glucose 280 mg/dL with dextrose added to IV fluids
Oriented to person, place, and time

questions.stem: A home health nurse is planning visits for the day. Which client should the nurse visit first?
questions.rationale: Rapid weight gain with new orthopnea indicates worsening heart failure that may require urgent intervention. The other visits are routine.

options.text: A client with heart failure who called to report a 3-lb weight gain overnight and new shortness of breath when lying down
A client with a healing venous leg ulcer due for a weekly dressing change
A client with type 2 diabetes who needs a monthly medication review
A client recovering from a hip replacement who has a scheduled physical therapy visit

questions.stem: A young adult is diagnosed with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Which instruction should the nurse include?
questions.rationale: Dehydration, vasodilators, and intense exertion can worsen outflow obstruction and trigger syncope or sudden death. Beta blockers are commonly prescribed, and first-degree relatives should be screened.

options.text: "Take nitroglycerin for chest pain."
"Stay well hydrated and avoid strenuous competitive sports as directed by your cardiologist."
"Take a sauna daily to relax the heart."
"Dehydration will improve your symptoms."

questions.stem: A client with a prosthetic heart valve is scheduled for a dental cleaning. What should the nurse advise?
questions.rationale: Clients at highest risk, including those with prosthetic valves, receive antibiotic prophylaxis before dental procedures that manipulate gum tissue. Anticoagulant changes are made only with provider direction.

options.text: "No special precautions are needed."
"Tell your dentist about your valve. You will likely need antibiotics before dental procedures to prevent endocarditis."
"Avoid all dental care."
"Stop your anticoagulant for a week before the cleaning without asking your provider."

questions.stem: A client at 30 weeks' gestation asks why she should receive the Tdap vaccine. What is the nurse's best response?
questions.rationale: Tdap is recommended during each pregnancy, ideally between 27 and 36 weeks, to transfer protective antibodies. Pertussis is most dangerous for young infants.

options.text: "It protects you from tetanus only."
"Antibodies you make pass to your baby and help protect against whooping cough in the first months, before the baby can be vaccinated."
"It's only needed if you've never had it."
"It should be given after delivery instead."

questions.stem: A client with a history of DVT is planning a 12-hour flight. Which advice should the nurse give?
questions.rationale: Prolonged immobility increases VTE risk. Movement, hydration, and compression promote venous return. Sedation reduces movement.

options.text: "Stay seated the whole flight to avoid falls."
"Walk and do calf exercises periodically, stay hydrated, avoid alcohol, and wear compression stockings if prescribed."
"Take a sleeping pill so you can sleep through the flight."
"Cross your legs to stay comfortable."

questions.stem: A client with myasthenia gravis has a new infection. Which prescription should the nurse question?
questions.rationale: Aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, magnesium, and some other drugs can impair neuromuscular transmission and precipitate myasthenic crisis.

options.text: IV gentamicin
Acetaminophen for fever
IV fluids
Pyridostigmine as scheduled

questions.stem: A client is starting carbamazepine for seizures. Which instruction should the nurse include?
questions.rationale: Carbamazepine can cause blood dyscrasias and severe skin reactions such as SJS, especially in people of Asian ancestry who carry HLA-B*1502. Grapefruit raises drug levels, and abrupt withdrawal can trigger seizures.

options.text: "No blood tests are needed."
"Report sore throat, fever, easy bruising, or any rash right away, and keep appointments for blood tests."
"Drink grapefruit juice daily."
"Stop it suddenly if you feel drowsy."

questions.stem: A 78-year-old client with coronary artery disease is starting levothyroxine for hypothyroidism. What does the nurse anticipate?
questions.rationale: Rapidly increasing metabolism raises myocardial oxygen demand and can trigger angina or MI in older adults with heart disease.

options.text: A full replacement dose on the first day
A low starting dose increased gradually, with teaching to report chest pain or palpitations
Stopping the client's cardiac medications
Taking it with calcium for better absorption

questions.stem: A newborn has excessive frothy drooling and coughs, chokes, and turns blue with the first feeding. What should the nurse do?
questions.rationale: These findings suggest esophageal atresia with tracheoesophageal fistula. Feeding risks aspiration. Diagnosis is confirmed when a catheter cannot pass into the stomach, and surgery is required.

options.text: Try feeding again more slowly
Stop feeding, keep the newborn NPO, suction the mouth, position with the head elevated, and notify the provider
Give water instead of formula
Place the newborn prone and continue feeding

questions.stem: A client recovering from acute kidney injury now has urine output of 4 L/day. Which complication should the nurse monitor for?
questions.rationale: During the diuretic phase, the tubules cannot yet concentrate urine, causing large fluid and electrolyte losses. Close monitoring of I&O, weight, and electrolytes is needed.

options.text: Fluid overload
Dehydration and electrolyte losses such as hypokalemia
Hyperkalemia only
Hypertension from excess fluid

questions.stem: An 82-year-old client started oxybutynin for overactive bladder 1 week ago. The family reports new confusion and constipation. What should the nurse do?
questions.rationale: Anticholinergic drugs cause confusion, constipation, urinary retention, dry mouth, and falls in older adults. They are on the Beers Criteria list. Alternatives may be considered.

options.text: Reassure the family that this is normal aging
Report the findings, because anticholinergic effects may be causing them
Increase the dose
Add a sedative for the confusion

questions.stem: A client with acute, nonspecific low back pain and no red-flag symptoms asks about activity. What should the nurse recommend?
questions.rationale: Evidence supports staying active over bed rest for acute low back pain. Red flags such as bowel or bladder changes, saddle numbness, or leg weakness require urgent evaluation.

options.text: "Stay in bed for 2 weeks."
"Stay as active as tolerated, use heat for comfort, and gradually return to usual activities."
"Avoid all movement until the pain is completely gone."
"Lift heavy objects to strengthen your back."

questions.stem: A client is receiving the first dose of IV iron dextran. Which action is most important?
questions.rationale: Iron dextran carries a risk of serious hypersensitivity reactions. A test dose and close observation are required, and newer IV iron formulations have lower risk.

options.text: Give the full dose rapidly
Administer a test dose per protocol and monitor closely for anaphylaxis, with emergency equipment available
Give it intramuscularly instead
Mix it with other IV medications

questions.stem: A client has just had a bone marrow aspiration and biopsy from the posterior iliac crest. Which action should the nurse take?
questions.rationale: Pressure and monitoring prevent hematoma, especially in clients with low platelets. Mild aching is expected, and increasing pain or bleeding should be reported.

options.text: Have the client walk immediately
Apply pressure to the site and monitor for bleeding and pain
Remove the dressing after 10 minutes
Place a heating pad on the site
