questions.stem: A client with suspected acute coronary syndrome has no aspirin allergy or active bleeding. How should the nurse give the prescribed aspirin?
questions.rationale: Chewing non-enteric-coated aspirin speeds absorption and antiplatelet effect in ACS. Enteric coating delays absorption.

options.text: Give 81 mg enteric-coated aspirin to swallow whole
Have the client chew non-enteric-coated aspirin (162–325 mg)
Give aspirin rectally only
Give aspirin IV push

questions.stem: A client's ankle-brachial index (ABI) is 0.62 in the right leg. How should the nurse interpret this?
questions.rationale: An ABI of about 1.0–1.4 is normal, 0.9 or below indicates PAD, and very low values (below about 0.4) indicate critical limb ischemia. Values above 1.4 suggest noncompressible, calcified arteries.

options.text: Normal arterial flow
Moderate peripheral arterial disease
Venous insufficiency
Falsely elevated reading from calcified vessels

questions.stem: A client with known right lung cancer suddenly coughs up large amounts of bright red blood. After calling for help, how should the nurse position the client?
questions.rationale: Positioning with the bleeding lung down uses gravity to protect the unaffected lung from blood. Airway protection, suction, and emergency interventions follow.

options.text: Lying on the left side with the right lung up
Lying on the right side (affected lung down)
Prone
Flat on the back

questions.stem: A client with severe ARDS is placed in the prone position. Which nursing action is most important?
questions.rationale: Prone positioning improves oxygenation and survival in severe ARDS, but it increases the risk of facial and anterior pressure injuries and tube dislodgement. Clients typically remain prone for 12–16 hours or more per day.

options.text: Turn the client prone only for 5 minutes each day
Frequently assess and protect pressure points on the face, chest, knees, and other bony areas, and secure all tubes and lines
Remove the endotracheal tube securing device
Stop all sedation

questions.stem: A 72-year-old reports a new temporal headache, scalp tenderness, and jaw pain when chewing. Which complication is the nurse most concerned about, and what treatment is anticipated?
questions.rationale: Giant cell (temporal) arteritis can cause sudden, irreversible blindness. Corticosteroids are started promptly, often before the temporal artery biopsy, and an elevated ESR supports the diagnosis.

options.text: Hearing loss; antibiotics
Permanent vision loss; urgent high-dose corticosteroids
Stroke; thrombolytics
Migraine; triptans

questions.stem: A client with diabetes has a plantar foot ulcer. Which intervention is most important for healing?
questions.rationale: Continued pressure prevents healing. Offloading, infection control, debridement, adequate circulation, and glucose control promote healing and reduce amputation risk.

options.text: Walking barefoot to toughen the skin
Offloading pressure from the ulcer as prescribed (such as a total contact cast or offloading boot), with glucose control and wound care
Soaking the foot in hot water daily
Applying a tight elastic bandage over the ulcer

questions.stem: A client had an endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) to remove a bile duct stone. Four hours later, the client reports severe epigastric pain radiating to the back. What does the nurse suspect?
questions.rationale: Pancreatitis is the most common complication after ERCP. The nurse reports severe pain, checks lipase as prescribed, and monitors for perforation and bleeding.

options.text: Expected mild discomfort
Post-ERCP pancreatitis
Gastroenteritis
Myocardial infarction only

questions.stem: A client is on an enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) pathway following colon resection. Which intervention does the nurse expect?
questions.rationale: ERAS pathways shorten length of stay and reduce complications through early feeding, mobility, limited opioids, and avoiding routine drains and tubes.

options.text: Prolonged NPO status for several days
Early oral intake, early ambulation, and multimodal pain control that minimizes opioids
Strict bed rest for 3 days
Routine NG tube for a week

questions.topic: ACE inhibitors and renal artery stenosis
questions.stem: A client with bilateral renal artery stenosis was started on lisinopril 1 week ago. The creatinine has risen from 1.1 to 2.4 mg/dL. What should the nurse do?
questions.rationale: In bilateral renal artery stenosis, the kidneys depend on angiotensin II to maintain filtration. Blocking it can sharply reduce kidney function.

options.text: Continue the medication and recheck in a month
Hold the medication and notify the provider, because ACE inhibitors can cause acute kidney injury in bilateral renal artery stenosis
Double the dose
Encourage a high-potassium diet

questions.stem: A client reports leg pain and numbness when walking that is relieved by sitting or bending forward. Pedal pulses are strong. What does the nurse suspect?
questions.rationale: Neurogenic claudication improves with spinal flexion, such as leaning on a shopping cart, because it opens the spinal canal. Vascular claudication improves with standing still and is associated with weak pulses.

options.text: Peripheral arterial disease
Lumbar spinal stenosis (neurogenic claudication)
Deep vein thrombosis
Gout

questions.stem: A client taking warfarin has an INR of 5.2 with no signs of bleeding. What does the nurse anticipate?
questions.rationale: For a supratherapeutic INR without bleeding, holding doses and close monitoring are usually sufficient. Rapid reversal is reserved for serious bleeding.

options.text: Administering IV vitamin K and plasma immediately
Holding one or more warfarin doses, rechecking the INR, and assessing for bleeding, with low-dose oral vitamin K considered by the provider
Increasing the warfarin dose
No change in management

questions.stem: A client receiving radiation therapy reports overwhelming fatigue. Which recommendation is best supported by evidence?
questions.rationale: Regular moderate exercise reduces cancer-related fatigue. Energy conservation, sleep hygiene, and treating contributing factors such as anemia also help.

options.text: Complete bed rest until treatment ends
Light to moderate physical activity as tolerated, such as short daily walks, with planned rest periods
Drink several energy drinks daily
Avoid all activity

questions.stem: A pregnant client with HIV asks how to reduce the chance of passing HIV to her baby. Which information should the nurse include?
questions.rationale: ART with viral suppression, newborn prophylaxis, and avoiding breastfeeding reduce perinatal transmission to below 1%. Current guidance supports shared decision-making about breastfeeding for people with sustained viral suppression.

options.text: "Stop your HIV medications during pregnancy."
"Take antiretroviral therapy throughout pregnancy. Your baby will receive antiretroviral medication after birth, and in the U.S., formula feeding is usually recommended."
"Breastfeeding is recommended to boost your baby's immunity."
"Transmission can't be prevented."

questions.stem: A veteran with PTSD is prescribed prazosin for nightmares. Which instruction should the nurse include?
questions.rationale: Prazosin, an alpha-1 blocker, can cause first-dose orthostatic hypotension. Bedtime dosing and gradual titration reduce risk.

options.text: "Take it in the morning."
"Take it at bedtime, and get up slowly, especially after the first dose, because it can cause dizziness or fainting."
"It will stop your nightmares immediately."
"Stop it suddenly if you feel dizzy."

questions.stem: An adolescent comes to the clinic with several superficial cuts on the forearm and says they "help me feel better." What is the nurse's best approach?
questions.rationale: A nonjudgmental approach builds trust. Self-injury may be a way of coping with distress and is associated with increased suicide risk, so a risk assessment and mental health referral are needed.

options.text: Express shock and disapproval
Provide wound care in a calm, nonjudgmental way, and directly assess for suicidal thoughts and emotional distress
Ignore the cuts to avoid reinforcing the behavior
Tell the adolescent to promise never to do it again

questions.stem: A client with postpartum hemorrhage from uterine atony has a history of severe asthma. Which uterotonic should the nurse question?
questions.rationale: Carboprost (a prostaglandin F2-alpha analog) can cause bronchospasm and is contraindicated in asthma. Methylergonovine is avoided in hypertension.

options.text: Oxytocin
Carboprost tromethamine
Misoprostol
Tranexamic acid

questions.stem: The parent of a thriving 2-month-old with frequent spitting up asks whether the baby should sleep on the stomach or with the head elevated. What should the nurse advise?
questions.rationale: Spitting up is common and usually resolves by about 12 months. Safe sleep recommendations still apply. Positioners and inclined sleepers increase suffocation risk. Poor weight gain or feeding refusal should be reported.

options.text: "Place the baby on the stomach to sleep."
"Continue placing the baby on the back on a flat, firm surface. Hold the baby upright after feedings, feed smaller amounts more often, and burp frequently."
"Use a wedge in the crib."
"Let the baby sleep in the car seat."

questions.stem: Highlight (circle) the findings that require immediate follow-up.
questions.rationale: Hypoxemia, increased work of breathing, and pulmonary edema from aspiration threaten respiratory function. Decreased responsiveness suggests hypoxic effects. Hypothermia and wet clothing need prompt correction. Sodium and BP are acceptable.
questions.answer_summary: SpO2 89%; tachypnea with retractions; crackles with frothy sputum; drowsiness; hypothermia; wet clothing
questions.correct_text: SpO2 89%; tachypnea with retractions; crackles with frothy sputum; drowsiness; hypothermia; wet clothing

questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it primarily reflects lung injury from aspiration or hypothermia.
questions.rationale: Aspirated water washes out surfactant and causes alveolar collapse and pulmonary edema. Immersion and wet clothing cause heat loss. Both require treatment.
questions.answer_summary: Lung injury: crackles/frothy sputum, hypoxemia, increased work of breathing. Hypothermia: low core temperature, shivering, cool mottled skin.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.rationale: Respiratory symptoms after drowning can worsen over hours as lung injury progresses. Symptomatic children are observed closely and admitted for monitoring.
questions.answer_summary: 1: a drowning event with aspiration-related lung injury and hypothermia; 2: worsening respiratory failure (such as ARDS)
questions.template: The child experienced ___1___ and is at risk for ___2___ over the next several hours.

options: a drowning event with aspiration-related lung injury and hypothermia
blanks.correct: a drowning event with aspiration-related lung injury and hypothermia

questions.stem: Which interventions does the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Care focuses on oxygenation, rewarming, and monitoring for deterioration. Abdominal thrusts do not remove water from the lungs and can cause vomiting and aspiration. Antibiotics are given only for signs of infection or grossly contaminated water.

options.text: High-flow oxygen with preparation for CPAP or other ventilatory support
Removing wet clothing and actively rewarming
Continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring and pulse oximetry
Frequent neurological assessments
Monitoring glucose and electrolytes
Abdominal thrusts to remove water from the lungs
Routine prophylactic antibiotics for all drowning victims

questions.stem: Which action should the nurse take first?
questions.rationale: Hypoxemia is the most immediate threat, so oxygen comes first. Removing wet clothing and rewarming follow right away and are often done simultaneously by the team.

options.text: Remove the child's wet clothing
Apply high-flow oxygen by nonrebreather mask
Obtain a repeat chest x-ray
Perform abdominal thrusts

questions.stem: The nurse evaluates the child over the next several hours. For each finding, indicate whether it shows improvement or requires follow-up.
questions.rationale: Initial improvement can be followed by delayed pulmonary edema, which is why observation continues. Drowning prevention teaching includes constant, close supervision, four-sided pool fencing, and CPR training for caregivers.
questions.answer_summary: Improved: oxygenation, normothermia, alert, normal RR at 2 hours. Follow-up: delayed respiratory deterioration at 6 hours; parent needs water safety teaching.

rows.text: SpO2 97% on 2 L/min nasal cannula at 2 hours
At 6 hours: RR 56/min, new retractions, and SpO2 decreasing
Parent says, "I'll only leave her alone by the pool for a minute next time"

questions.stem: The nurse in a pulmonary clinic receives four phone calls. Which client should the nurse call back first?
questions.rationale: Needing a rescue inhaler repeatedly with persistent symptoms indicates a severe, poorly controlled exacerbation that needs urgent evaluation. The other calls are routine.

options.text: A client with asthma who has used the albuterol inhaler every hour for 6 hours and still feels short of breath
A client with COPD requesting a refill of tiotropium
A client with sleep apnea whose CPAP mask is uncomfortable
A client with a cough asking whether to get a flu shot

questions.stem: A client with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, who does not have diabetes, is prescribed dapagliflozin. The client asks why a "diabetes pill" was prescribed. What is the nurse's best response?
questions.rationale: SGLT2 inhibitors are now a core part of heart failure therapy. The nurse teaches genital hygiene, hydration, and sick-day precautions.

options.text: "This must be a mistake."
"This medication class has been shown to reduce hospitalizations and death in heart failure, whether or not a person has diabetes."
"It will lower your blood sugar to prevent diabetes."
"It replaces all your other heart medications."

questions.stem: A client is receiving an IV nitroglycerin infusion for unstable angina. Which nursing action is correct?
questions.rationale: Standard PVC tubing can absorb nitroglycerin, reducing the delivered dose. Hypotension and headache are common side effects, and PDE-5 inhibitor use is a contraindication.

options.text: Titrate without monitoring BP
Use the manufacturer-supplied or non-PVC tubing if required, and monitor BP closely while titrating to relieve chest pain
Give it by IV push
Stop the infusion abruptly if pain resolves

questions.stem: A client's spirometry shows a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.58. How should the nurse interpret this?
questions.rationale: A post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.70 confirms persistent airflow limitation, consistent with COPD. Restrictive diseases reduce both values proportionally.

options.text: Normal lung function
Airflow obstruction consistent with COPD
A restrictive lung disease pattern
Improved asthma control

questions.stem: A client with a cervical spine fracture has a halo vest. Which item must be kept with the client at all times?
questions.rationale: The wrench allows rapid access to the chest for CPR. The nurse also performs pin site care, checks the skin under the vest, and never uses the halo frame to lift or turn the client.

options.text: A pair of scissors
The wrench (or tool) to release the vest's anterior bars in an emergency such as CPR
A cervical collar
Extra pins

questions.stem: A client with Parkinson's disease has postoperative nausea. Which prescribed antiemetic should the nurse question?
questions.rationale: Metoclopramide, haloperidol, and prochlorperazine block dopamine and can worsen parkinsonian symptoms. Ondansetron is generally preferred.

options.text: Ondansetron
Metoclopramide
Nonpharmacological measures such as ginger
Trimethobenzamide

questions.stem: A client with pheochromocytoma is scheduled for adrenalectomy. Which medication sequence does the nurse anticipate before surgery?
questions.rationale: Starting a beta blocker first leaves alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed and can cause a hypertensive crisis. Alpha blockade with volume expansion comes first.

options.text: A beta blocker first, then an alpha blocker
An alpha blocker (such as phenoxybenzamine) first, then a beta blocker if needed for tachycardia
A beta blocker alone
No medications before surgery

questions.stem: A client with cirrhosis and recurrent hepatic encephalopathy is prescribed rifaximin in addition to lactulose. How does the nurse explain its purpose?
questions.rationale: Rifaximin is minimally absorbed and acts locally in the gut. It is often combined with lactulose to reduce encephalopathy recurrence.

options.text: "It lowers your blood pressure."
"It is an antibiotic that reduces ammonia-producing bacteria in the gut and helps prevent episodes of confusion."
"It replaces the need for lactulose."
"It treats liver scarring."

questions.stem: A client had a pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple procedure) for pancreatic cancer. Which finding requires prompt follow-up?
questions.rationale: Drainage high in amylase suggests a pancreatic anastomotic leak (fistula), a serious complication. The nurse also monitors glucose closely because pancreatic tissue was removed.

options.text: Glucose of 118 mg/dL
Clear, amber-colored drainage from the abdominal drain that tests high in amylase, with increasing abdominal pain
Incisional pain rated 4/10 with medication
Hypoactive bowel sounds on day 1

questions.stem: After hemodialysis needles are removed, a client's arteriovenous fistula site continues to bleed steadily. What should the nurse do first?
questions.rationale: Direct pressure controls bleeding. Complete occlusion or a tourniquet can clot the fistula. Prolonged bleeding may indicate excess anticoagulation or access problems.

options.text: Apply a tourniquet above the fistula
Apply firm, direct pressure to the site without occluding flow through the fistula, and notify the provider if bleeding persists
Elevate the arm and leave it uncovered
Apply ice and walk away

questions.stem: A 66-year-old with a 40 pack-year smoking history reports painless blood in the urine. What should the nurse recognize?
questions.rationale: Gross hematuria in adults requires evaluation, often including cystoscopy and imaging. Smoking cessation lowers bladder cancer risk.

options.text: Painless hematuria is always harmless
Painless hematuria is the most common sign of bladder cancer, and smoking is its leading risk factor, so evaluation is needed
The hematuria is likely from dehydration only
Only painful hematuria needs evaluation

questions.stem: A client with a tibial fracture asks what might slow bone healing. Which factor should the nurse emphasize?
questions.rationale: Smoking impairs blood flow and bone formation, increasing the risk of delayed healing and nonunion. Diabetes, malnutrition, and steroids also slow healing.

options.text: Drinking milk
Cigarette smoking
Wearing the cast as directed
Taking prescribed vitamin D

questions.stem: A client's WBC is 2,000/mm³ with 20% segmented neutrophils and 5% bands. What is the absolute neutrophil count, and what precautions are needed?
questions.rationale: ANC = WBC × (% neutrophils + % bands) = 2,000 × 0.25 = 500/mm³. An ANC of 500 or below is severe neutropenia with high infection risk.

options.text: ANC 500; severe neutropenia requiring neutropenic precautions
ANC 1,000; no risk
ANC 2,000; normal
ANC 100; no precautions needed

questions.stem: A 35-year-old with normal previous results asks how often she needs cervical cancer screening. Which response by the nurse reflects current guidance for average-risk adults?
questions.rationale: For ages 30–65, USPSTF recommends a Pap test every 3 years, primary HPV testing every 5 years, or co-testing every 5 years. For ages 21–29, a Pap test is done every 3 years.

options.text: "Every year with a Pap test."
"Every 5 years with an HPV test (alone or with a Pap test), or every 3 years with a Pap test alone."
"Screening stops at age 30."
"Only if you have symptoms."

questions.stem: A client taking cyclosporine after a kidney transplant has several findings. Which one is most concerning?
questions.rationale: Cyclosporine is nephrotoxic and causes hypertension. Rising creatinine may indicate toxicity or rejection and requires drug level monitoring and provider evaluation. Hair growth, gum hyperplasia, and tremor are known side effects.

options.text: Mild increase in hair growth
Gum overgrowth
Rising serum creatinine and BP
Mild tremor

questions.stem: Which client has the highest risk for suicide?
questions.rationale: Older age, male sex, being widowed, chronic illness or pain, substance use, and access to lethal means (especially firearms) all increase suicide risk.

options.text: A 30-year-old woman with seasonal allergies
A 78-year-old widowed man with chronic pain, alcohol use, and access to a firearm
A 22-year-old college student with exam stress and strong family support
A 45-year-old with well-controlled hypertension

questions.stem: A client at 37 weeks' gestation is scheduled for external cephalic version for breech presentation. Which action does the nurse anticipate?
questions.rationale: Version can cause fetal heart rate changes, placental abruption, or fetal-maternal bleeding. Monitoring, uterine relaxation, and Rh prophylaxis are standard.

options.text: No fetal monitoring is needed
A nonstress test or ultrasound before and fetal monitoring after, a tocolytic as prescribed, and Rh immune globulin if the client is Rh-negative
A vaginal exam every 5 minutes during the procedure
Discharge immediately without monitoring

questions.stem: A child with poor weight gain, frequent respiratory infections, and salty-tasting skin is being evaluated for cystic fibrosis. Which test confirms the diagnosis?
questions.rationale: Elevated sweat chloride confirms CF. Newborn screening and genetic testing are also used.

options.text: Sweat chloride test
Tuberculin skin test
Hemoglobin electrophoresis
Urine culture

questions.stem: A 9-month-old is prescribed an iron supplement. Which instruction is most important for the nurse to give?
questions.rationale: Iron is a leading cause of poisoning deaths in young children. Milk reduces absorption, and missed doses are not doubled.

options.text: "Give it with milk."
"Store it locked and out of reach, because iron overdose is dangerous for young children. Give it between meals with juice if tolerated."
"Double the dose if a dose is missed."
"Mix it into a full bottle."

questions.stem: Highlight (circle) the findings that require immediate follow-up.
questions.rationale: Pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis, and coldness (the 6 P's) indicate acute arterial occlusion. Sensory and motor loss mean the limb is threatened. AF without anticoagulation is the likely embolic source.
questions.answer_summary: Pale, cold leg; absent pulses and Doppler signals; numbness; weakness; AF with rapid rate; stopped anticoagulant

passage_segments.text: Pale, cold left foot and lower leg
Absent pulses with no Doppler signal
Weak dorsiflexion of the left foot
Right leg warm with palpable pulses

questions.correct_text: Pale, cold leg; absent pulses and Doppler signals; numbness; weakness; AF with rapid rate; stopped anticoagulant

questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is more consistent with acute arterial occlusion or deep vein thrombosis.
questions.rationale: Arterial occlusion blocks inflow, so the limb is cold, pale, and pulseless. DVT blocks venous outflow, causing a warm, swollen, congested limb with intact pulses. Positioning and treatment differ for each.
questions.answer_summary: Arterial: pale cold limb, absent pulses, neuro deficits, sudden onset with AF. DVT: warm red swollen calf, pitting edema.

rows.text: Pitting edema of the lower leg
Sudden onset in a client with atrial fibrillation not on anticoagulation

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.rationale: AF allows clots to form in the left atrium and travel to peripheral arteries. Skeletal muscle and nerves tolerate ischemia for only about 4–6 hours before permanent damage occurs.
questions.answer_summary: 1: acute limb ischemia from an arterial embolism related to atrial fibrillation; 2: irreversible tissue damage and limb loss within hours
questions.template: The client has ___1___, and without prompt treatment is at risk for ___2___.

options: acute limb ischemia from an arterial embolism related to atrial fibrillation
blanks.correct: acute limb ischemia from an arterial embolism related to atrial fibrillation

options: irreversible tissue damage and limb loss within hours
blanks.correct: irreversible tissue damage and limb loss within hours

questions.stem: Which interventions does the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Heparin prevents clot extension, and urgent revascularization restores flow. A level or slightly dependent position helps arterial flow. Heat can burn ischemic tissue and increases metabolic demand. Elevation reduces arterial perfusion.

options.text: IV heparin bolus and infusion as prescribed
Preparation for emergency revascularization, such as embolectomy or catheter-directed therapy
Keep the affected leg level or slightly dependent
Protect the limb from pressure and injury, with no heat applied
Frequent neurovascular checks of both legs
Elevate the affected leg above heart level
Apply a heating pad to warm the foot

questions.stem: What is the nurse's priority action?
questions.rationale: Acute limb ischemia with sensory and motor deficits is a vascular emergency. Time to revascularization determines whether the limb can be saved.

options.text: Apply a warm compress to the left leg
Elevate the left leg on pillows
Notify the provider immediately so emergency revascularization can be arranged
Encourage the client to walk to improve circulation

questions.stem: After surgical embolectomy, the nurse monitors the client. For each finding, indicate whether it shows effective treatment or requires immediate follow-up.
questions.rationale: Restored perfusion shows success. Reperfusion can cause muscle swelling and compartment syndrome, which may require fasciotomy. Myoglobin released from damaged muscle can cause acute kidney injury, so aggressive IV fluids and monitoring are needed.
questions.answer_summary: Effective: pulse restored, warm pink foot, brisk capillary refill, sensation returned. Follow-up: reperfusion compartment syndrome; rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuria.

rows.text: Sensation returned to the left toes
Severe calf pain with passive toe stretch and a tense, swollen calf
Dark, tea-colored urine with CK 18,000 units/L

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four clients. Which client should the nurse assess first?
questions.rationale: Severe hyponatremia with neurological changes can progress to seizures and cerebral edema. The other clients are stable.

options.text: A client with SIADH whose sodium is 118 mEq/L, with new confusion and muscle twitching
A client with central diabetes insipidus who is stable on desmopressin
A client with hypothyroidism who started levothyroxine yesterday
A client with Cushing's syndrome whose glucose is 190 mg/dL

questions.stem: A client with a large pericardial effusion is being evaluated for cardiac tamponade. Which finding supports tamponade?
questions.rationale: Pulsus paradoxus (an exaggerated inspiratory drop in systolic BP) is a classic sign of tamponade, along with Beck's triad of hypotension, JVD, and muffled heart sounds. Pericardiocentesis is the treatment.

options.text: Systolic BP that falls more than 10 mm Hg during inspiration
Bradycardia with hypertension
Bounding peripheral pulses
A loud S4 heart sound

questions.stem: A client took an overdose of propranolol and has HR 38/min and BP 70/40 mm Hg despite atropine and IV fluids. Which medication does the nurse anticipate?
questions.rationale: Glucagon increases heart rate and contractility through a pathway that bypasses beta receptors. High-dose insulin with dextrose, vasopressors, and pacing may also be used.

options.text: Glucagon IV
Naloxone
Flumazenil
Protamine sulfate

questions.stem: A client with a massive pulmonary embolism and hypotension is being considered for systemic thrombolysis. Which finding in the history is a contraindication the nurse should report?
questions.rationale: Prior intracranial hemorrhage, recent ischemic stroke, active bleeding, recent major surgery or trauma, and intracranial tumors are contraindications to thrombolysis because of bleeding risk.

options.text: Seasonal allergies
A hemorrhagic stroke 2 months ago
Controlled hypertension
A history of appendectomy 20 years ago

questions.stem: A client with a brain tumor is prescribed dexamethasone. Which action is most important for the nurse to include?
questions.rationale: Dexamethasone reduces vasogenic cerebral edema but causes hyperglycemia, immunosuppression, and GI irritation. It is taken with food, usually in the morning, and tapered rather than stopped abruptly.

options.text: Restrict the client to bed rest
Monitor blood glucose and watch for signs of infection
Give it at bedtime on an empty stomach
Stop it abruptly once the headache improves

questions.stem: A 40-year-old who has never received a tetanus vaccine steps on a rusty nail in a barn. What does the nurse anticipate?
questions.rationale: For dirty or contaminated wounds, people with fewer than three prior tetanus doses or an unknown history need both a vaccine and tetanus immune globulin for immediate passive protection.

options.text: No treatment is needed
A tetanus-containing vaccine (Tdap) plus tetanus immune globulin, with the vaccine series completed later
Antibiotics only
Tetanus immune globulin only

questions.stem: A hospitalized client with type 2 diabetes who is eating regular meals has glucose values in the 250s. Which regimen does the nurse anticipate based on current recommendations?
questions.rationale: Sliding-scale insulin alone is discouraged because it reacts to hyperglycemia instead of preventing it. Basal-bolus regimens improve glycemic control in eating clients.

options.text: Sliding-scale regular insulin alone
Scheduled basal insulin plus mealtime (prandial) insulin, with correction doses as needed
Stopping all insulin
Oral glucose tablets

questions.stem: A client has a single-lumen (Levin) nasogastric tube for gastric decompression. Which suction setting does the nurse expect?
questions.rationale: Continuous suction through a single-lumen tube can pull the gastric mucosa against the tube and damage it. Double-lumen sump tubes (Salem sump) can use low continuous suction because the air vent protects the mucosa.

options.text: High continuous suction
Low intermittent suction
No suction ever
Wall suction at 200 mm Hg continuous

questions.stem: A client with compensated cirrhosis asks about pain relief for a headache. Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
questions.rationale: Low-dose acetaminophen is often preferred in cirrhosis. NSAIDs can cause kidney injury, GI bleeding, and fluid retention in liver disease.

options.text: "Take ibuprofen, since it's safest for your liver."
"Acetaminophen may be used at a reduced maximum dose, often no more than 2 g per day, as directed by your provider. Avoid alcohol."
"Take as much acetaminophen as you need."
"No pain relievers are ever safe."

questions.stem: During recovery from a transurethral resection of the prostate, the client becomes confused and nauseated, with bradycardia and hypertension. The sodium is 124 mEq/L. What does the nurse suspect?
questions.rationale: Absorption of hypotonic irrigation fluid during TURP can cause fluid overload and dilutional hyponatremia. It is managed with fluid restriction, diuretics, and cautious sodium correction.

options.text: Normal postoperative confusion
Transurethral resection (TUR) syndrome from absorption of irrigation fluid
Urinary tract infection
Hypoglycemia

questions.stem: A client with cancer metastatic to bone is starting IV zoledronic acid. Which teaching point is most important?
questions.rationale: Osteonecrosis of the jaw is a rare but serious effect, especially with IV bisphosphonates and invasive dental procedures. Kidney function and calcium are also monitored, because the drug can cause hypocalcemia.

options.text: "Avoid dental care entirely."
"Have a dental exam before starting, keep up with good oral hygiene, and tell your dentist you take this drug, because it increases the risk of jaw osteonecrosis."
"Take it with orange juice."
"It will increase your calcium level."

questions.stem: A client has had two previous febrile reactions (fever and chills without hemolysis) during transfusions. Which strategy does the nurse anticipate for future transfusions?
questions.rationale: Febrile nonhemolytic reactions are caused by cytokines and white cells in the product. Leukoreduction reduces risk. Any fever during a transfusion still requires stopping the transfusion to rule out hemolysis.

options.text: No blood transfusions ever
Leukocyte-reduced blood products and premedication with an antipyretic as prescribed
Transfusing faster
Using D5W to prime the tubing

questions.stem: A client receiving paclitaxel reports numbness and tingling in the feet. Which instruction should the nurse include?
questions.rationale: Decreased sensation increases the risk of injuries and burns. Worsening neuropathy may require a dose adjustment.

options.text: "Walk barefoot to improve sensation."
"Inspect your feet daily, wear protective shoes, check bath water temperature with your elbow or a thermometer, and report worsening symptoms."
"Use a heating pad on your feet."
"The numbness means the chemotherapy isn't working."

questions.stem: A client with a history of hives after IV contrast is scheduled for a contrast CT. What does the nurse anticipate?
questions.rationale: Prior reactions increase risk. Premedication protocols or alternative imaging reduce risk, and emergency medications must be available.

options.text: Proceed without any changes
Notify the radiology team and provider, who may prescribe premedication (such as a corticosteroid and antihistamine) or an alternative study
Give the contrast faster
Cancel all future imaging permanently

questions.stem: A 15-year-old is starting fluoxetine for depression. Which instruction is most important for the nurse to give the parents?
questions.rationale: Antidepressants carry a boxed warning for increased suicidal thinking in children, adolescents, and young adults. Close monitoring is essential, especially early in treatment.

options.text: "It works within 24 hours."
"Watch closely for worsening depression, agitation, or suicidal thoughts, especially in the first few weeks and after dose changes, and report them immediately."
"Stop it if your teen feels better after a week."
"No monitoring is needed."

questions.stem: A client being discharged offers the nurse an expensive watch as thanks. What is the nurse's best response?
questions.rationale: Accepting significant gifts can blur professional boundaries. Most policies allow only small tokens, such as cards or treats shared with the unit.

options.text: Accept the watch to avoid offending the client
Thank the client warmly, explain that nurses can't accept gifts like this, and follow facility policy
Ask the client for a different gift
Accept it but don't tell anyone

questions.stem: An Rh-negative client with a negative antibody screen is at 28 weeks' gestation. What does the nurse anticipate?
questions.rationale: Routine prophylaxis at about 28 weeks prevents sensitization from small fetal-maternal bleeds in the third trimester. A postpartum dose is given within 72 hours if the newborn is Rh-positive.

options.text: No Rh immune globulin until after delivery
Administering Rh(D) immune globulin now, with another dose after birth if the newborn is Rh-positive
Administering Rh immune globulin to the partner
Giving it only if bleeding occurs

questions.topic: Newborn of a mother with hepatitis B
questions.stem: A newborn's mother is positive for hepatitis B surface antigen. What does the nurse anticipate for the newborn?
questions.rationale: Prompt vaccination with HBIG greatly reduces perinatal transmission. Breastfeeding is not contraindicated. The infant completes the vaccine series and is tested afterward.

options.text: No treatment until age 1
Hepatitis B vaccine and hepatitis B immune globulin within 12 hours of birth
Formula feeding is required
Isolation from the mother

questions.stem: Which findings in a 3-month-old should the nurse report as possible signs of hydrocephalus?
questions.rationale: Because infant skulls can expand, increasing head size is an early sign. Irritability, poor feeding, and a high-pitched cry may also occur.

options.text: A flat anterior fontanel and steady head growth
Rapidly increasing head circumference, a bulging fontanel, separated sutures, and eyes deviated downward (sunset eyes)
Head circumference in the 50th percentile
A social smile

questions.stem: Highlight (circle) the 1030 findings that require immediate follow-up.
questions.rationale: Sudden relief of appendicitis pain followed by diffuse rigidity suggests perforation. Fever, tachycardia, hypotension, lethargy, and poor perfusion indicate peritonitis with septic shock. Hypotension is a late sign in children.
questions.answer_summary: Sudden pain relief; rigid distended abdomen; absent bowel sounds; lethargy; high fever; tachycardia with hypotension; delayed capillary refill
questions.correct_text: Sudden pain relief; rigid distended abdomen; absent bowel sounds; lethargy; high fever; tachycardia with hypotension; delayed capillary refill

questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is more consistent with uncomplicated appendicitis or perforation with peritonitis.
questions.rationale: Perforation releases pressure, briefly relieving pain, then spreads infection throughout the peritoneum. Younger children perforate more often because symptoms are harder to recognize.
questions.answer_summary: Uncomplicated: migrating pain, localized rebound tenderness, anorexia and vomiting. Perforation: sudden pain relief, diffuse rigidity with absent bowel sounds, sepsis signs.

rows.text: Pain migrating from the umbilicus to the right lower quadrant
Diffusely rigid abdomen with absent bowel sounds
High fever with tachycardia and hypotension

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.rationale: Pain relief does not mean the appendicitis has resolved when it is followed by worsening abdominal and systemic findings. Hypotension with poor perfusion in a febrile child indicates septic shock.
questions.answer_summary: 1: a ruptured appendix with peritonitis; 2: septic shock
questions.template: The child is most likely experiencing ___1___ with ___2___.

questions.stem: Which interventions does the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Perforated appendicitis requires resuscitation, antibiotics, pain control, and surgery. Heat and laxatives or enemas can spread infection and are contraindicated. Analgesia does not mask the diagnosis enough to justify withholding it.

options.text: Keep the child NPO
Isotonic IV fluid bolus of 20 mL/kg with reassessment
Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics
IV analgesia, such as morphine
Preparation for emergency surgery
A heating pad on the abdomen
A laxative or enema

questions.stem: At 1030, when the child reports suddenly feeling better and then becomes lethargic with a rigid abdomen, what should the nurse do first?
questions.rationale: Signs of perforation and shock require immediate escalation for resuscitation and emergency surgery. The child remains NPO.

options.text: Document the pain improvement and continue routine care
Offer clear liquids now that the pain is better
Notify the surgeon and provider immediately and call for rapid response
Apply a warm pack to the abdomen

questions.stem: After appendectomy and antibiotic therapy, the nurse evaluates the child. For each finding, indicate whether it shows expected recovery or requires follow-up.
questions.rationale: Perforated appendicitis carries a higher risk of wound infection and abscess. New fever, pain, and diarrhea after initial improvement suggest a pelvic abscess needing imaging and possible drainage.
questions.answer_summary: Expected: afebrile, advancing diet, ambulating, controlled pain. Follow-up: surgical site infection; possible intra-abdominal (pelvic) abscess.

rows.text: Tolerating clear liquids and advancing diet
Incision red, warm, and draining thick yellow fluid
Day 5: new fever of 102.2°F (39°C), pelvic pain, and diarrhea

questions.stem: The nurse in an endoscopy recovery area is caring for four clients. Which client should the nurse assess first?
questions.rationale: Severe pain with a rigid, distended abdomen and tachycardia after colonoscopy suggests bowel perforation, a surgical emergency. Gas, mild bloating, and a sore throat are expected.

options.text: A client 1 hour after colonoscopy with polyp removal who reports severe abdominal pain, with a rigid, distended abdomen and HR 122/min
A client after upper endoscopy who reports a mild sore throat
A client after colonoscopy who is passing gas and reports mild bloating
A client who is drowsy but arousable after moderate sedation, with stable vital signs

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a client with a continuous-flow left ventricular assist device (LVAD). The client has no palpable radial pulse. What should the nurse do?
questions.rationale: Continuous-flow LVADs produce little or no pulsatile flow, so pulses may be absent in a well-perfused client. The nurse assesses perfusion, mental status, device parameters, and Doppler MAP, often targeted around 70–90 mm Hg.

options.text: Begin chest compressions immediately
Measure BP by Doppler, which reflects the mean arterial pressure, and check device flow, alarms, and perfusion
Call a code because the client is pulseless
Remove the driveline to reset the device

questions.stem: A client is scheduled for an exercise stress test. Which instruction should the nurse include?
questions.rationale: Caffeine interferes with pharmacologic stress agents, and beta blockers can blunt the heart rate response. Comfortable shoes and clothing are worn, and a light meal a few hours beforehand is usually allowed.

options.text: "Drink extra coffee the morning of the test."
"Avoid caffeine for about 24 hours, and ask your provider whether to hold medications such as beta blockers before the test."
"Eat a large meal right before the test."
"Wear dress shoes."

questions.stem: A chest tube is inserted for a traumatic hemothorax. The initial output is 1,700 mL of blood, followed by 250 mL/hr for the next 2 hours. What does the nurse anticipate?
questions.rationale: Large initial output (often more than 1,500 mL) or ongoing bleeding of about 200 mL/hr or more suggests major vascular injury that may require surgery. Clamping would trap blood in the chest.

options.text: Clamping the chest tube to stop the bleeding
Notifying the surgeon for possible thoracotomy, and preparing blood products
Removing the chest tube
Continuing to observe for 24 hours

questions.stem: A client with COPD is prescribed tiotropium by dry powder inhaler. Which instruction should the nurse include?
questions.rationale: Tiotropium is a long-acting anticholinergic maintenance drug. Powder in the eyes can precipitate narrow-angle glaucoma. Dry mouth and urinary retention are other side effects. Capsules are placed in the device, not swallowed.

options.text: "Use it as a rescue inhaler during attacks."
"Use it once daily, avoid getting the powder in your eyes, and report eye pain or blurred vision."
"Swallow the capsule."
"Use it every 2 hours as needed."

questions.stem: A client with a complete C6 spinal cord injury asks what level of independence to expect. Which statement by the nurse is most accurate?
questions.rationale: At C6, shoulder movement, elbow flexion, and wrist extension are typically preserved, allowing tenodesis grasp and assisted self-care with devices. Ventilator dependence is more typical of injuries at C3 and above.

options.text: "You will be able to walk independently."
"With adaptive equipment such as wrist splints and utensil holders, you may be able to feed yourself and help with some self-care."
"You will need a ventilator for breathing."
"You won't be able to move your arms at all."

questions.stem: A mechanically ventilated client with a traumatic brain injury has a stable ICP. What PaCO2 range does the nurse expect the team to maintain?
questions.rationale: Routine hyperventilation causes cerebral vasoconstriction and can worsen ischemia. Brief hyperventilation is reserved for signs of impending herniation.

options.text: 20–25 mm Hg (aggressive hyperventilation)
About 35–45 mm Hg (normocapnia)
50–60 mm Hg
Above 65 mm Hg

questions.stem: A client with type 2 diabetes and worsening chronic kidney disease has had several episodes of hypoglycemia on the same insulin dose. What is the most likely explanation?
questions.rationale: The kidneys clear a significant portion of insulin. As kidney function declines, insulin lasts longer, and doses often need to be reduced. Some oral agents also accumulate.

options.text: Increased insulin resistance
Reduced kidney clearance of insulin, which prolongs its action
Excess dietary sugar
Improved pancreatic function

questions.stem: Which findings are characteristic of primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease)?
questions.rationale: Low cortisol and aldosterone cause hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hypoglycemia. High ACTH stimulates melanocytes, causing hyperpigmentation.

options.text: Weight gain, moon face, and hypertension
Fatigue, weight loss, darkened skin (especially in creases and gums), salt craving, and low BP
Heat intolerance and exophthalmos
Hyperglycemia and hypokalemia

questions.stem: A client with Crohn's disease had most of the terminal ileum removed. Which long-term supplement does the nurse anticipate?
questions.rationale: Vitamin B12 is absorbed in the terminal ileum. Without it, clients develop B12 deficiency with anemia and neuropathy. Bile acid malabsorption can also cause diarrhea.

options.text: Vitamin C
Vitamin B12 by injection or another non-oral route
Iron only
Vitamin K only

questions.stem: An older adult has a sudden, painless passage of a large amount of maroon and bright red blood from the rectum. Which cause is most likely?
questions.rationale: Diverticular bleeding is a common cause of painless lower GI hemorrhage in older adults. The nurse assesses hemodynamic status and prepares for resuscitation and colonoscopy.

options.text: Peptic ulcer
Diverticular bleeding
Esophageal varices
Appendicitis

questions.stem: A client with normal kidney function has renal colic from a ureteral stone. Which medication is commonly used first-line for pain?
questions.rationale: NSAIDs reduce ureteral spasm and inflammation and are effective first-line analgesics for renal colic when kidney function allows. Opioids are added if needed.

options.text: Oral acetaminophen only
An NSAID such as IV ketorolac
Meperidine
No pain medication until the stone passes

questions.stem: A client with a history of lumbar disc disease reports new numbness in the groin and inner thighs, difficulty urinating, and bilateral leg weakness. What should the nurse do?
questions.rationale: Saddle anesthesia, bladder or bowel dysfunction, and bilateral leg symptoms indicate cauda equina compression, a surgical emergency. Delayed decompression can cause permanent loss of function.

options.text: Recommend rest and heat at home
Recognize possible cauda equina syndrome and arrange emergency evaluation
Give a muscle relaxant and reassess in a week
Encourage vigorous stretching

questions.stem: An adult in sickle cell pain crisis has a prescription for meperidine. What should the nurse do?
questions.rationale: Normeperidine accumulates and lowers the seizure threshold. Opioids such as morphine or hydromorphone, often by PCA, are preferred.

options.text: Administer it as prescribed
Question the prescription, since meperidine is avoided because its metabolite can cause seizures, especially with repeated doses
Give it intramuscularly every hour
Combine it with an MAOI

questions.stem: A client receiving radiation to the pelvis develops frequent loose stools. Which dietary recommendation should the nurse give?
questions.rationale: Radiation enteritis causes diarrhea. Low-residue foods, hydration, and avoiding irritants help, along with prescribed antidiarrheals and skin care.

options.text: "Eat more raw vegetables and bran."
"Follow a low-fiber (low-residue) diet, drink plenty of fluids, and avoid greasy and spicy foods."
"Drink large amounts of milk."
"Stop drinking fluids to reduce diarrhea."

questions.stem: A client who recently received a kidney transplant enjoys gardening and has a cat. Which instruction should the nurse include?
questions.rationale: Soil and animal waste can carry organisms such as fungi and Toxoplasma that cause serious infections in immunosuppressed clients. Precautions allow safe enjoyment of hobbies.

options.text: "Give up all hobbies."
"Wear gloves and a mask when gardening or handling soil, and have someone else clean the litter box."
"Change the litter box yourself daily without gloves."
"Soil exposure is harmless."

questions.stem: A client with bipolar disorder is starting valproic acid. Which symptoms should the nurse instruct the client to report immediately?
questions.rationale: Valproate can cause hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, and thrombocytopenia. It is highly teratogenic, so contraception is discussed. Liver function, platelets, and drug levels are monitored.

options.text: Mild weight gain
Severe abdominal pain, vomiting, jaundice, or unusual bleeding or bruising
Improved mood
Mild hair thinning

questions.stem: A client at 30 weeks' gestation with placenta previa and no active bleeding is discharged home. Which instruction should the nurse include?
questions.rationale: Pelvic rest reduces the risk of bleeding. Previa covering the cervix requires cesarean birth. Any bleeding requires urgent evaluation.

options.text: "Resume all normal activities, including intercourse."
"Avoid intercourse and anything inserted into the vagina, and go to the hospital immediately for any bleeding or contractions."
"Use tampons for any spotting."
"Plan for a vaginal birth."

questions.stem: A 2-year-old with sickle cell disease suddenly becomes pale and lethargic. The spleen is markedly enlarged, and the child has tachycardia and hypotension. What does the nurse suspect?
questions.rationale: In splenic sequestration, blood pools in the spleen, causing rapid anemia and hypovolemic shock. It requires emergency transfusion. Parents are taught to palpate the spleen.

options.text: Vaso-occlusive pain crisis only
Acute splenic sequestration crisis
Iron deficiency anemia
Viral gastroenteritis

questions.stem: Highlight (circle) the findings that require immediate follow-up.
questions.rationale: Falling respiratory measurements and dysphagia signal risk of respiratory failure and aspiration. Wide heart rate and BP swings show autonomic dysfunction, which can cause dangerous dysrhythmias. A normal SpO2 can be falsely reassuring in neuromuscular respiratory weakness.
questions.answer_summary: Declining FVC; weakening NIF; dysphagia; heart rate swings; BP swings; ascending weakness

passage_segments.text: BP ranging from 88/50 to 182/104 mm Hg

questions.correct_text: Declining FVC; weakening NIF; dysphagia; heart rate swings; BP swings; ascending weakness

questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is more consistent with Guillain-Barré syndrome or acute stroke.
questions.rationale: GBS is an immune-mediated polyneuropathy, often following Campylobacter or viral infection. Albuminocytologic dissociation in the CSF supports it. Stroke causes sudden, focal, usually one-sided deficits.
questions.answer_summary: GBS: symmetric ascending weakness, areflexia, recent infection, elevated CSF protein with normal cells. Stroke: sudden one-sided weakness, facial droop with aphasia.

rows.text: Symmetric weakness ascending from the legs
Sudden weakness of one side of the body
Facial droop on one side with aphasia
Elevated CSF protein with a normal cell count

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.rationale: Myasthenia causes fatigable weakness with intact reflexes, and MS rarely produces this acute ascending pattern. In GBS, respiratory muscle involvement and autonomic instability are the main causes of death.
questions.answer_summary: 1: Guillain-Barré syndrome; 2: respiratory failure and life-threatening autonomic dysfunction
questions.template: The client has ___1___ and is at greatest risk for ___2___.

options: respiratory failure and life-threatening autonomic dysfunction
blanks.correct: respiratory failure and life-threatening autonomic dysfunction

questions.stem: Which interventions does the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: IVIG or plasma exchange shortens the course. Close respiratory monitoring allows controlled intubation before crisis. Autonomic instability requires cardiac monitoring, immobility requires VTE prevention, and dysphagia requires aspiration precautions. Corticosteroids are not effective in GBS, and overexertion is avoided during the acute phase.

options.text: IV immunoglobulin or plasma exchange
Frequent FVC and NIF measurements with plans for elective intubation if values decline
Continuous cardiac monitoring
VTE prophylaxis
Swallow evaluation, with alternative nutrition if needed
High-dose oral corticosteroids as primary therapy
Vigorous resistance exercise of the weak muscles

questions.stem: Two days later, the client is intubated. During endotracheal suctioning, the HR suddenly drops from 88 to 36/min and BP falls to 76/40 mm Hg. What should the nurse do first?
questions.rationale: Autonomic dysfunction in GBS can cause severe bradycardia with vagal stimulation such as suctioning. The nurse stops the stimulus and oxygenates. Atropine or temporary pacing may be required.

options.text: Continue suctioning to clear all secretions
Stop suctioning, oxygenate the client, and prepare atropine while notifying the provider
Increase the suction pressure
Reposition the client prone

questions.stem: Over the following weeks, the nurse evaluates the client. For each finding, indicate whether it shows expected progress or requires follow-up.
questions.rationale: Recovery in GBS often proceeds in the reverse order of onset. Immobility increases DVT risk, and dysphagia with tube feeding increases aspiration risk. Both need prompt evaluation.
questions.answer_summary: Expected: returning strength, improving VC, effective communication, pain controlled. Follow-up: possible DVT; possible aspiration pneumonia.

rows.text: Arm strength returning, followed by leg strength
Vital capacity improving, allowing a weaning trial
Communicates effectively using a letter board
New swelling, warmth, and pain in the left calf
Fever and new coarse crackles after tube feedings

questions.stem: The pediatric emergency nurse is triaging four children. Which child should the nurse see first?
questions.rationale: Stridor at rest with retractions indicates moderate to severe upper airway obstruction from croup, which requires immediate treatment. The other children are stable.

options.text: A 2-year-old with a barking cough, stridor at rest, and suprasternal retractions
A 4-year-old with a runny nose and a temperature of 100.2°F (37.9°C)
A 6-year-old with an ear infection who is playing in the waiting room
A 9-year-old with a forearm laceration that has stopped bleeding

questions.stem: A child with moderate to severe croup receives nebulized racemic epinephrine and oral dexamethasone. Which action is most important after the epinephrine treatment?
questions.rationale: Racemic epinephrine works quickly but wears off in about 1–2 hours, and symptoms may return. Dexamethasone reduces airway swelling over several hours.

options.text: Discharge the child immediately once stridor improves
Observe the child for at least 2–4 hours for a return of symptoms as the epinephrine wears off
Give a second dose of dexamethasone every hour
Place the child flat to rest

questions.stem: A client's ECG shows regular "sawtooth" waves between QRS complexes at an atrial rate of about 300/min, with a ventricular rate of 150/min. How should the nurse interpret this rhythm?
questions.rationale: Atrial flutter produces organized flutter waves. Like atrial fibrillation, it carries stroke risk and may need rate control, anticoagulation, cardioversion, or ablation.

options.text: Atrial fibrillation
Atrial flutter with 2:1 conduction
Ventricular tachycardia
Sinus tachycardia

questions.stem: A client with a new mechanical mitral valve asks about anticoagulation. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
questions.rationale: Mechanical valves require lifelong warfarin. Direct oral anticoagulants are contraindicated with mechanical valves because they have been associated with more clots and bleeding.

options.text: "You can take apixaban instead of warfarin."
"You will need warfarin long term, with regular INR checks. A higher target range, often 2.5–3.5, is common for mechanical mitral valves."
"Anticoagulation is only needed for 3 months."
"Aspirin alone is enough."

questions.stem: A client with COPD and chronic resting hypoxemia is prescribed home oxygen. Which statement indicates understanding of how to get the most benefit?
questions.rationale: Long-term oxygen used at least 15 hours per day improves survival in COPD with severe resting hypoxemia. The flow rate is used as prescribed.

options.text: "I'll use it only when I feel short of breath."
"I'll use my oxygen at least 15 hours a day, including while I sleep."
"I'll turn it up to 10 liters when I feel tired."
"I'll stop using it once my breathing feels better."

questions.stem: A teenager with exercise-induced bronchoconstriction plays soccer. Which instruction should the nurse include?
questions.rationale: Pre-exercise short-acting beta agonist use and a gradual warm-up prevent symptoms. Clients should carry their rescue inhaler during activity.

options.text: "Avoid all sports."
"Use your albuterol inhaler about 15 minutes before exercise and warm up gradually."
"Use your inhaled steroid right before games as a rescue."
"Only use albuterol after you finish playing."

questions.stem: A client with severe spasticity has an intrathecal baclofen pump. The pump alarms for a low reservoir, and the client reports itching, increased spasticity, and fever. What should the nurse do?
questions.rationale: Intrathecal baclofen withdrawal can progress to high fever, altered mental status, rhabdomyolysis, and death. Prompt pump evaluation and refill are needed.

options.text: Wait until the next scheduled refill
Notify the provider immediately, because abrupt baclofen withdrawal can be life-threatening
Give oral acetaminophen and reassess tomorrow
Turn off the pump

questions.stem: The nurse uses the Confusion Assessment Method (CAM) to screen an older adult for delirium. Which combination of findings is required for a positive screen?
questions.rationale: The CAM identifies delirium, which requires prompt evaluation for causes such as infection, medications, hypoxia, or electrolyte imbalance.

options.text: Chronic memory loss only
Acute onset or fluctuating course and inattention, plus either disorganized thinking or an altered level of consciousness
Depressed mood and poor appetite
Hallucinations only

questions.stem: A client with hypothyroidism who takes levothyroxine has just learned she is pregnant. What does the nurse anticipate?
questions.rationale: Thyroid hormone needs rise early in pregnancy, and adequate levels are important for fetal brain development. Many clients are told to increase the dose as soon as pregnancy is confirmed.

options.text: Stopping levothyroxine during pregnancy
An increase in the levothyroxine dose, often right away, with TSH checked every few weeks
No change until after delivery
Switching to methimazole

questions.stem: A client who has taken metformin for 8 years reports numbness and tingling in the feet. Which lab test should the nurse anticipate?
questions.rationale: Long-term metformin use can reduce B12 absorption, which can cause neuropathy that may be mistaken for diabetic neuropathy. Periodic B12 monitoring is recommended.

options.text: Serum amylase
Vitamin B12 level
Thyroid antibodies
Uric acid

questions.stem: A client with a new ileostomy has had 2,400 mL of watery output in 24 hours and reports dizziness and thirst. What is the nurse's priority concern?
questions.rationale: High ileostomy output (often more than about 1.5–2 L/day) can quickly cause dehydration, hyponatremia, hypokalemia, and kidney injury. Oral rehydration solutions, IV fluids, and antimotility drugs may be needed.

options.text: Constipation
Dehydration and electrolyte loss
Hypertension
Stomal prolapse

questions.stem: A client with achalasia reports difficulty swallowing both solids and liquids and regurgitation of undigested food. Which instruction should the nurse include?
questions.rationale: Achalasia is failure of the lower esophageal sphincter to relax. Gravity helps food pass, and head elevation reduces nighttime regurgitation and aspiration risk.

options.text: "Lie down right after eating."
"Eat small meals slowly, sit upright during and after meals, and raise the head of your bed at night."
"Eat large, dry meals quickly."
"Drink ice-cold drinks with meals."

questions.stem: Which annual screening test is recommended to detect early kidney disease in adults with diabetes?
questions.rationale: Albuminuria is an early marker of diabetic kidney disease. Early detection allows treatment such as ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or SGLT2 inhibitors to slow progression.

options.text: Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio and eGFR
Kidney ultrasound
24-hour urine for cortisol
Urine culture

questions.stem: A postmenopausal client is prescribed raloxifene for osteoporosis. Which history should the nurse report before the first dose?
questions.rationale: Raloxifene increases the risk of venous thromboembolism and is contraindicated with a history of VTE. It may also worsen hot flashes.

options.text: Seasonal allergies
A previous deep vein thrombosis
Hypothyroidism controlled with medication
Mild osteoarthritis

questions.stem: A client reports craving and chewing large amounts of ice. Which condition should the nurse suspect?
questions.rationale: Pica, especially craving ice (pagophagia), is associated with iron deficiency. The nurse also looks for the cause, such as heavy menstrual bleeding or GI blood loss.

options.text: Hypercalcemia
Iron deficiency anemia
Hypothyroidism
Diabetes insipidus

questions.stem: A client in hospice with advanced lung cancer is very short of breath and anxious. Which intervention is commonly used to relieve dyspnea?
questions.rationale: Low-dose opioids reduce the sensation of breathlessness without significantly shortening life when titrated appropriately. Cool airflow and upright positioning also help.

options.text: Withholding all opioids
Low-dose opioids (such as morphine) as prescribed, along with positioning, a fan directed at the face, and oxygen if helpful
Encouraging the client to walk
Keeping the room hot and closed

questions.stem: A client with paranoid thinking is pacing and suspicious of staff. Which approach by the nurse is most appropriate?
questions.rationale: Unexpected touch and closeness can be perceived as threatening by a paranoid client. Clear, honest communication and respecting personal space build trust.

options.text: Approach quickly and touch the client's arm to reassure them
Maintain personal space, speak calmly and clearly, and explain actions before doing them
Whisper to other staff in front of the client
Stand very close to show support

questions.stem: In which situation should the nurse recognize that breastfeeding is generally contraindicated in the United States?
questions.rationale: Active untreated TB requires temporary separation from direct breastfeeding, although expressed milk can usually be given. Other contraindications include classic galactosemia in the infant and certain drug use. HIV guidance now emphasizes shared decision-making for mothers with sustained viral suppression.

options.text: A mother with a cold
A mother with active, untreated tuberculosis until treatment is established (expressed milk may be given)
A mother taking acetaminophen
A mother who had a cesarean birth

questions.stem: The parent of a 2-year-old with sickle cell disease asks why the child takes penicillin every day. What is the nurse's best response?
questions.rationale: Functional asplenia greatly increases the risk of pneumococcal sepsis. Prophylactic penicillin and vaccinations reduce this risk. Any fever still requires urgent evaluation.

options.text: "It treats pain crises."
"Children with sickle cell disease have a weakened spleen, so daily penicillin (usually until about age 5) helps prevent life-threatening bacterial infections."
"It increases red blood cells."
"It is only needed during fever."

questions.stem: Highlight (circle) the findings that require immediate follow-up.
questions.rationale: These are severe features of preeclampsia, indicating high risk for eclampsia, stroke, and HELLP syndrome. The fetal heart rate tracing is currently reassuring.
questions.answer_summary: Severe-range BP; refractory headache; visual changes; RUQ pain; hyperreflexia with clonus; low platelets; elevated liver enzymes

passage_segments.text: BP 172/114 mm Hg, confirmed on repeat

questions.correct_text: Severe-range BP; refractory headache; visual changes; RUQ pain; hyperreflexia with clonus; low platelets; elevated liver enzymes

questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is a severe feature of preeclampsia or can be a normal finding in late pregnancy.
questions.rationale: Dependent edema and heartburn are common in pregnancy. Severe-range BP, neurological symptoms, thrombocytopenia, liver involvement, pulmonary edema, and kidney dysfunction define severe features.
questions.answer_summary: Severe features: SBP 160 or higher, refractory headache, falling platelets, RUQ/epigastric pain. Can be normal: mild dependent edema, heartburn.
columns: Can be normal in late pregnancy

rows.text: Systolic BP of 160 mm Hg or higher
Mild ankle edema at the end of the day
rows.correct_column: Can be normal in late pregnancy
Can be normal in late pregnancy

rows.text: Right upper quadrant or epigastric pain

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.rationale: Severe-range BP with proteinuria, neurological symptoms, and lab abnormalities confirms preeclampsia with severe features. Uncontrolled BP is a leading cause of maternal stroke.
questions.answer_summary: 1: preeclampsia with severe features; 2: eclamptic seizures and stroke
questions.template: The client has ___1___ and is at immediate risk for ___2___.

questions.stem: Which interventions does the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Management includes seizure prophylaxis with magnesium, prompt antihypertensive treatment, monitoring for magnesium toxicity, fetal surveillance, and delivery planning (recommended at 34 weeks or later with severe features). Clients are at risk for pulmonary edema, so fluids are restricted.

options.text: IV magnesium sulfate loading dose followed by a maintenance infusion
IV labetalol or hydralazine (or oral immediate-release nifedipine) to lower severe-range BP within 30–60 minutes
Seizure precautions and a quiet environment
Strict intake and output with close monitoring of reflexes and respirations
Continuous fetal monitoring and planning for delivery
Encourage the client to ambulate in the hallway
Give IV fluids rapidly at 250 mL/hr

questions.stem: Before magnesium is started, the client has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. What should the nurse do first?
questions.rationale: During an eclamptic seizure, side-lying positioning protects the airway and improves placental perfusion, and the client is protected from injury. After the seizure, oxygen is given, magnesium is started, and the fetus is assessed. Fetal bradycardia commonly recovers afterward.

options.text: Insert an oral airway between the client's teeth
Turn the client onto her side, protect her from injury, call for help, and note the time
Restrain the client's arms and legs
Begin chest compressions immediately

questions.stem: Six hours after treatment begins, the nurse reassesses the client. For each finding, indicate whether it shows effective treatment or requires follow-up.
questions.rationale: Improved BP, normal reflexes, and adequate respirations and urine output show response. A magnesium level above the therapeutic range (about 4.8–8.4 mg/dL) risks toxicity. Recurrent late decelerations suggest uteroplacental insufficiency and may prompt expedited delivery.
questions.answer_summary: Effective: BP out of severe range, reflexes 2+, RR 16, adequate urine output. Follow-up: supratherapeutic magnesium level; recurrent late decelerations.

rows.text: Recurrent late decelerations on the fetal monitor

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four clients. Which client should the nurse assess first?
questions.rationale: Inability to pass a suction catheter with falling SpO2 suggests tracheostomy tube obstruction (such as a mucus plug) or displacement, an airway emergency.

options.text: A client with a tracheostomy who suddenly cannot pass a suction catheter, has high-pitched breath sounds, and SpO2 dropping to 84%
A client with COPD on 2 L/min oxygen with SpO2 91%
A client with pneumonia requesting cough medicine
A client 2 days after lobectomy who reports incisional pain of 5/10

questions.stem: A client returns from cardiac catheterization through the right radial artery with a compression band in place. Which action is correct?
questions.rationale: Radial access allows early mobility but requires monitoring for hand ischemia, bleeding, and hematoma. Stepwise band deflation per protocol prevents rebleeding. BP and blood draws are avoided on that arm.

options.text: Keep the client flat for 6 hours with the leg straight
Monitor the hand for color, warmth, capillary refill, and sensation, and deflate the band gradually per protocol
Take blood pressure on the right arm every 15 minutes
Remove the band all at once after 30 minutes

questions.stem: A client taking enalapril reports a persistent, dry, tickling cough that is disrupting sleep. The lungs are clear. What does the nurse anticipate?
questions.rationale: ACE inhibitors increase bradykinin, which can cause a dry cough. ARBs do not increase bradykinin to the same extent. Angioedema, although rare, can also occur.

options.text: Adding a cough suppressant and continuing enalapril indefinitely
The provider may switch to an ARB such as losartan, which is less likely to cause cough
Doubling the enalapril dose
Starting antibiotics

questions.stem: A client with a severe asthma exacerbation has not improved after repeated albuterol-ipratropium nebulizers and systemic corticosteroids. Which additional medication may the nurse anticipate in the emergency department?
questions.rationale: IV magnesium relaxes bronchial smooth muscle and is used for severe exacerbations that don't respond to initial therapy. Sedatives are avoided because they depress breathing.

options.text: IV magnesium sulfate
Oral montelukast only
Inhaled fluticasone as the rescue drug
A sedative to calm breathing

questions.stem: A client with ARDS is mechanically ventilated. Which tidal volume setting reflects lung-protective ventilation?
questions.rationale: Low tidal volumes reduce ventilator-induced lung injury and improve survival in ARDS. Some rise in CO2 may be accepted (permissive hypercapnia).

options.text: About 10–12 mL/kg of actual body weight
About 6 mL/kg of predicted (ideal) body weight, with plateau pressure kept at or below about 30 cm H2O
The highest volume tolerated
About 15 mL/kg

questions.stem: A family member is concerned about an older adult's memory. Which finding is more concerning for dementia than normal aging?
questions.rationale: Disorientation in familiar places, difficulty managing daily tasks, and poor judgment suggest cognitive impairment and need evaluation. Mild slowing and occasional forgetfulness are common with aging.

options.text: Occasionally forgetting a name but remembering it later
Getting lost while driving to a familiar grocery store
Taking longer to learn a new phone
Misplacing glasses once in a while

questions.stem: A client had gestational diabetes that resolved after delivery. Which follow-up does the nurse recommend?
questions.rationale: Gestational diabetes significantly raises lifetime risk of type 2 diabetes. Healthy weight, activity, and breastfeeding lower that risk.

options.text: "No follow-up is needed because it went away."
"Have a glucose test (often a 75-g oral glucose tolerance test) at about 4–12 weeks postpartum, and ongoing screening at least every 3 years because your risk of type 2 diabetes is higher."
"Check your glucose only if you become pregnant again."
"Start insulin now."

questions.stem: A client with long-standing GERD is diagnosed with Barrett's esophagus. Which teaching point is most important?
questions.rationale: Barrett's esophagus increases the risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma. Surveillance endoscopy allows early detection and treatment.

options.text: "This condition is harmless and needs no follow-up."
"You'll need periodic endoscopy to watch for precancerous changes, and continuing acid-reducing treatment is important."
"You should stop all medications."
"It will go away on its own in a week."

questions.stem: A client is diagnosed with a first episode of Clostridioides difficile infection. Which prescription does the nurse expect?
questions.rationale: IV vancomycin does not reach the colon in meaningful amounts, so oral therapy is used. Antidiarrheals are avoided, and unnecessary antibiotics are stopped when possible.

options.text: IV vancomycin
Oral vancomycin or oral fidaxomicin
Loperamide to stop the diarrhea
Oral ciprofloxacin

questions.stem: A client at 24 weeks' gestation has fever, flank pain, and costovertebral angle tenderness. Why is prompt treatment important?
questions.rationale: Urinary stasis in pregnancy increases the risk of upper UTI. Complications include sepsis, respiratory distress, and preterm labor. Screening for bacteria in the urine helps prevent it.

options.text: It is a minor infection that resolves on its own
Pyelonephritis in pregnancy can lead to sepsis and preterm labor, so it usually requires hospitalization and IV antibiotics
It only affects the mother's comfort
Treatment should wait until after delivery

questions.stem: A client is recovering from an open nephrectomy through a flank incision. Which complication should the nurse especially work to prevent?
questions.rationale: Flank incisions near the diaphragm make deep breathing painful. Pain control, splinting, incentive spirometry, and ambulation prevent pulmonary complications. The nurse also monitors urine output from the remaining kidney.

options.text: Hypoglycemia
Atelectasis and pneumonia from shallow breathing because of incisional pain near the diaphragm
Constipation only
Hearing loss

questions.stem: A 6-year-old is diagnosed with juvenile idiopathic arthritis. Which ongoing screening is especially important?
questions.rationale: Uveitis can occur silently in JIA and cause vision loss if untreated. Slit-lamp exams are scheduled based on risk.

options.text: Hearing tests
Regular eye exams by an ophthalmologist to detect uveitis, which often has no symptoms
Annual chest x-rays
Monthly colonoscopy

questions.stem: After a topical benzocaine spray before a procedure, a client appears cyanotic with SpO2 of about 85% that does not improve with oxygen. The blood drawn appears chocolate-brown. What does the nurse suspect, and which treatment is anticipated?
questions.rationale: Methemoglobin cannot carry oxygen. Benzocaine, dapsone, and some other drugs can cause it. Methylene blue restores normal hemoglobin but is used cautiously in G6PD deficiency.

options.text: Pulmonary embolism; heparin
Methemoglobinemia; IV methylene blue
Carbon monoxide poisoning; hyperbaric oxygen
Anemia; iron

questions.stem: A client taking capecitabine reports red, swollen, tender palms and soles. Which instruction should the nurse include?
questions.rationale: Hand-foot syndrome is a common effect of some chemotherapy drugs. Protective measures reduce severity, and a dose adjustment may be needed.

options.text: "Take hot showers and scrub your feet."
"Avoid heat and friction, keep your hands and feet cool and moisturized, wear loose shoes, and report blistering or pain that limits activity."
"Walk long distances to toughen your feet."
"This means the drug is not working."

questions.stem: A client at 33 weeks' gestation in September asks which vaccines are recommended during pregnancy. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
questions.rationale: Maternal Tdap, influenza, and seasonal RSV vaccination protect both the pregnant person and the newborn through antibody transfer. Live vaccines such as MMR are avoided in pregnancy. COVID-19 vaccination is also recommended.

options.text: "No vaccines are safe during pregnancy."
"Tdap and the inactivated flu vaccine are recommended, and a maternal RSV vaccine is recommended between 32 and 36 weeks during RSV season to protect your baby."
"You should get MMR now."
"Only get vaccines after delivery."

questions.stem: A client prescribed zolpidem for insomnia reports waking to find the kitchen messy with no memory of cooking. What should the nurse do?
questions.rationale: Complex sleep behaviors can cause serious injury. Zolpidem should be taken only when the client can get a full night's sleep and should never be combined with alcohol or other CNS depressants.

options.text: Reassure the client that this is harmless
Report it, because complex sleep behaviors such as sleep-driving and sleep-cooking are a boxed warning for zolpidem, and the drug should be stopped
Suggest taking it with alcohol to sleep more deeply
Double the dose

questions.stem: A client jumps from topic to topic while describing several stressors. Which response by the nurse demonstrates the technique of focusing?
questions.rationale: Focusing helps the client concentrate on a key concern and explore it in more depth.

options.text: "Let's talk about something else."
"You mentioned your job loss several times. Let's talk more about that."
"Everything will work out."
"Why are you so stressed?"

questions.stem: After delivery of the newborn, which findings indicate the placenta is separating?
