questions.rationale: These signs usually appear within minutes to 30 minutes after birth. The placenta is examined for completeness, because retained fragments cause hemorrhage.

options.text: The uterus becomes soft and flat
A gush of blood, lengthening of the umbilical cord, and the uterus rising and becoming more globular
Maternal bradycardia
Absence of bleeding for 2 hours

questions.stem: A 5-year-old weighing 20 kg is diagnosed with a severe peanut allergy. Which epinephrine auto-injector dose does the nurse expect to be prescribed?
questions.rationale: The 0.15-mg auto-injector is generally used for children about 15–30 kg, and 0.3 mg for those 30 kg or more. A 0.1-mg device exists for infants and toddlers weighing about 7.5–15 kg.

options.text: 0.3 mg
1 mg
0.5 mg

questions.stem: Highlight (circle) the findings that require immediate follow-up.
questions.rationale: A core temperature of 86°F indicates moderate to severe hypothermia with depressed cardiac, respiratory, and neurological function. Loss of shivering signals worsening hypothermia. Frostbite and hypoglycemia also need treatment. Potassium is normal.
questions.answer_summary: Core temp 86°F; bradycardia with irregular rhythm; RR 8; hypotension; absence of shivering; frostbitten fingers; hypoglycemia
questions.correct_text: Core temp 86°F; bradycardia with irregular rhythm; RR 8; hypotension; absence of shivering; frostbitten fingers; hypoglycemia

questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it primarily reflects systemic hypothermia or local cold injury (frostbite).
questions.rationale: Hypothermia slows metabolism and cardiac conduction. Frostbite is freezing of local tissue. Blister type after rewarming helps estimate depth: clear blisters suggest superficial injury, and hemorrhagic blisters suggest deeper injury.
questions.answer_summary: Systemic: bradycardia, no shivering, J waves. Frostbite: white waxy hard skin, numbness, blisters after rewarming.

rows.text: Blisters on the fingers after rewarming

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.rationale: Below about 90°F (32°C), shivering stops and the myocardium becomes irritable. Rough handling or rapid position changes can trigger VF. Alcohol worsens heat loss by causing vasodilation.
questions.answer_summary: 1: moderate to severe accidental hypothermia with frostbite; 2: ventricular fibrillation
questions.template: The client has ___1___ and is at high risk for ___2___.

options: moderate to severe accidental hypothermia with frostbite
blanks.correct: moderate to severe accidental hypothermia with frostbite

questions.stem: Which interventions does the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Rewarming (external and core), gentle handling, cardiac monitoring, and correcting hypoglycemia are key. Frostbitten tissue is never rubbed, because rubbing damages it. Rapid rewarming of frostbite is done later in warm water. Oral intake is unsafe with decreased consciousness.

options.text: Handle the client gently and keep them horizontal
Remove wet clothing and begin active external rewarming (such as forced-air warming blankets)
Warmed IV fluids and warmed, humidified oxygen
Continuous cardiac monitoring
IV dextrose for hypoglycemia
Rub the frostbitten fingers vigorously to restore circulation
Give hot coffee by mouth

questions.stem: The client needs to be moved from the stretcher to the emergency department bed. What is most important for the nurse to do?
questions.rationale: The cold heart is very prone to ventricular fibrillation with rough movement. Keeping the client horizontal also helps prevent hypotension.

options.text: Have the client sit up and pivot to the bed
Move the client gently while keeping them horizontal, with minimal jostling
Walk the client to the bed to generate body heat
Move the client quickly to save time

questions.stem: Four hours after rewarming begins, the nurse reassesses the client. For each finding, indicate whether it shows effective treatment or requires follow-up.
questions.rationale: Gradual rewarming with restored rhythm and mentation shows success. Hemorrhagic blisters indicate deep frostbite that may need specialized care, such as thrombolytics in select cases. Severe hyperkalemia can signal tissue damage and needs urgent treatment.
questions.answer_summary: Effective: core temp 95°F, sinus rhythm, improved mentation, stable BP. Follow-up: deep frostbite (hemorrhagic blisters); severe hyperkalemia.

questions.stem: A school nurse (RN) has four students waiting. Which student should the nurse see first?
questions.rationale: Throat tightness after possible allergen exposure may be the beginning of anaphylaxis. Epinephrine should be given without delay according to the student's emergency plan.

options.text: A student with a known peanut allergy who says, "My throat feels itchy and tight," after eating lunch
A student with a scraped knee
A student with type 1 diabetes due for a scheduled glucose check before lunch
A student who reports a mild headache

questions.stem: A client is going home with a 48-hour Holter monitor. Which instruction should the nurse include?
questions.rationale: The Holter records continuous ECG data during usual activities. The symptom diary allows providers to match symptoms with rhythm changes.

options.text: "Stay in bed while wearing the monitor."
"Continue your normal activities, keep a diary of symptoms and activities with times, and don't shower or get the monitor wet unless told otherwise."
"Remove the electrodes at night."
"Only record symptoms if they are severe."

questions.stem: A client taking warfarin for atrial fibrillation is scheduled for elective hip replacement. What does the nurse anticipate?
questions.rationale: Warfarin's effect lasts several days. Bridging with heparin is reserved for high-risk clients, such as those with mechanical valves or recent stroke, because it increases bleeding.

options.text: Continuing warfarin up to the morning of surgery
Stopping warfarin about 5 days before surgery, with bridging anticoagulation only if the provider determines high thrombotic risk, and an INR check before surgery
Doubling warfarin the week before
Stopping warfarin permanently

questions.stem: A client recovering from a spontaneous pneumothorax asks about travel and hobbies. Which instruction should the nurse include?
questions.rationale: Pressure changes during flight and diving can expand residual air or cause recurrence. Smoking greatly increases recurrence risk.

options.text: "You can fly and go scuba diving right away."
"Avoid air travel until your provider confirms resolution, often a few weeks, and avoid scuba diving unless cleared by a specialist. Stop smoking to reduce recurrence."
"Smoking has no effect on recurrence."
"Recurrence is impossible."

questions.stem: A 6-week-old is brought in with a cough for a week. Which finding is most concerning for pertussis in this infant?
questions.rationale: Young infants with pertussis may not whoop but can have life-threatening apnea. They are hospitalized for monitoring, placed on droplet precautions, and treated with a macrolide antibiotic.

options.text: Clear nasal discharge only
Episodes of apnea and cyanosis after coughing fits, sometimes without a "whoop"
Occasional sneezing
Mild fussiness after feeding

questions.stem: A client reports an irresistible urge to move the legs in the evening that improves with walking. Which lab test does the nurse anticipate?
questions.rationale: Iron deficiency is associated with restless legs syndrome, and iron replacement may improve symptoms when ferritin is low. Caffeine, alcohol, and some antidepressants and antihistamines can worsen it.

options.text: Serum ferritin (iron studies)
Hemoglobin A1C
Serum amylase
Thyroid antibodies only

questions.stem: A client is scheduled for an EEG. Which instruction should the nurse include?
questions.rationale: Hair products interfere with electrode contact, and caffeine can affect results. Sleep deprivation may be ordered to increase the chance of capturing abnormal activity. The test is painless.

options.text: "Apply hair conditioner the morning of the test."
"Wash your hair the night before without conditioner or styling products, avoid caffeine as instructed, and follow any sleep deprivation instructions."
"Fast for 24 hours."
"Take an extra dose of your sedative."

questions.stem: A client with an insulin pump has unexplained high glucose readings. The infusion site is red and was placed 5 days ago. What should the nurse advise?
questions.rationale: Old or infected sites absorb insulin poorly and can cause hyperglycemia and DKA. Regular site changes and rotation prevent problems.

options.text: "Keep the same site to avoid wasting supplies."
"Change the infusion set and site now, usually every 2–3 days, rotate sites, and check glucose and ketones closely."
"Stop checking glucose."
"Increase carbohydrate intake."

questions.stem: A client is scheduled for a urea breath test for Helicobacter pylori. Which instruction should the nurse include?
questions.rationale: PPIs, bismuth, and antibiotics suppress H. pylori and can cause false-negative results. Fasting before the test is also typical.

options.text: "Take your omeprazole the morning of the test."
"Stop proton pump inhibitors about 2 weeks before and antibiotics about 4 weeks before the test, unless your provider instructs otherwise."
"Eat a large meal right before the test."
"No preparation is needed."

questions.stem: A client with gallstones develops fever with chills, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain. What does the nurse suspect?
questions.rationale: Charcot's triad (fever, jaundice, RUQ pain) suggests infection of the bile ducts from obstruction. Treatment includes antibiotics, fluids, and urgent biliary drainage, often by ERCP. Confusion and hypotension indicate severe disease.

options.text: Uncomplicated biliary colic
Acute cholangitis, which can rapidly progress to sepsis
Hepatitis A
Gastroenteritis

questions.stem: An older man with benign prostatic hyperplasia took an over-the-counter cold medicine containing pseudoephedrine and diphenhydramine. He now cannot urinate and has lower abdominal pain. What is the likely cause?
questions.rationale: Decongestants tighten bladder neck muscles, and anticholinergics weaken bladder contraction, causing retention in men with BPH. Catheterization is needed, and clients are taught to avoid these products.

options.text: Dehydration
Acute urinary retention caused by the decongestant and antihistamine
Kidney stones
Normal aging

questions.stem: A client with a history of gout has a hot, swollen knee and a temperature of 101.8°F (38.8°C). Which test is most important to distinguish gout from a septic joint?
questions.rationale: Serum uric acid can be normal during a gout flare. Septic arthritis destroys the joint rapidly and requires prompt drainage and antibiotics, and gout and infection can occur together.

options.text: Serum uric acid alone
Joint aspiration with fluid analysis, Gram stain, and culture
X-ray only
Urinalysis

questions.stem: The nurse starts a unit of packed red blood cells for a stable adult. Which approach to the infusion rate is correct?
questions.rationale: Severe reactions such as hemolysis and anaphylaxis usually occur early. A slow start limits the volume given if a reaction occurs. Clients at risk for fluid overload may need slower rates.

options.text: Infuse at the maximum rate from the beginning
Infuse slowly for the first 15 minutes (often about 2 mL/min) while observing closely, then increase to complete within 4 hours if there is no reaction
Infuse over 6 hours
Pause every 5 minutes

questions.stem: A client who received doxorubicin for breast cancer 2 years ago reports new shortness of breath with activity and ankle swelling. What should the nurse recognize?
questions.rationale: Doxorubicin cardiotoxicity is dose-related and can appear years later. Cardiac monitoring is part of cancer survivorship care.

options.text: These symptoms are unrelated to past treatment
Anthracyclines can cause cardiomyopathy and heart failure, so an echocardiogram evaluation is needed
This is normal aging
The symptoms mean the cancer has returned

questions.stem: A client has an expanding bull's-eye rash 10 days after a tick bite. Which treatment does the nurse anticipate?
questions.rationale: Erythema migrans is diagnosed clinically and treated with oral antibiotics such as doxycycline. The nurse teaches sun protection and taking doxycycline with water while remaining upright.

options.text: No treatment is needed
Oral doxycycline for early Lyme disease
IV vancomycin
A topical steroid only

questions.stem: A client with methamphetamine use disorder is admitted. Which findings are commonly associated with chronic methamphetamine use?
questions.rationale: Methamphetamine is a potent stimulant. Acute toxicity can cause hyperthermia, dysrhythmias, stroke, and psychosis. Care includes safety, cooling, benzodiazepines for agitation, and referral for treatment.

options.text: Pinpoint pupils and bradycardia
Severe dental decay, weight loss, skin sores from picking, paranoia, and hypertension
Weight gain and hypothermia
Constricted pupils and respiratory depression

questions.stem: A client is diagnosed with panic disorder. Which long-term treatment approach does the nurse expect?
questions.rationale: SSRIs and SNRIs plus CBT are first-line for panic disorder. Long-term benzodiazepine use carries a risk of dependence, falls, and cognitive effects.

options.text: Daily benzodiazepines indefinitely as the only treatment
An SSRI or SNRI with cognitive behavioral therapy, and short-term benzodiazepine use only if needed
Avoiding all treatment
Antipsychotics as first-line

questions.stem: A client with cervical insufficiency had a cerclage placed at 14 weeks. Which instruction should the nurse include?
questions.rationale: Labor with a cerclage in place can cause cervical tearing. Signs of labor, rupture of membranes, or infection require prompt evaluation.

options.text: "The stitch stays in during vaginal birth."
"Report contractions, leaking fluid, bleeding, or fever right away. The stitch is usually removed around 36–37 weeks."
"You can't feel anything if the stitch fails."
"Use tampons for any spotting."

questions.stem: A 4-month-old has constipation for several days, a weak cry, poor feeding, and decreased muscle tone. The parent says they sweetened the pacifier with honey. What does the nurse suspect?
questions.rationale: Clostridium botulinum spores in honey can colonize an infant's immature gut and produce toxin, causing descending weakness. Honey is avoided before age 1. The nurse monitors breathing and swallowing.

options.text: Teething
Infant botulism
Colic
Gastroesophageal reflux

questions.stem: Highlight (circle) the findings that require immediate follow-up.
questions.rationale: Severe pain with a relatively benign exam is the classic sign of early mesenteric ischemia. Elevated lactate and acidosis indicate tissue hypoperfusion. AF without anticoagulation is the embolic source. SpO2 is acceptable.
questions.answer_summary: Pain out of proportion to exam; AF with rapid rate; borderline BP; elevated lactate; metabolic acidosis; leukocytosis; no anticoagulation

passage_segments.text: Pain 10/10 with only mild tenderness on exam

questions.correct_text: Pain out of proportion to exam; AF with rapid rate; borderline BP; elevated lactate; metabolic acidosis; leukocytosis; no anticoagulation

questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is more typical of early mesenteric ischemia or progression to bowel infarction.
questions.rationale: Early ischemia causes intense pain and gut spasm before the full bowel wall is damaged. Peritoneal signs, bleeding, and sepsis indicate transmural necrosis, which greatly increases mortality.
questions.answer_summary: Early: pain out of proportion, forceful bowel emptying, hyperactive bowel sounds. Infarction: peritoneal signs, bloody stools, fever with hypotension.

rows.text: Severe pain with a soft abdomen

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.rationale: An SMA embolus cuts off blood flow to much of the small bowel and right colon. Every hour of delay increases bowel death and mortality.
questions.answer_summary: 1: acute mesenteric ischemia from an embolus related to atrial fibrillation; 2: bowel necrosis, perforation, and sepsis
questions.template: The client has ___1___ and is at high risk for ___2___.

options: acute mesenteric ischemia from an embolus related to atrial fibrillation
blanks.correct: acute mesenteric ischemia from an embolus related to atrial fibrillation

questions.stem: Which interventions does the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Management includes resuscitation, anticoagulation to prevent clot extension, antibiotics for bacterial translocation, and urgent restoration of blood flow with removal of dead bowel. Enemas and delays are harmful.

options.text: Keep the client NPO with nasogastric decompression
IV isotonic fluid resuscitation
IV heparin as prescribed
Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics
Preparation for emergency revascularization and possible bowel resection
A cleansing enema
Waiting 24 hours for the pain to localize before further action

questions.stem: Which prescription should the nurse implement first?
questions.rationale: Restoring circulating volume supports bowel perfusion and treats hypoperfusion shown by the elevated lactate. The client remains NPO.

options.text: Establish large-bore IV access and begin isotonic fluid resuscitation
Insert a urinary catheter
Obtain a stool sample
Encourage sips of clear liquids

questions.stem: The client undergoes embolectomy and bowel resection and is on a heparin infusion. On postoperative day 1, the nurse reassesses. For each finding, indicate whether it shows expected recovery or requires immediate follow-up.
questions.rationale: A falling lactate and stable vital signs show restored perfusion. A rising lactate with distention suggests ongoing ischemia, and a planned second-look surgery may be needed. Bleeding with a supratherapeutic aPTT requires adjusting the heparin.
questions.answer_summary: Expected: normalized lactate, controlled HR, adequate urine output, controlled pain. Follow-up: recurrent ischemia; excessive anticoagulation with bleeding.

rows.text: Rising lactate with increasing abdominal distention
Oozing from the incision and gums with an aPTT of 118 seconds

questions.stem: The nurse in a psychiatric emergency department is caring for four clients. Which client should the nurse assess first?
questions.rationale: An unknown ingestion within the past hour may be life-threatening even if the client appears calm. Some drugs, such as acetaminophen and extended-release medications, show delayed toxicity. Immediate medical evaluation is needed.

options.text: A calm client who says they swallowed "a handful of pills" from a friend about an hour ago
A client with schizophrenia who reports hearing voices that are not giving commands
A client with anxiety pacing in the waiting area
A client with depression requesting a sandwich

questions.stem: A client with chronic hypertension who takes lisinopril tells the nurse she is 6 weeks pregnant. What does the nurse anticipate?
questions.rationale: ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated in pregnancy because they can cause fetal kidney damage and other harm. Labetalol, nifedipine, and methyldopa are commonly used instead.

options.text: Continuing lisinopril
Stopping lisinopril and switching to a pregnancy-compatible antihypertensive such as labetalol or nifedipine
Stopping all BP medications
Adding an ARB

questions.stem: During a code for pulseless electrical activity, the team reviews the H's and T's. Which condition is one of the reversible causes the team should consider?
questions.rationale: The H's are hypovolemia, hypoxia, hydrogen ion (acidosis), hypo- or hyperkalemia, and hypothermia. The T's are tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, and thrombosis (pulmonary or coronary). Treating the cause can restore circulation.

options.text: Hypothermia
Hypercalcemia only
Hyperthyroidism
Hypertension

questions.stem: A client with a new proximal DVT had a hemorrhagic stroke last week. Which intervention does the nurse anticipate?
questions.rationale: An IVC filter traps clots and helps prevent pulmonary embolism when anticoagulation is contraindicated, such as after a recent intracranial hemorrhage. Anticoagulation is started when safe.

options.text: Full-dose heparin infusion
Placement of an inferior vena cava (IVC) filter
Thrombolytic therapy
Massage of the leg

questions.stem: A client with obstructive sleep apnea is receiving IV opioids after surgery. Which monitoring does the nurse anticipate?
questions.rationale: Clients with OSA are at high risk for opioid-induced respiratory depression. Continuous monitoring, CPAP, head elevation or side-lying positioning, and opioid-sparing analgesia reduce risk.

options.text: Vital signs once per shift
Continuous pulse oximetry and, when available, capnography, with the client's home CPAP used while sleeping
No additional monitoring
Keeping the client flat on the back

questions.stem: A client is started on gabapentin for neuropathic pain. Which instruction should the nurse include?
questions.rationale: Gabapentin commonly causes sedation and dizziness, increasing fall risk. Abrupt discontinuation can cause withdrawal or seizures. Combining it with opioids increases the risk of respiratory depression.

options.text: "It works immediately like an opioid."
"It may cause dizziness and drowsiness, so be careful when standing or driving, and don't stop it suddenly."
"Take it with alcohol for better effect."
"It cures nerve damage."

questions.stem: A hospitalized client with Parkinson's disease takes carbidopa-levodopa at 0600, 1000, 1400, and 1800. Why is on-time administration important?
questions.rationale: Parkinson's medications are time-critical. Missed or delayed doses can cause "off" periods and serious complications such as aspiration. Hospitals often schedule these doses at the client's home times.

options.text: Timing doesn't matter
Late doses can cause sudden worsening of rigidity, tremor, swallowing problems, and fall risk as medication levels drop
Late doses cause hypoglycemia
It only affects sleep

questions.stem: A frail 86-year-old with diabetes, dementia, and a history of falls has an A1C of 7.8%. How should the nurse interpret this in light of current guidelines?
questions.rationale: A1C goals are individualized. Tight control increases hypoglycemia risk in frail older adults, which can cause falls and cognitive decline. Many healthy adults target below 7%.

options.text: It must be lowered below 6% immediately
A less strict goal (often below 8%) may be appropriate for older adults with frailty or hypoglycemia risk
Diabetes no longer needs any management
The goal for all adults is below 5%

questions.stem: Which group of findings is consistent with metabolic syndrome?
questions.rationale: Metabolic syndrome is diagnosed when three or more of these five criteria are present. It increases the risk of cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes, and lifestyle change is the cornerstone of treatment.

options.text: Low BP, low triglycerides, and high HDL
Increased waist circumference, elevated triglycerides, low HDL, elevated BP, and elevated fasting glucose
Weight loss and hypoglycemia
Low cholesterol only

questions.stem: A client with cirrhosis and ascites is being discharged. Which instruction should the nurse include?
questions.rationale: Sodium restriction and diuretics (often spironolactone with furosemide) control ascites. Daily weights track fluid, and NSAIDs can cause kidney injury in cirrhosis.

options.text: "Follow a high-sodium diet."
"Limit sodium (often to about 2 g/day), weigh yourself daily, take your diuretics as prescribed, and avoid alcohol and NSAIDs."
"Drink as much fluid as possible."
"Stop your diuretics if you lose weight."

questions.stem: A client who had a laparoscopic cholecystectomy asks about diet. Which response by the nurse is best?
questions.rationale: Bile flows continuously into the intestine after gallbladder removal. Most people tolerate a normal diet, although large fatty meals may cause diarrhea initially.

options.text: "You must avoid all fat forever."
"You can usually return to a normal diet, starting with lower-fat meals and adding fat gradually as tolerated. Some people have loose stools at first."
"Eat only liquids for a month."
"Eat very high-fat meals to help digestion."

questions.stem: A client started hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension. Which lab changes should the nurse monitor for?
questions.rationale: Thiazides cause potassium and sodium loss and calcium retention, and they can raise glucose and uric acid. Gout flares may occur, and older adults are at risk for hyponatremia.

options.text: Hyperkalemia and hypocalcemia
Hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hypercalcemia, hyperglycemia, and hyperuricemia
Hypoglycemia only
No lab changes occur

questions.stem: A client is scheduled for a nuclear medicine bone scan. Which instruction should the nurse include?
questions.rationale: The small tracer dose is cleared mainly through the kidneys. Frequent voiding reduces bladder exposure and improves image quality. There is a waiting period of a few hours between injection and scanning.

options.text: "You will need to be isolated for a week."
"After the tracer injection, drink extra fluids and urinate often to help clear the tracer. Remove metal objects before the scan."
"Avoid all fluids before the scan."
"The scan requires general anesthesia."

questions.stem: A client with beta-thalassemia major receives regular transfusions and has a very high ferritin level. Which treatment does the nurse anticipate?
questions.rationale: Repeated transfusions cause iron overload that can damage the heart, liver, and endocrine organs. Chelators bind excess iron for removal. Iron supplements are avoided.

options.text: Oral iron supplements
Iron chelation therapy, such as deferasirox or deferoxamine
Vitamin C megadoses
Stopping all transfusions

questions.stem: A client with cancer is prescribed a transmucosal fentanyl product for breakthrough pain. Which information is most important for the nurse to verify?
questions.rationale: Transmucosal immediate-release fentanyl is restricted to opioid-tolerant clients. Safe storage away from children is essential, because accidental exposure can be fatal.

options.text: That the client has never taken opioids
That the client is opioid-tolerant (already taking around-the-clock opioids), because these products can cause fatal respiratory depression in opioid-naive people
That the client takes it with grapefruit juice
That the client can chew and swallow it

questions.stem: A nurse sustains a needlestick from a client with hepatitis C. After immediate wound care and reporting, what follow-up does the nurse expect?
questions.rationale: There is no vaccine or post-exposure prophylaxis for hepatitis C. Early detection allows treatment with direct-acting antivirals, which are highly curative.

options.text: No follow-up is needed
Baseline testing, with follow-up HCV RNA and antibody testing over the following weeks to months, and treatment if infection develops
Immediate hepatitis C vaccine
Hepatitis C immune globulin

questions.stem: A client reports depressed mood, fatigue, oversleeping, and carbohydrate cravings every winter that resolve in spring. Which treatment should the nurse expect to be discussed?
questions.rationale: Morning light therapy with a specialized light box helps regulate circadian rhythms. Tanning beds emit UV radiation and are not a substitute.

options.text: Staying indoors in a dark room
Bright light therapy, typically in the morning, along with other treatments such as psychotherapy or antidepressants
Using a tanning bed daily
Avoiding all exercise

questions.stem: A newborn is receiving phototherapy for hyperbilirubinemia. Which nursing action is correct?
questions.rationale: Maximal skin exposure increases effectiveness, and eye shields protect the retina. Phototherapy increases fluid loss, so feeding and hydration are maintained. Lotions can cause burns under the lights.

options.text: Keep the infant fully clothed under the lights
Place eye protection on the infant, expose as much skin as possible, reposition regularly, monitor temperature and hydration, and continue frequent feedings
Apply lotion to the skin before phototherapy
Stop feedings during treatment

questions.stem: A parent asks why the newborn needs a hepatitis B vaccine before discharge when the mother tested negative. What is the nurse's best response?
questions.rationale: The universal birth dose, given within 24 hours, is a safety net against missed or unrecognized exposures. Infants infected early have a high risk of chronic infection.

options.text: "It isn't recommended if the mother tested negative."
"The birth dose is recommended for all medically stable newborns. It protects against infection from unknown exposures and starts the vaccine series early."
"It prevents jaundice."
"It's only for babies born by cesarean."

questions.stem: Highlight (circle) the findings that require immediate follow-up.
questions.rationale: These findings indicate placental abruption with fetal compromise, maternal hemorrhage, and developing coagulopathy. Rh-negative status requires Rh immune globulin after trauma. Pregnancy's increased blood volume can hide significant blood loss until late.
questions.answer_summary: Rigid uterus; dark bleeding with constant pain; fetal tachycardia with minimal variability and late decels; maternal tachycardia with falling BP; low fibrinogen; falling platelets; Rh-negative status

passage_segments.text: Rigid, tender uterus that doesn't relax
Dark red vaginal bleeding with constant pain
FHR 170/min with minimal variability and late decelerations

questions.correct_text: Rigid uterus; dark bleeding with constant pain; fetal tachycardia with minimal variability and late decels; maternal tachycardia with falling BP; low fibrinogen; falling platelets; Rh-negative status

questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is more consistent with placental abruption or placenta previa.
questions.rationale: In abruption, the placenta separates from the uterine wall, causing pain and blood that may be concealed behind the placenta. In previa, the placenta covers or is near the cervix and bleeds painlessly as the cervix changes.
questions.answer_summary: Abruption: painful rigid uterus, dark bleeding, trauma. Previa: painless bright red bleeding, soft uterus, low-lying placenta.

rows.text: Placenta low in the uterus near or over the cervix

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.rationale: Abruption releases tissue factor that consumes clotting factors, causing a falling fibrinogen. A fibrinogen below 200 mg/dL is associated with severe hemorrhage. Fetal tachycardia, minimal variability, and late decelerations indicate hypoxia.
questions.answer_summary: 1: placental abruption; 2: fetal compromise, maternal hemorrhage, and early DIC
questions.template: The client is experiencing ___1___ with ___2___.

options: fetal compromise, maternal hemorrhage, and early DIC
blanks.correct: fetal compromise, maternal hemorrhage, and early DIC

questions.stem: Which interventions does the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Management includes positioning to improve placental perfusion, hemorrhage and coagulopathy resuscitation, fetal surveillance, and expedited delivery when mother or fetus is compromised. A Kleihauer-Betke test guides the Rh immune globulin dose after trauma. Tocolytics are contraindicated in abruption, and delay risks fetal death.

options.text: Left lateral positioning or manual uterine displacement
Two large-bore IVs with blood products, including cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen as prescribed
Continuous fetal monitoring
Preparation for emergency cesarean birth
Rh immune globulin, with testing to determine the dose needed
Tocolytics to stop the contractions
Delaying delivery until 34 weeks for corticosteroids

questions.stem: Which action should the nurse take first?
questions.rationale: Lateral positioning relieves aortocaval compression, improving venous return, maternal cardiac output, and placental blood flow. The other actions follow.

options.text: Position the client on her left side (or tilt the uterus to the left)
Obtain a Kleihauer-Betke test
Administer Rh immune globulin
Perform a digital cervical exam

questions.stem: After emergency cesarean birth and transfusion, the nurse reassesses the client. For each finding, indicate whether it shows effective treatment or requires immediate follow-up.
questions.rationale: A firm uterus, stabilized hemodynamics, and corrected fibrinogen show response. Oozing from multiple sites suggests continuing coagulopathy, and low urine output suggests inadequate perfusion or kidney injury.
questions.answer_summary: Effective: firm fundus, stable BP, improved fibrinogen, stable newborn. Follow-up: oozing (possible ongoing DIC); oliguria (possible hypoperfusion or AKI).

rows.text: BP 118/72 mm Hg after 2 units of packed red cells
Oozing from IV sites and around the incision

questions.stem: The nurse in the neonatal intensive care unit is caring for four infants. Which infant should the nurse assess first?
questions.rationale: Apnea longer than 20 seconds with bradycardia is a life-threatening event requiring immediate stimulation and respiratory support. Caffeine citrate is commonly used for apnea of prematurity.

options.text: A 30-week preterm infant with repeated apnea spells longer than 20 seconds and heart rate drops to 70/min
A 34-week infant tolerating gavage feedings
A term infant receiving phototherapy for mild jaundice
A 36-week infant in an open crib with stable temperature

questions.stem: A 22-year-old with hypertension is being evaluated for coarctation of the aorta. Which finding supports this diagnosis?
questions.rationale: Narrowing of the aorta, usually beyond the left subclavian artery, causes high pressure proximal to it and reduced flow below it. Normally, leg pressures are equal to or slightly higher than arm pressures.

options.text: BP higher in the legs than the arms
BP higher in the arms than the legs, with weak or delayed femoral pulses
Equal pulses in all extremities
Bradycardia with a narrow pulse pressure

questions.stem: A 35-year-old who smokes is diagnosed with thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger's disease) with painful fingertip ulcers. Which intervention is most important?
questions.rationale: Buerger's disease is strongly linked to tobacco use. Complete abstinence is the only intervention proven to halt progression and prevent amputation.

options.text: Increase smoking to reduce stress
Complete cessation of all tobacco and nicotine products
Apply ice to the fingers
Begin high-intensity exercise immediately

questions.stem: The nurse notes that fluctuation (tidaling) in the water-seal chamber of a client's chest tube has stopped. What should the nurse do?
questions.rationale: Loss of tidaling may mean the lung has fully re-expanded (a chest x-ray confirms) or that the tube is blocked. Dependent loops, kinks, and clots are checked, and new respiratory distress is reported.

options.text: Clamp the tube
Assess whether the lung has re-expanded or the tubing is kinked, clotted, or obstructed, and check breath sounds and the client's respiratory status
Strip the tubing vigorously
Increase the suction to maximum

questions.stem: A client with pulmonary tuberculosis has been on treatment for 2 weeks. When can airborne isolation generally be discontinued in the hospital?
questions.rationale: These criteria indicate the client is unlikely to be infectious. Treatment continues for the full course, often with directly observed therapy.

options.text: As soon as the cough improves
When the client is improving clinically on effective therapy and has three consecutive negative sputum AFB smears collected per protocol
After 24 hours of antibiotics
Only after 6 months of treatment

questions.stem: A client had a craniotomy for a tumor in the posterior fossa (infratentorial). Which position does the nurse anticipate after surgery?
questions.rationale: Infratentorial surgery may require flatter positioning to reduce pressure on the incision and brainstem. Supratentorial procedures typically use head-of-bed elevation of about 30 degrees. Surgeon orders guide positioning.

options.text: High-Fowler's at 90 degrees
Positioning as prescribed by the surgeon, often flat or with slight elevation, lying to the side and avoiding neck flexion
Prone with the neck flexed
Trendelenburg

questions.stem: A client with a large-vessel ischemic stroke arrives 10 hours after last known well and is outside the window for IV alteplase. Which treatment may still be considered?
questions.rationale: Thrombectomy can benefit selected clients with large-vessel occlusion and salvageable brain tissue on imaging well beyond the alteplase window. Rapid transfer to a stroke center is key.

options.text: No treatment is available after 4.5 hours
Mechanical thrombectomy, for selected clients up to 24 hours after last known well based on imaging
IV heparin bolus
Oral aspirin only, immediately, before imaging

questions.stem: A client with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), insulin resistance, and irregular periods is prescribed metformin. How does the nurse explain its purpose?
questions.rationale: Insulin resistance drives many PCOS features. Lifestyle changes and metformin improve metabolic health, and hormonal contraceptives may also be used to regulate cycles.

options.text: "It is a hormone that stops ovulation."
"It improves insulin sensitivity, which may help regulate cycles and lower the risk of type 2 diabetes."
"It causes weight gain to balance hormones."
"It is only for pain."

questions.stem: A client is going home after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass. Which long-term instruction is most important?
questions.rationale: Bypass surgery reduces absorption of several nutrients, leading to deficiencies such as anemia, bone loss, and neuropathy if not supplemented.

options.text: "You won't need vitamins after surgery."
"Take lifelong supplements as prescribed, including a multivitamin, calcium with vitamin D, vitamin B12, and iron, and have regular lab monitoring."
"Eat large meals to prevent weight loss."
"Drink carbonated drinks with meals."

questions.stem: A client had a hemorrhoidectomy this morning. Which instruction should the nurse include?
questions.rationale: Delaying bowel movements leads to hard stool and more pain. Softeners, fluids, analgesia, and warm sitz baths ease recovery. Heavy bleeding or inability to void is reported.

options.text: "Avoid having a bowel movement for a week."
"Take the prescribed stool softener and pain medication, use sitz baths, drink fluids, and don't delay your first bowel movement, although it may be uncomfortable."
"Strain to empty your bowels completely."
"Sit on a hard chair for long periods."

questions.stem: A 20-kg child is recovering from surgery. What is the minimum acceptable urine output per hour?
questions.rationale: Children generally should produce at least about 1 mL/kg/hr, and infants about 1–2 mL/kg/hr. Lower output suggests inadequate perfusion or dehydration.

options.text: About 5 mL/hr
About 20 mL/hr (1 mL/kg/hr)
About 100 mL/hr
About 200 mL/hr

questions.stem: A toddler is in a hip spica cast. Which instruction should the nurse give the parents?
questions.rationale: Keeping urine and stool away from the cast prevents soiling and skin breakdown. The bar is not a handle. Small objects placed inside the cast can cause pressure injuries.

options.text: "Put the diaper over the cast."
"Tuck a small diaper inside the cast edges at the perineal opening, cover it with a larger diaper, check the skin at the cast edges often, and never lift the child by the abduction bar."
"Let the child stand on the cast right away."
"Stuff small toys inside the cast for comfort."

questions.stem: A trauma client is receiving a massive transfusion of many units of blood products. Which complications should the nurse monitor for?
questions.rationale: Citrate binds calcium. Cold blood causes hypothermia, which worsens bleeding. Replacing red cells without enough plasma and platelets dilutes clotting factors. Blood warmers, calcium replacement, and balanced ratios are used.

options.text: Hyperglycemia and hypernatremia
Hypocalcemia from citrate, hypothermia, and coagulopathy
Hypokalemia only
Hypertension and bradycardia only

questions.stem: A postmenopausal client is taking anastrozole after treatment for breast cancer. Which monitoring does the nurse expect?
questions.rationale: Lowering estrogen accelerates bone loss. Calcium, vitamin D, weight-bearing exercise, and sometimes bisphosphonates help. Joint aches are also common.

options.text: Weekly INR checks
Baseline and periodic bone density testing, since aromatase inhibitors can cause bone loss
Daily blood glucose checks
Monthly chest x-rays

questions.stem: A 45-year-old receiving immunosuppressive therapy for rheumatoid arthritis asks about the shingles vaccine. Which response is accurate?
questions.rationale: The recombinant zoster vaccine is non-live, so it is safe and recommended for immunocompromised adults 19 and older. Timing may be coordinated with immunosuppressive therapy.

options.text: "You can't get any shingles vaccine because you're immunocompromised."
"The recombinant (non-live) shingles vaccine is recommended for adults 19 and older with weakened immune systems, so ask your provider about timing."
"You need the live shingles vaccine."
"Only people over 80 can get it."

questions.stem: A client has taken lithium for many years. In addition to lithium levels, which labs should the nurse expect to be monitored?
questions.rationale: Lithium can cause hypothyroidism, chronic kidney disease, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, and hyperparathyroidism. Regular monitoring detects these problems early.

options.text: Liver enzymes only
Thyroid function (TSH) and kidney function (creatinine/eGFR), plus calcium
Hemoglobin A1C only
Amylase and lipase

questions.stem: A client is at 41 weeks and 3 days of gestation. Which concern guides the nurse's teaching and the planned monitoring?
questions.rationale: After 41 weeks, placental aging increases the risk of stillbirth, macrosomia, and meconium aspiration. Nonstress tests, amniotic fluid assessment, and induction are commonly offered.

options.text: Postterm pregnancy has no added risk
Risk of decreasing placental function and amniotic fluid (oligohydramnios), with increased risk of fetal compromise and meconium, so fetal surveillance and discussion of induction are recommended
Risk of the fetus being too small to deliver
Risk of preterm labor

questions.stem: Immediately after the provider performs an amniotomy (artificial rupture of membranes), what should the nurse do first?
questions.rationale: Rupture of membranes can cause cord prolapse, which shows as FHR changes. Green (meconium-stained), bloody, or foul-smelling fluid requires further evaluation.

options.text: Document the time only
Assess the fetal heart rate and note the color, amount, and odor of the amniotic fluid
Encourage the client to walk right away
Administer oxytocin immediately

questions.stem: A 2-month-old with a large ventricular septal defect is being monitored for heart failure. Which findings should the nurse report?
questions.rationale: Feeding is exertion for infants. Tachypnea, diaphoresis, and fatigue during feeds with poor growth suggest heart failure. Management includes diuretics and high-calorie feeds, often with surgical repair.

options.text: Steady weight gain and feeding in 15 minutes
Sweating and fast breathing during feedings, tiring before finishing bottles, and poor weight gain
Sleeping 16 hours a day
Pink mucous membranes

questions.stem: Highlight (circle) the findings that require immediate follow-up.
questions.rationale: These are the hallmark metabolic abnormalities of tumor lysis syndrome, which can cause lethal dysrhythmias, seizures, and kidney failure. G6PD status matters before rasburicase. SpO2 is normal.
questions.answer_summary: Hyperkalemia with ECG changes; PVCs; hypocalcemia with Chvostek's sign; hyperphosphatemia; hyperuricemia; acute kidney injury with oliguria; unknown G6PD status

passage_segments.text: Potassium 6.6 mEq/L with peaked T waves
Calcium 6.8 mg/dL with positive Chvostek's sign
Creatinine 2.3 mg/dL with urine output 20 mL/hr

questions.correct_text: Hyperkalemia with ECG changes; PVCs; hypocalcemia with Chvostek's sign; hyperphosphatemia; hyperuricemia; acute kidney injury with oliguria; unknown G6PD status

questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it primarily reflects hyperkalemia, hypocalcemia, or acute kidney injury.
questions.rationale: Lysed tumor cells release potassium, phosphate, and nucleic acids. Phosphate binds calcium, and uric acid and calcium-phosphate crystals damage the kidneys, which further impairs potassium excretion.
questions.answer_summary: Hyperkalemia: peaked T waves, ectopy with K 6.6. Hypocalcemia: cramps and tingling, Chvostek's sign. AKI: rising creatinine, oliguria.

rows.text: Weakness with frequent PVCs and a potassium of 6.6

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.rationale: Burkitt lymphoma is highly chemosensitive and carries a high risk of TLS. Hyperkalemia with ECG changes can progress to ventricular fibrillation.
questions.answer_summary: 1: tumor lysis syndrome; 2: a cardiac dysrhythmia from hyperkalemia
questions.template: The client has ___1___, and the most immediate threat to life is ___2___.

questions.stem: Which interventions does the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Hydration improves kidney excretion, rasburicase rapidly lowers uric acid, and hyperkalemia is treated urgently. Dialysis may be needed for refractory abnormalities or kidney failure. Potassium supplementation and fluid restriction would worsen the condition.

options.text: Aggressive IV hydration with close monitoring of urine output
Rasburicase, after G6PD status is confirmed
Continuous cardiac monitoring
Treatment of hyperkalemia as prescribed (calcium gluconate for ECG changes, insulin with dextrose)
Nephrology consultation for possible dialysis
Adding potassium chloride to the IV fluids
Restricting all fluids

questions.stem: Rasburicase is prescribed. Which action is essential before the nurse administers it?
questions.rationale: Rasburicase generates hydrogen peroxide and can cause severe hemolysis and methemoglobinemia in people with G6PD deficiency. Testing is required before use.

options.text: Confirm the client's G6PD status
Give it with grapefruit juice
Confirm that the client has eaten
Check a hemoglobin A1C

questions.stem: Twenty-four hours later, the nurse reassesses the client. For each finding, indicate whether it shows effective treatment or requires follow-up.
questions.rationale: Normalized electrolytes and improving kidney function show response. Aggressive hydration can cause pulmonary edema, requiring diuretics or dialysis. Dark urine with falling hemoglobin suggests hemolysis, which occurs with unrecognized G6PD deficiency.
questions.answer_summary: Effective: normal potassium and ECG, good urine output, normal uric acid, improving creatinine. Follow-up: fluid overload; possible hemolysis.

rows.text: Potassium 4.8 mEq/L with normal T waves
New crackles and SpO2 88% on room air
Dark brown urine with a falling hemoglobin after rasburicase

questions.stem: The obstetric triage nurse receives four phone calls. Which client should the nurse call back first?
questions.rationale: Decreased fetal movement can signal fetal compromise and needs prompt evaluation, such as a nonstress test. The other concerns are routine.

options.text: A client at 38 weeks who reports the baby has moved much less than usual for the past 12 hours
A client at 12 weeks with morning nausea
A client at 28 weeks asking about a glucose test appointment
A client at 34 weeks with mild ankle swelling in the evening

questions.stem: A client with peripheral arterial disease has calf pain when walking one block. Which recommendation is most effective for improving walking distance?
questions.rationale: Structured walking programs promote collateral circulation and significantly increase pain-free walking distance. Smoking cessation and medications are also important.

options.text: "Avoid walking to prevent pain."
"Join a supervised exercise program: walk until moderate pain, rest until it resolves, then repeat, for about 30–45 minutes at least three times a week."
"Elevate your legs above your heart when they hurt."
"Use a heating pad on your legs daily."

questions.stem: A client is going home after coronary artery bypass surgery through a median sternotomy. Which instruction should the nurse include?
questions.rationale: Sternal precautions protect the healing sternum from separation. Some programs now use individualized "move in the tube" guidance, but heavy strain is still avoided early on.

options.text: "Push yourself up from the bed with both arms."
"Avoid lifting, pushing, or pulling more than about 5–10 lb, and don't drive until cleared. Hug a pillow when you cough."
"Resume weightlifting next week."
"Reach over your head often to stretch the incision."

questions.stem: A client with a low clinical probability of pulmonary embolism has a normal D-dimer result. How should the nurse interpret this?
questions.rationale: D-dimer is sensitive but not specific. A normal result makes a clot unlikely in low-risk clients. An elevated result is nonspecific and occurs with surgery, pregnancy, infection, and older age.

options.text: PE is confirmed
A normal D-dimer in a low-probability client helps rule out PE
The test must be repeated daily
D-dimer is only used for heart attacks

questions.stem: A client has a stab wound to the chest with air bubbling and a sucking sound during breathing. What should the nurse do first?
questions.rationale: A vented dressing prevents air from entering during inspiration while allowing trapped air to escape, reducing the risk of tension pneumothorax. Chest tube placement follows.

options.text: Pack the wound tightly with gauze
Cover the wound with a vented chest seal or a sterile occlusive dressing taped on three sides, and monitor for tension pneumothorax
Leave the wound open
Have the client lie on the uninjured side and walk

questions.stem: An 80-year-old taking apixaban fell 3 weeks ago without apparent injury. The family now reports gradually worsening confusion, headaches, and unsteady walking. What does the nurse suspect?
questions.rationale: Brain atrophy stretches bridging veins in older adults, and anticoagulation increases the risk of slow bleeding. Symptoms can develop weeks after minor trauma and may be mistaken for dementia. A CT scan is needed.

options.text: Normal aging
A chronic subdural hematoma
An acute epidural hematoma
Urinary tract infection only

questions.stem: A client with an acute ischemic stroke is not eligible for thrombolytics or thrombectomy. BP is 196/104 mm Hg. What does the nurse anticipate?
questions.rationale: Lowering BP too quickly can extend the infarct. Clients receiving alteplase have stricter targets (below 185/110 before and 180/105 after).

options.text: Rapidly lowering BP to 120/80 mm Hg
Permissive hypertension, avoiding treatment unless BP exceeds about 220/120 mm Hg in the first 24–48 hours, to preserve blood flow to at-risk brain tissue
Giving IV nitroprusside immediately to normalize BP
Stopping all monitoring

questions.stem: A client with long-standing type 1 diabetes no longer feels shaky or sweaty before low glucose readings and had a severe low while driving. Which intervention should the nurse anticipate?
questions.rationale: Repeated hypoglycemia blunts warning symptoms. Avoiding lows for 2–3 weeks can restore awareness. CGM alarms and checking glucose before driving improve safety.

options.text: Tightening glucose targets further
Strictly avoiding hypoglycemia for several weeks, raising glucose targets temporarily, using a CGM with alerts, and checking glucose before driving
Stopping insulin
Driving only at night

questions.stem: A client with chronic pancreatitis has greasy, foul-smelling stools and weight loss. Which instruction is most important?
questions.rationale: Loss of exocrine function causes fat malabsorption, and loss of endocrine function can cause diabetes. Alcohol cessation slows progression, and fat-soluble vitamins may be needed.

options.text: "Take pancreatic enzymes with every meal and snack, avoid alcohol completely, and have your glucose checked regularly."
"Eat a very high-fat diet."
"Drink alcohol in moderation."
"Take enzymes once a week."

questions.stem: A client with long-standing ulcerative colitis in remission on mesalamine asks about follow-up. Which information should the nurse include?
questions.rationale: Surveillance usually begins about 8 years after diagnosis. Maintenance therapy reduces flares and may lower cancer risk.

options.text: "No follow-up is needed once symptoms go away."
"Continue your maintenance medication, and plan regular surveillance colonoscopies because long-standing UC increases colon cancer risk."
"Stop mesalamine when you feel well."
"Colon cancer risk is lower with UC."

questions.stem: A client receives intravesical BCG for superficial bladder cancer. Which instruction should the nurse include?
questions.rationale: BCG is a live, attenuated bacterium. Retention allows contact with the bladder lining. Disinfection protects household members. Fever or flu-like symptoms lasting more than 48 hours should be reported.

options.text: "Urinate immediately after the treatment."

"Hold the solution in your bladder for about 2 hours as instructed. For about 6 hours afterward, sit to urinate, add bleach to the toilet for 15 minutes before flushing, and wash your hands and genitals."
"BCG is not infectious."
"Drink no fluids for 24 hours."

questions.stem: A 72-year-old with osteoporosis reports sudden mid-back pain after lifting a laundry basket. Height has decreased by 1.5 inches since last year. What does the nurse suspect?
questions.rationale: Osteoporotic vertebral fractures can occur with minimal stress and cause height loss and kyphosis. Pain management, early mobility, and osteoporosis treatment are important.

options.text: A muscle strain only
A vertebral compression fracture
Kidney stones
Normal aging with no fracture

questions.stem: Ten days after a transfusion, a client has fever, mild jaundice, and a hemoglobin that has dropped below the post-transfusion level. What does the nurse suspect?
questions.rationale: Delayed hemolysis occurs 3–14 days later when antibodies to minor red cell antigens develop. It is usually milder than acute hemolysis. The blood bank is notified, and future transfusions need antigen-matched blood.

options.text: An acute hemolytic reaction
A delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction
Iron deficiency anemia
Hepatitis A

questions.stem: A client received highly emetogenic chemotherapy yesterday and is now having nausea at home on day 2. Which teaching is most important?
questions.rationale: Delayed nausea commonly peaks days 2–3. Scheduled prophylaxis works better than treating established nausea. Dehydration needs prompt intervention.

options.text: "Nausea only happens on the day of treatment."
"Take your prescribed antiemetics on schedule for the full number of days, not just when nausea is severe, and call if you can't keep fluids down."
"Stop eating for 3 days."
"Take antiemetics only once a week."

questions.stem: A 5-day-old newborn is brought in with poor feeding, lethargy, and a temperature of 96.5°F (35.8°C). What does the nurse suspect?
questions.rationale: Newborns with serious infection may have hypothermia, lethargy, poor feeding, or apnea. Urgent evaluation with cultures and empiric antibiotics is needed.

options.text: Normal newborn behavior
Possible neonatal sepsis, which often causes temperature instability, including low temperature, rather than fever
Teething
Overdressing

questions.stem: A transgender client's legal name in the record differs from the name they use. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
questions.rationale: Respecting chosen names and pronouns supports dignity and trust. Two-identifier verification still uses legal information to ensure safety.

options.text: Use the legal name in all conversations
Ask the client which name and pronouns they use, use them consistently, and document per facility policy while using legal identifiers for safety checks
Avoid addressing the client by name
Ask the client's family instead

questions.stem: During delivery of the placenta, the nurse sees a mass protruding from the vagina, and the client has sudden hemorrhage and hypotension. The fundus cannot be felt abdominally. What should the nurse do?
questions.rationale: Uterine inversion is a life-threatening emergency. Oxytocin is stopped until the uterus is repositioned, and then given to keep it contracted. Traction on the cord before separation is a risk factor.

options.text: Pull on the umbilical cord to deliver the placenta
Call for emergency help immediately, stop any oxytocin infusion, and prepare for immediate uterine repositioning and resuscitation
Massage the fundus vigorously
Place the client in high-Fowler's position

questions.stem: A newborn is born through meconium-stained amniotic fluid and is crying vigorously with good tone. What does the nurse anticipate under current neonatal resuscitation guidelines?
questions.rationale: Vigorous newborns need no special intervention. Routine intubation for suctioning is no longer recommended, even for nonvigorous newborns. The team monitors for respiratory distress.

options.text: Immediate intubation and tracheal suctioning
Routine newborn care with the mother, including clearing secretions from the mouth and nose as needed
Deep suctioning of the stomach
Transfer to the NICU regardless of condition

questions.stem: A 4-month-old has a fever of 102.4°F (39.1°C) without an obvious source. Which test does the nurse anticipate?
questions.rationale: UTI is a common cause of fever without a source in infants, who often have nonspecific symptoms. Bag specimens are unreliable for culture. Imaging may follow to evaluate for reflux.

options.text: Chest x-ray only
Urinalysis and urine culture, collected by catheterization
Throat culture
Stool culture

questions.stem: Highlight (circle) the findings that support the suspected diagnosis and require follow-up.
questions.rationale: Fever of 5 or more days plus at least four of five features (conjunctival injection, oral changes, rash, extremity changes, cervical lymphadenopathy) meets criteria for Kawasaki disease. Clear lungs and normal perfusion are reassuring.
questions.answer_summary: Prolonged fever; bilateral conjunctival injection; oral changes; extremity changes; cervical lymphadenopathy; rash

passage_segments.text: Fever for 6 days unresponsive to antipyretics

questions.correct_text: Prolonged fever; bilateral conjunctival injection; oral changes; extremity changes; cervical lymphadenopathy; rash

questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it typically occurs in the acute phase or the subacute phase of Kawasaki disease.
questions.rationale: The acute phase lasts about 1–2 weeks. The subacute phase (about weeks 2–4) brings periungual peeling, rising platelets, and the greatest risk of coronary aneurysm and thrombosis.
questions.answer_summary: Acute: fever, conjunctivitis, extremity swelling. Subacute: desquamation, thrombocytosis, peak aneurysm risk.

rows.text: Peeling skin on the fingers and toes
Highest risk of coronary artery aneurysm development

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.rationale: Kawasaki disease is an acute vasculitis and a leading cause of acquired heart disease in children. Scarlet fever and measles have different features, such as a sandpaper rash with strep or a cough with Koplik spots, and would not persist despite appropriate care.
questions.template: The child most likely has ___1___, and the most serious complication to prevent is ___2___.

questions.stem: Which interventions does the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: IVIG given within 10 days of fever onset greatly reduces aneurysm risk. Aspirin provides anti-inflammatory and antiplatelet effects. Live vaccines are delayed about 11 months after IVIG, and ibuprofen interferes with aspirin's antiplatelet effect.

options.text: IV immunoglobulin (IVIG) as a single high-dose infusion
High- or moderate-dose aspirin initially, followed by low-dose aspirin
Echocardiograms at diagnosis and follow-up
Monitoring for IVIG infusion reactions and fluid overload
Comfort measures such as lip care and a calm environment
Live vaccines (such as MMR) next week as scheduled
Ibuprofen along with aspirin

questions.stem: While the child is taking aspirin, the parent reports that a sibling at home was just diagnosed with influenza. What should the nurse do?
questions.rationale: Aspirin plus influenza or varicella infection is associated with Reye's syndrome, which can cause liver failure and encephalopathy. The provider may adjust therapy, and inactivated influenza vaccination is recommended.

options.text: Reassure the parent that no action is needed
Notify the provider, because influenza or varicella during aspirin therapy increases the risk of Reye's syndrome
Double the aspirin dose
Give the child the live intranasal flu vaccine

questions.stem: After IVIG, the nurse evaluates the child. For each finding, indicate whether it shows expected response or requires follow-up.
questions.rationale: Fever lasting more than 36 hours after IVIG suggests resistance, which usually requires a second dose or other therapy. Coronary changes require cardiology management and closer follow-up.
questions.answer_summary: Expected: fever resolves, improved behavior, fingertip peeling (expected subacute finding), falling CRP. Follow-up: persistent fever (IVIG resistance), coronary dilation.

rows.text: Fever persisting 40 hours after the IVIG infusion ended

questions.stem: The nurse in an outpatient hemodialysis unit is caring for four clients. Which client should the nurse assess first?
questions.rationale: Chest pain with sudden hypotension during dialysis may indicate cardiac ischemia, hemorrhage, air embolism, or a reaction. The nurse stops or slows ultrafiltration, places the client in Trendelenburg or supine position, and escalates. Leg cramps are common and less urgent.

options.text: A client 1 hour into treatment who reports new chest pain, with BP falling from 138/80 to 82/50 mm Hg
A client reporting mild leg cramps near the end of treatment
A client asking for a snack
A client whose fistula has a strong thrill and bruit

questions.stem: A 20-year-old college athlete is recovering from viral myocarditis. Which instruction is most important?
questions.rationale: Myocarditis is a known cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes. Return to sport requires evaluation that may include ECG, echocardiogram, and exercise testing.

options.text: "You can return to competitive sports next week."
"Avoid competitive sports and strenuous exercise for several months, typically 3–6, until cleared by cardiology, because exertion increases the risk of dangerous heart rhythms."
"Exercise will speed healing of the heart muscle."
"Myocarditis never causes lasting effects."

questions.stem: A client who had a drug-eluting coronary stent placed 2 months ago tells the nurse they plan to stop clopidogrel before a dental cleaning. What is the nurse's best response?
questions.rationale: Premature discontinuation of dual antiplatelet therapy is a major cause of stent thrombosis, which can cause MI or death. Most dental cleanings can be done while continuing antiplatelets.

options.text: "That's fine; stop it a week before."
"Don't stop clopidogrel without talking to your cardiologist, because stopping early greatly increases the risk of a clot forming in the stent."
"Stop aspirin instead."
"Double the dose after the cleaning."

questions.stem: A client with COPD is given high-flow oxygen by mistake. The client becomes drowsy and has a headache, and the skin is warm and flushed. What does the nurse suspect?
questions.rationale: Hypercapnia causes vasodilation (flushed skin, headache) and CNS depression. The nurse obtains an ABG, adjusts oxygen to the target range, and prepares for ventilatory support if needed.

options.text: Hypoglycemia
Rising carbon dioxide levels (hypercapnia)
Anaphylaxis
Hypothermia

questions.stem: During a thoracentesis, 1,500 mL of fluid has been removed. The client develops coughing and chest tightness. What should the nurse anticipate?
questions.rationale: Many providers limit removal to about 1–1.5 L at a time. Coughing, chest discomfort, and dyspnea are signals to stop. The nurse monitors for hypoxemia and hypotension.

options.text: Continuing to drain until no more fluid remains
Stopping the procedure, because removing large volumes quickly can cause re-expansion pulmonary edema
Increasing the drainage rate
Having the client lie flat

questions.stem: A client with essential tremor is prescribed propranolol. Which condition in the client's history should the nurse report before the first dose?
questions.rationale: Propranolol is a nonselective beta blocker that can trigger bronchospasm. It can also mask hypoglycemia and cause bradycardia and fatigue. Primidone is an alternative.

options.text: Seasonal allergies
Asthma with frequent bronchospasm
Mild osteoarthritis
Hypothyroidism controlled with medication

questions.stem: A client with suspected meningitis has papilledema, new confusion, and a focal neurological deficit. What does the nurse anticipate before any lumbar puncture?
questions.rationale: Removing CSF when ICP is elevated from a mass lesion can cause brain herniation. Empiric antibiotics are not delayed for imaging.

options.text: Proceeding with the lumbar puncture immediately
A head CT to rule out a mass or raised ICP before the lumbar puncture, with antibiotics given without delay
Delaying antibiotics until after the lumbar puncture
Performing the lumbar puncture with the client sitting upright only

questions.stem: A client with type 1 diabetes plans to become pregnant next year. Which recommendation should the nurse emphasize?
questions.rationale: High glucose during organ formation in early pregnancy increases the risk of birth defects and miscarriage. Preconception care improves outcomes. Some medications, such as ACE inhibitors and statins, are stopped.

options.text: "Glucose control doesn't matter until the third trimester."
"Aim for tight glucose control before conception (often an A1C below 6.5% if safely achievable), take folic acid, and review medications with your provider."
"Stop insulin when you become pregnant."
"Pregnancy will cure your diabetes."

questions.stem: A 66-year-old with long-standing GERD reports that swallowing has become harder over several months, first with solids and now with soft foods, along with a 15-lb weight loss. What should the nurse do?
questions.rationale: Progressive dysphagia from solids to liquids suggests a narrowing, such as a tumor or stricture. Endoscopy is needed.

options.text: Recommend drinking more water with meals
Refer promptly for evaluation, because progressive difficulty swallowing with weight loss is a warning sign of esophageal cancer
Suggest eating faster
Reassure the client that this is normal aging

questions.topic: GI bleeding risk with combined drugs
questions.stem: An older adult takes daily naproxen for arthritis and was recently started on sertraline. Why is the nurse concerned?
questions.rationale: NSAIDs damage the gastric lining, and SSRIs impair platelet function. Together they raise bleeding risk. The provider may consider a safer analgesic or a PPI.

options.text: The combination causes hypertension
The combination increases the risk of GI bleeding
The combination causes hyperglycemia
There is no concern

questions.stem: A client with acute epididymitis has a painful, swollen scrotum. Which comfort measures should the nurse recommend with the prescribed antibiotics?
questions.rationale: Support and cold reduce swelling and pain. Sexually transmitted causes require partner treatment. Sudden severe pain in younger males must be distinguished from testicular torsion.

options.text: Heat applied directly for hours
Scrotal support or elevation, cold packs, rest, and pain relief
Vigorous exercise
Tight-fitting clothing

questions.stem: An 80-year-old with knee osteoarthritis and chronic kidney disease asks about pain relief. Which option has lower systemic risk than oral NSAIDs?
questions.rationale: Topical NSAIDs provide local relief with much lower blood levels, which reduces GI, kidney, and cardiovascular risks. Acetaminophen is another option.

options.text: High-dose oral ibuprofen
Topical diclofenac gel applied to the knee as directed
Oral naproxen twice daily
Aspirin 1,000 mg four times daily

questions.stem: A client is prescribed rivaroxaban 20 mg daily for atrial fibrillation. Which instruction should the nurse include?
questions.rationale: The 15-mg and 20-mg rivaroxaban doses are absorbed better with food. INR monitoring is not used, and doses are not stopped without provider guidance.

options.text: "Take it on an empty stomach."
"Take this dose with your evening meal for proper absorption, and report any unusual bleeding."
"Have weekly INR checks."
"Stop it before dental work without asking."

questions.stem: A client receiving androgen deprivation therapy for prostate cancer asks about side effects. Which should the nurse include?
questions.rationale: Lowering testosterone causes these effects. Bone density monitoring, calcium and vitamin D, exercise, and cardiovascular risk management are recommended.

options.text: Increased muscle mass
Hot flashes, decreased libido, bone loss, fatigue, and increased metabolic and cardiovascular risk
Improved bone density
Weight loss

questions.stem: A client is diagnosed with early (primary) syphilis and has no penicillin allergy. Which treatment does the nurse anticipate?
questions.rationale: Benzathine penicillin G is the treatment of choice. Clients are monitored for a Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction, and partners are notified and treated. Follow-up blood tests confirm the response.

options.text: Oral amoxicillin for 3 days
A single IM injection of benzathine penicillin G
Topical antifungal cream
No treatment

questions.stem: A client says to the nurse, "You're just like my mother. You never listen to me," although the nurse has only just met the client. What is this an example of?
questions.rationale: Transference occurs when a client unconsciously directs feelings from past relationships onto the nurse. Countertransference is the nurse's emotional reaction to the client. The nurse stays professional and explores the client's feelings.

options.text: Countertransference
Transference
Projection of the nurse's feelings
Sublimation

questions.stem: A laboring client chooses self-administered nitrous oxide for pain relief. Which instruction should the nurse give?
questions.rationale: Self-administration is a built-in safety feature, because a drowsy client lets go of the mask. Starting before the contraction lets the gas peak with the pain. It reduces but does not eliminate pain.

options.text: "The nurse will hold the mask tightly on your face continuously."
"Hold the mask yourself and start breathing the gas about 30 seconds before a contraction begins. If you get drowsy, you'll naturally drop the mask."
"It will completely eliminate all pain."
"You'll need to stay NPO for a week."

questions.stem: A term newborn born by scheduled cesarean has a respiratory rate of 80/min with mild grunting at 2 hours of age. SpO2 is 94%, and the chest x-ray shows fluid in the fissures. What does the nurse suspect?
questions.rationale: Delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid, which is more common after cesarean birth without labor, causes TTN. It usually resolves in 24–72 hours with supportive care. The infant is monitored for worsening distress.

options.text: Meconium aspiration
Transient tachypnea of the newborn
Respiratory distress syndrome of prematurity
Congenital heart disease only

questions.stem: A parent notices that in flash photos, one of the 18-month-old's pupils looks white instead of red. What should the nurse advise?
questions.rationale: Leukocoria is the most common presenting sign of retinoblastoma. Early detection preserves vision and life. Strabismus can be another sign.

options.text: "It's just the camera angle."
"Schedule a prompt eye exam, because a white pupillary reflex can be a sign of retinoblastoma, a childhood eye cancer."
"Check again when your child is 5."
"Use eye drops."

questions.stem: Highlight (circle) the findings that require immediate follow-up.
questions.rationale: A seizure lasting 5 minutes or more defines status epilepticus. Airway compromise, hypoxemia, and hypoglycemia need immediate correction, and without IV access, an IM or intranasal benzodiazepine is needed. Incontinence is expected during seizures, and sodium is normal.
questions.answer_summary: Seizure lasting over 5 minutes; airway secretions; hypoxemia; hypoglycemia; missed antiepileptic; no IV access

passage_segments.text: Ran out of levetiracetam 4 days ago

questions.correct_text: Seizure lasting over 5 minutes; airway secretions; hypoxemia; hypoglycemia; missed antiepileptic; no IV access

questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is more likely a consequence of the prolonged seizure or a possible cause or trigger to identify and treat.
questions.rationale: Prolonged convulsions cause sympathetic surge, heat production, and injury. Common triggers include antiepileptic nonadherence, hypoglycemia, electrolyte disturbances, alcohol withdrawal, and infection, and these must be identified and corrected.
questions.answer_summary: Consequences: tachycardia/hypertension, hyperthermia, tongue laceration. Causes: missed doses, hypoglycemia, subtherapeutic drug level.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.rationale: Ongoing convulsions increase neuronal injury, aspiration risk, muscle breakdown, and metabolic acidosis. Seizures become harder to stop the longer they continue.
questions.answer_summary: 1: convulsive status epilepticus; 2: hypoxic brain injury, aspiration, and rhabdomyolysis
questions.template: The client is experiencing ___1___ and is at risk for ___2___.

options: hypoxic brain injury, aspiration, and rhabdomyolysis
blanks.correct: hypoxic brain injury, aspiration, and rhabdomyolysis

questions.stem: Which interventions does the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Status epilepticus treatment is time-sensitive: a benzodiazepine first, then a second-line agent, while supporting the airway and correcting glucose. Restraints cause injury, and nothing is given by mouth during a seizure.

options.text: IM midazolam now (or IV lorazepam once access is obtained)
Dextrose for hypoglycemia, with thiamine if alcohol use or malnutrition is suspected
A second-line IV antiepileptic, such as levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, or valproate, if seizures continue
Side-lying positioning, suctioning, and high-flow oxygen
Labs including electrolytes, CK, and antiepileptic drug level
Restraining the client's limbs
Giving the missed oral levetiracetam by mouth during the seizure

questions.stem: As the client arrives, which action should the nurse take first?
questions.rationale: Protecting the airway and correcting hypoxemia are the first priorities, done at the same time as preparing medications. Forcing objects between clenched teeth causes injury, and a nasal airway may be used if needed.

options.text: Draw a levetiracetam level
Turn the client onto the side, suction the airway, and apply high-flow oxygen
Force an oral airway between the clenched teeth
Obtain a detailed seizure history from EMS

questions.stem: After IM midazolam, dextrose, and IV levetiracetam, the nurse reassesses the client. For each finding, indicate whether it shows effective treatment or requires immediate follow-up.
questions.rationale: Ending the seizure, restoring oxygenation and glucose, and gradual recovery of consciousness show response. Very high CK with dark urine indicates rhabdomyolysis, which requires aggressive IV fluids. Recurrent seizures without recovery indicate refractory status epilepticus, which may need intubation and continuous infusion therapy.
questions.answer_summary: Effective: seizures stopped, oxygenation restored, glucose corrected, expected postictal recovery. Follow-up: rhabdomyolysis; recurrent status epilepticus.

rows.text: Groggy but responds to voice 30 minutes later
CK 24,000 units/L with dark, tea-colored urine
New convulsions 20 minutes later without regaining consciousness

questions.stem: A rheumatology clinic nurse receives four phone messages. Which client should the nurse call back first?
questions.rationale: Fever with mouth sores in a client taking methotrexate may indicate bone marrow suppression (neutropenia) and serious infection, which requires urgent evaluation.

options.text: A client taking methotrexate who reports a sore throat, mouth sores, and a temperature of 101.5°F (38.6°C)
A client with osteoarthritis asking about a knee brace
A client with gout requesting a refill of allopurinol
A client with lupus asking about sunscreen

questions.stem: A young adult with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) asks how to manage symptoms. Which recommendations should the nurse include?
questions.rationale: POTS involves an excessive heart rate increase when standing. Volume expansion, compression, and graded exercise improve tolerance. Heat and prolonged standing worsen symptoms.

options.text: "Restrict fluids and salt."
"Increase fluid and salt intake as directed by your provider, wear compression garments, rise slowly, and gradually build up exercise, starting with recumbent activities."
"Stand still for long periods to adapt."
"Take hot baths to relax."

questions.stem: Where should the nurse place the V1 electrode for a 12-lead ECG?
questions.rationale: V1 is at the fourth intercostal space at the right sternal border, and V2 is at the same level on the left. Accurate placement prevents misleading tracings.

options.text: Fifth intercostal space, left midclavicular line
Fourth intercostal space, right sternal border
Second intercostal space, left sternal border
Left midaxillary line at the level of V4

questions.stem: A client who aspirated while lying upright develops pneumonia. In which area is the infiltrate most likely?
questions.rationale: The right main bronchus is wider, shorter, and more vertical, so aspirated material in an upright person tends to enter the right lower lobe.

options.text: Left upper lobe
Right lower lobe
Left lingula
Both apices equally
